## You Grieve for Those Not to Be Grieved, Yet Speak Wise Words
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.11

You grieve for those who should not be grieved, and you speak words of wisdom. The wise do not mourn for the dead or the living.

---

### Devanagari
श्री भगवानुवाच

अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे।

गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः

### IAST
śrī bhagavānuvāca

aśocyānanvaśocastvaṃ prajñāvādāṃśca bhāṣase|

gatāsūnagatāsūṃśca nānuśocanti paṇḍitāḥ

### Pratibha Translation
The Blessed Lord said: “You have grieved for those who should not be grieved, and you utter words that sound like wisdom. The learned do not mourn for those whose breath has gone or for those whose breath has not.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Kṛṣṇa’s first doctrinal cut is epistemological: Arjuna mixes true-sounding speech (*prajñā-vāda*) with misplaced grief. The contested claim is that some objects of mourning are *aśocya* — not appropriate loci of *śoka* — not because death is trivial, but because the wise locate identity beyond the breath’s coming and going. *Paṇḍita* here is not academic credential; it is one who sees. This verse does not yet explain why; it asserts a standard against which Arjuna’s ethic will be tested. Existentially, notice when your eloquence is grief wearing the mask of philosophy. The Gītā refuses to let polished moral language exempt you from deeper seeing.

Naming misplaced grief is the first cut of wisdom-speech. Eloquence is not evidence of seeing. The paṇḍita standard inaugurates a whole chapter that will redefine what is worth mourning and what is confusion wearing moral clothes.

Test your next eloquent complaint against this cut: does it see, or does it decorate grief? The chapter will not forbid care; it will forbid care that misidentifies what death and life are.

### Key Terms
**aśocya (अशोच्य)** — not to be mourned → persons/conditions wrongly taken as grief’s proper object when Self is unseen → “not worth grieving” sounds callous; the point is mislocated sorrow.

**prajñā-vāda (प्रज्ञावाद)** — speech that sounds like wisdom → eloquence without corresponding vision → “wise words” misses the critique of wisdom-talk.

**paṇḍita (पण्डित)** — the truly learned seer → one who does not mourn across the living/dead binary as ultimate → “scholar” is a category error.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Epictetus, Enchiridion 3 / 11:** Both relocate grief by correcting what one takes the beloved/lost to be.
*Divergence:* Stoicism emphasizes judgment about externals; the Gītā will ground the claim in the deathless Self.

**Katha Upaniṣad 1.2.18–22:** Both deny that the wise treat embodied life-death as the final term of sorrow.
*Divergence:* Katha teaches via Yama’s secret; here the teaching addresses a warrior mid-refusal.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Write one grief you are elaborating with sophisticated reasons. Ask: “What exactly am I taking as ultimately lost?” Sit with the question before answering.

---

## Never Was I Not, Nor You, Nor These Kings
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.12

There was never a time when I was not, nor you, nor these lords of men; nor shall we all ever cease to be hereafter.

---

### Devanagari
न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः।

न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम्

### IAST
na tvevāhaṃ jātu nāsaṃ na tvaṃ neme janādhipāḥ|

na caiva na bhaviṣyāmaḥ sarve vayamataḥ param

### Pratibha Translation
“Never was there a time when I was not, nor you, nor these lords of peoples; nor is it that we all shall not exist from this time forward.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Kṛṣṇa asserts continuity of being across the apparent absolute of death. The contested move is plural: not only a solitary ātman, but “I, you, and these kings” share never-not-being. This is not yet full Advaita reduction; it is a claim that personal identities implicated in the war are not extinguishable by battle. Grief that treats killing as ontological annihilation is thus misframed. Within Sāṅkhya-inflected reading, conscious principles persist through bodily change. Existentially, the verse asks whether your fear of loss is fear of change or fear of absolute erasure. If the latter, the Gītā begins to dissolve the premise.

Plural continuity — I, you, these kings — blocks both solitary mysticism and collective annihilation panic. The war’s persons are not extinguished by the war’s chronology. Act inside time without letting time’s endings dictate the Real.

This continuity claim also refuses the fantasy that killing ends the moral relationship. Persons persist as loci of meaning beyond the breath’s schedule. Duty must be framed without annihilation metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**jātu na (जातु न)** — never at any time → absolute temporal negation of non-existence → “never” in English is weaker than this sealed “not ever.”

**janādhipa (जनाधिप)** — lord of peoples → the kings on the field included in ontological continuity → “rulers” misses their inclusion in the never-not-being claim.

**ataḥ param (अतः परम्)** — from this point forward → future continuity asserted with past continuity → “hereafter” is fine; the symmetry of past/future is the point.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Phaedo 70c–72e (cyclical argument):** Both argue that death cannot be simple absolute end if life-death are structured transitions.
*Divergence:* Plato argues toward Forms and soul immortality philosophically; Kṛṣṇa asserts as Lord within dialogic authority.

**Dao De Jing 16:** Both orient the mind to what abides through arising and perishing.
*Divergence:* Laozi emphasizes return to the root in quietude; the Gītā asserts personal continuity amid duty to act.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Contemplate one relationship you fear losing. For two minutes, hold: “What in this was never merely the perishable form?” Write one sentence of what abides.

---

## As Boyhood, Youth, and Age to the Embodied, So Is Attainment of Another Body
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.13

As boyhood, youth, and old age befall the embodied in this body, so does the attaining of another body; the firm one is not confused about this.

---

### Devanagari
देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा।

तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति

### IAST
dehino'sminyathā dehe kaumāraṃ yauvanaṃ jarā|

tathā dehāntaraprāptirdhīrastatra na muhyati

### Pratibha Translation
“Just as boyhood, youth, and old age come to the embodied one in this body, so does the attaining of another body; the steadfast is not deluded about that.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Death is placed on a continuum with aging. The contested analogy: if you already survive childhood’s end into youth, the wise (*dhīra*) are not bewildered by the body’s further transition. *Dehāntara-prāpti* — attaining another body — is presented as structurally akin to life-stage change. This neither trivializes bereavement nor denies pain; it challenges the metaphysics that makes bodily end absolute personal end. Existentially, notice that you have already “died” to earlier forms of yourself without ceasing. The verse asks for the same steadiness toward the larger change.

Aging already taught you transition; death asks for the same literacy at larger scale. The dhīra’s non-delusion is practiced long before the funeral, in every released childhood. Steady people are those who stopped confusing form-change with self-erasure.

Confusion at death is often confusion rehearsed at every smaller ending. Practice non-delusion when a role ends, a season ends, a body-ability ends. The dhīra is trained in increments.

Train non-delusion at small endings so the larger transition does not invent a false absolute.

### Key Terms
**dehin (देहिन्)** — the embodied one → conscious identity wearing a body → “soul in a body” can dualize too crudely; the term centers the one who *has* a body.

**dehāntara-prāpti (देहान्तरप्राप्ति)** — attainment of another body → rebirth as transition analogous to aging → “reincarnation” is doctrinally thick; the verse’s force is analogical continuity.

**dhīra (धीर)** — steadfast/firm-wise → one who does not fall into *moha* at transition → “wise man” misses the courage-steadiness in *dhī*.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Phaedo 87b–88b (cloak/weaver analogy and its critique):** Both explore whether the person outlasts a particular bodily “garment.”
*Divergence:* Plato’s dialogue problematizes the analogy carefully; Kṛṣṇa asserts it pedagogically to remove battlefield *moha*.

**Zhuangzi, butterfly / skull passages:** Both relativize identity across transformations of form.
*Divergence:* Zhuangzi plays with perspectival transformation; the Gītā stabilizes a continuing embodied Self through change.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Look at a photo of yourself ten years younger. Name three continuities and three discontinuities, then ask what “you” the *dhīra* would refuse to confuse with either list alone.

---

## Sense Contacts Come and Go — Endure Them
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.14–2.15

Contacts of the senses with their objects, son of Kuntī, giving cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come and go; they are impermanent — endure them, Bhārata. The person whom these do not torment, O best of men — the steadfast one alike in pain and pleasure — that one is fit for immortality.

---

### Devanagari
मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः।

आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत

यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ।

समदुःखसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते

### IAST
mātrāsparśāstu kaunteya śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkhadāḥ|

āgamāpāyino'nityāstāṃstitikṣasva bhārata

yaṃ hi na vyathayantyete puruṣaṃ puruṣarṣabha|

samaduḥkhasukhaṃ dhīraṃ so'mṛtatvāya kalpate

### Pratibha Translation
“Contacts of measure — sense and object — O son of Kuntī, give cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go; they are impermanent. Endure them, Bhārata. The person whom these do not torment, best of men — the steadfast one for whom pain and pleasure are equal — that one is fit for deathlessness.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Before denying death’s ultimacy further, Kṛṣṇa trains affect: *titikṣasva* — endure. Sense-object contacts (*mātrā-sparśa*) are framed as transient givers of paired opposites. The contested claim is that fitness for *amṛtatva* depends on not being tormented by these pairs — *sama-duḥkha-sukha*. Equanimity is not numbness; it is non-torment under inevitable contact. This is proto-yoga psychology inside Sāṅkhya dualities. Existentially, the verse relocates spiritual dignity from controlling outcomes to how you meet weather — outer and inner. Immortality begins as a way of being touched without being unseated.

Endurance is not the opposite of sensitivity; it is sensitivity without torment. Fitness for deathlessness begins as weather-skill. The pairs will keep arriving; the question is whether they get to own your posture.

Titikṣā is active hospitality to impermanence. You do not freeze sensation; you refuse to let sensation write your metaphysics. That refusal is already a rehearsal of amṛtatva.

Let today’s sensory weather be curriculum for amṛtatva rather than a verdict that owns your posture.

### Key Terms
**mātrā-sparśa (मात्रास्पर्श)** — contact of sense-measures with objects → structured sensation events → “sense contacts” is right; “measure” hints at limited, quantifiable impacts.

**titikṣā (तितिक्षा)** — endurance/forbearance → active capacity to bear without collapse → “tolerance” is too passive and modern.

**amṛtatva (अमृतत्व)** — deathlessness / immortality → fitness for which depends on equanimity → “immortality” can sound mythic; here it is a capacity-status.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 2.1 / 2.32 (tapas and titikṣā-adjacent disciplines):** Both treat endurance of opposite sensations as formative for steadiness.
*Divergence:* YS embeds endurance in eight-limbed method; here it is immediate battlefield counsel.

**Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.39 / 8.28:** Both train the mind to meet pleasure-pain as transient contacts.
*Divergence:* Marcus grounds in Stoic physics/providence; the Gītā aims toward *amṛtatva* and later karma-yoga.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
At the next unpleasant sensation (heat, cold, annoyance), label it “coming-and-going contact” three times and refrain from the first reactive story for thirty seconds.

---

## Of the Unreal There Is No Being; of the Real, No Non-Being
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.16

Of the non-existent there is no being; of the existent there is no non-being. The truth of both has been seen by the seers of the essence.

---

### Devanagari
नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः।

उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः

### IAST
nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ|

ubhayorapi dṛṣṭo'ntastvanayostattvadarśibhiḥ

### Pratibha Translation
“Of the unreal there is no being; of the real there is no non-being. The conclusion of both has been seen by the seers of thatness.”

### Pratibha Commentary
This is the metaphysical axiom of the chapter. *Asat* has no *bhāva*; *sat* has no *abhāva*. The contested move is ontological sorting: what truly is cannot cease; what merely appears cannot claim being. *Tattva-darśin* — seers of thatness — have seen the *anta*, the decisive end/settlement of both. Applied to Arjuna’s grief, bodies and roles participate in the asat’s flux; the Self as sat is not killable. Existentially, the verse demands a ruthless inventory: what in your panic is asat wearing the mask of absolute stakes? Seeing that is not coldness; it is the beginning of freedom from false emergencies.

Sat/asat sorting is the chapter’s knife. Use it on your emergencies: which stakes are Real, which are vivid asat? Grief that treats the perishable as absolute will mis-teach every duty that follows.

Seers of thatness are not collectors of opinions about sat and asat; they have settled the issue in seeing. Aim for settlement, not for a more sophisticated panic.

### Key Terms
**sat / asat (सत् / असत्)** — real/existent vs. unreal/non-existent → ontological polarity grounding grief-critique → “true/false” is propositional; here the issue is modes of being.

**bhāva / abhāva (भाव / अभाव)** — being / non-being → presence vs. absence as metaphysical statuses → “existence/nonexistence” is approximate.

**tattva-darśin (तत्त्वदर्शिन्)** — seer of thatness/principle → one who sees the essence-settlement of sat/asat → “philosopher” is too broad and secular.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Parmenides, On Nature (fr. 2–8):** Both deny that what-is can not-be, and that what-is-not can be.
*Divergence:* Parmenides freezes a monistic “is”; the Gītā uses the axiom to free action amid embodied change.

**Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.2:** Both reject production of being from non-being as ultimate account.
*Divergence:* Chāndogya unfolds sat as creative “may I be many”; here sat underwrites the deathless Self in war counsel.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Divide a current fear into “what can cease” and “what cannot cease.” Act only after naming which side your panic has confused.

---

## Know That by Which All This Is Pervaded as Indestructible
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.17–2.19

Know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded. No one can bring about the destruction of this imperishable. These bodies of the eternal embodied one are said to have an end — of the imperishable, immeasurable one; therefore fight, Bhārata. Who thinks this to be the killer and who thinks this to be killed — both do not know; this does not kill and is not killed.

---

### Devanagari
अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम्।

विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित् कर्तुमर्हति

अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ताः शरीरिणः।

अनाशिनोऽप्रमेयस्य तस्माद्युध्यस्व भारत

य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम्।

उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते

### IAST
avināśi tu tadviddhi yena sarvamidaṃ tatam|

vināśamavyayasyāsya na kaścit kartumarhati

antavanta ime dehā nityasyoktāḥ śarīriṇaḥ|

anāśino'prameyasya tasmādyudhyasva bhārata

ya enaṃ vetti hantāraṃ yaścainaṃ manyate hatam|

ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyaṃ hanti na hanyate

### Pratibha Translation
“Know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded. No one can effect the destruction of this imperishable. These bodies of the eternal embodied one are said to have an end — of the indestructible, immeasurable; therefore fight, Bhārata. Who thinks this the killer, and who thinks this killed — both do not know. This does not kill and is not killed.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Pervasion (*tatam*) grounds invulnerability: what saturates all cannot be locally destroyed. Bodies end; the *śarīrin* is eternal, indestructible, immeasurable — therefore fight. The contested inference is famous and dangerous: metaphysical deathlessness used to authorize battlefield action. The Gītā’s claim is not that killing is unreal as event, but that the Self is not the true patient or agent of killing in the ultimate register. Both “I am killer” and “this is killed” as ultimate statements are ignorance. Existentially, hold both edges: do not use this verse to numb conscience; do use it to stop treating the Self as a perishable token in your panic. The command to fight follows from duty clarified by ontology, not from ontology abolishing ethics.

Pervasion grounds invulnerability, and invulnerability is then yoked to duty rather than to numbness. The denial of ultimate killer/killed clears panic so relative responsibility can be clean. Ontology here is in service of non-deluded action, not of moral sleep.

Hold invulnerability and responsibility together: no numbness, and no panic that the Self can be erased by weapons.

### Key Terms
**avināśin (अविनाशिन्)** — indestructible → that which cannot be brought to ruin → “immortal” blends this with *amṛta*; here the stress is non-destructibility.

**tatam (ततम्)** — spread/pervaded → all-this saturated by the imperishable → “permeated” is good; the image is field-filling.

**hantṛ / hata (हन्तृ / हत)** — killer / killed → ultimate agency-patient ascriptions denied of the Self → “murderer/victim” moralizes what the verse ontologizes.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Katha Upaniṣad 1.2.18–19:** Both declare the Self unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain.
*Divergence:* Katha teaches a seeker toward inner yajña; here the same insight is harnessed to restore Kṣatriya action.

**Plotinus, Enneads IV.7:** Both argue the soul’s nature is not subject to bodily destruction.
*Divergence:* Plotinus orients toward contemplative ascent; the Gītā orients toward non-deluded participation in dharma-war.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Before a harsh necessary action, say aloud: “Bodies end; the pervading one does not.” Then ask what duty remains when panic about erasure is removed — and do only that.

---

## Unborn, Eternal, Ancient — Not Slain When the Body Is Slain
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.20

This is never born and never dies, nor having been will it ever not be again. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient — it is not slain when the body is slain.

---

### Devanagari
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचि

न्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः।

अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो

न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे

### IAST
na jāyate mriyate vā kadāci

nnāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ|

ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṃ purāṇo

na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre

### Pratibha Translation
“It is never born, nor does it ever die; nor having come to be will it not be again. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, this ancient one is not slain when the body is being slain.”

### Pratibha Commentary
The verse stacks negations until birth-death chronology fails. *Na jāyate, na mriyate* — and the difficult middle: it is not that having been, it will later fail to be. Epithets accumulate: *aja, nitya, śāśvata, purāṇa*. The contested image is simultaneous: the body is *being slain* (*hanyamāne śarīre*) while the Self is not slain. This is the classic Upaniṣadic claim pressed into war counsel. Existentially, the verse does not ask you to deny funerals; it asks you to stop mistaking the funeral for the end of what a person most is. Grief remains; ontological panic need not.

Stacked negations build a Self that chronology cannot own. When the body is being slain, the ancient one is not. Practice is learning to speak of persons without collapsing them into their woundable surfaces.

Speak of the ancient one without denying the body’s vulnerability. The verse’s compassion is ontological precision: mourn forms, stop cursing being. That precision leaves room for courage.

Mourn forms without cursing being; ontological precision is a form of compassion under fire.

### Key Terms
**aja (अज)** — unborn → without origination in time → “unborn” is literal; the force is exemption from genesis.

**śāśvata (शाश्वत)** — everlasting/perpetual → continuity without term → “eternal” overlaps *nitya*; here the stress is age-long persistence.

**purāṇa (पुराण)** — ancient → primordial rather than newly produced → “old” is comic understatement; it means aboriginal.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Katha Upaniṣad 1.2.18:** Near-verbal kinship: unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain.
*Divergence:* Katha’s context is inner attainment; Gītā 2.20 is already mid-argument for Arjuna’s return to duty.

**Gospel of John 8:58 / 11:25–26:** Both speak a life not measured by ordinary birth-death chronology.
*Divergence:* John personalizes in Christological “I am”; the Gītā speaks the Self’s nature as teaching for action.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
When mortality intrudes today, say to yourself: “The body can be slain; what I most am is not born into that vulnerability.” Then choose the next kind act and do it.

---

## Knowing the Indestructible — Whom Does He Slay
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.21

Who knows this as indestructible, eternal, unborn, imperishable — how can that person, Pārtha, cause anyone to be slain, whom does he kill?

---

### Devanagari
वेदाविनाशिनं नित्यं य एनमजमव्ययम्।

कथं स पुरुषः पार्थ कं घातयति हन्ति कम्

### IAST
vedāvināśinaṃ nityaṃ ya enamajamavyayam|

kathaṃ sa puruṣaḥ pārtha kaṃ ghātayati hanti kam

### Pratibha Translation
“Who knows this as indestructible, eternal, unborn, imperishable — how does that person, Pārtha, cause anyone to be killed, and whom does he kill?”

### Pratibha Commentary
Knowledge transforms the grammar of agency. The knower of the unborn cannot ultimately *ghātayati* or *hanti* anyone as Self-destroyer. The contested reading is ethical: does this abolish responsibility? The Gītā’s trajectory says no — it abolishes the delusion that the Self is a perishable combatant, while still commanding dharma-action. The rhetorical questions clear false ultimate agency so right relative agency can return without panic. Existentially, use the verse to drop the fantasy that you can annihilate what another most is — and to drop the despair that you yourself can be so annihilated — then face the finite harms and duties that remain.

Knowing revises agency-language. You still act; you stop fantasizing ultimate erasure as your power or your doom. The rhetorical questions clear the field for dharma without the metaphysics of annihilation.

If ultimate killing is impossible, cruelty does not become permitted; panic becomes unnecessary. Clean relative harm-assessment replaces cosmic despair. That is the ethical yield of the rhetorical questions.

After clearing ultimate killer/killed language, audit residual rationalizations of cruelty and discard them.

### Key Terms
**veda (वेद)** — knows/has come to know → knowledge as transformative seeing, not information → “knows” understates realization-force.

**avyaya (अव्यय)** — imperishable/inexhaustible → not subject to dwindling → “unchanging” is related but not identical.

**ghātayati / hanti (घातयति / हन्ति)** — causes to be slain / slays → dual agency verbs emptied at the ultimate level → the pair covers direct and causative killing.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Īśā Upaniṣad 1–3:** Both relocate agency and appropriation once the Self/Lord is known as filling all.
*Divergence:* Īśā emphasizes renunciation-in-enjoyment; here the focus is the impossibility of ultimate killing.

**Plotinus, Enneads I.1:** Both ask what truly acts and suffers when body and soul are distinguished.
*Divergence:* Plotinus analyzes for contemplative purification; Kṛṣṇa analyzes to unblock Arjuna’s duty.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Before speaking of someone as ruined or finished, ask: “Whom exactly am I declaring killed?” Separate finite harm from ultimate erasure in one written line.

---

## As a Man Casts Off Worn Garments and Takes New Ones
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.22

As a man casts off worn-out garments and takes other new ones, so the embodied casts off worn-out bodies and goes to other new ones.

---

### Devanagari
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय

नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि।

तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णा-

न्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही

### IAST
vāsāṃsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya

navāni gṛhṇāti naro'parāṇi|

tathā śarīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇā-

nyanyāni saṃyāti navāni dehī

### Pratibha Translation
“As a man casts off worn-out clothes and takes other new ones, so the embodied one casts off worn-out bodies and goes onward to other new ones.”

### Pratibha Commentary
The garment simile makes rebirth intimate and ordinary. *Jīrṇa* — worn out — frames bodily end as exhaustion of a vehicle, not annihilation of the wearer. The contested softness of the image risks sentimentalizing death; its philosophical work is to restore agency to the *dehī* as one who goes (*saṃyāti*) to new forms. Within the argument, this is pedagogy for a warrior who sees only corpses. Existentially, the verse asks whether you live as garment or wearer — as costume desperately defended, or as the one who can release what is worn through.

Garments are for wearing and releasing. The dehī’s dignity is the capacity to go on, not the terror of fabric. Live as wearer enough that worn roles can be set down without apocalypse.

The simile also softens grasping at youth and status-fabrics. What is worn through may be released without self-hatred. The dehī’s journey is continuity through responsible release.

Release one worn role this week as garment-release — continuity without apocalyptic self-talk.

### Key Terms
**vāsas (वासस्)** — garment/clothing → body as wearable → “clothes” is apt; the domesticity of the image is intentional.

**jīrṇa (जीर्ण)** — worn out/aged → fitness exhausted → “old” misses the used-up readiness for release.

**dehī (देही)** — the embodied one → traveler through bodies → “soul” imports later theology; here it is the body-haver who goes on.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Phaedo 87b (cloak analogy):** Both compare body to garment relative to a continuing self.
*Divergence:* Plato’s interlocutors immediately pressure-test the analogy; the Gītā asserts it to relieve *moha*.

**Milarepa, songs on the illusory body:** Both treat the body as temporary clothing of awareness.
*Divergence:* Milarepa aims at recognition in meditation; here the simile serves dharma-courage in war.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
While changing clothes today, move slowly and say: “Worn forms are releasable.” Apply the same sentence once to a role you are clutching.

## Weapons Do Not Cut It, Fire Does Not Burn It
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.23–2.25

Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, waters do not wet it, wind does not dry it. It cannot be cut, burned, wetted, or dried. Eternal, all-going, firm, unmoving, everlasting. It is called unmanifest, unthinkable, unchanging. Therefore, knowing it thus, you should not grieve.

---

### Devanagari
नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः।

न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः

अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च।

नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातनः

अव्यक्तोऽयमचिन्त्योऽयमविकार्योऽयमुच्यते।

तस्मादेवं विदित्वैनं नानुशोचितुमर्हसि

### IAST
nainaṃ chindanti śastrāṇi nainaṃ dahati pāvakaḥ|

na cainaṃ kledayantyāpo na śoṣayati mārutaḥ

acchedyo'yamadāhyo'yamakledyo'śoṣya eva ca|

nityaḥ sarvagataḥ sthāṇuracalo'yaṃ sanātanaḥ

avyakto'yamacintyo'yamavikāryo'yamucyate|

tasmādevaṃ viditvainaṃ nānuśocitumarhasi

### Pratibha Translation
“Weapons do not cut this, fire does not burn this, waters do not wet this, wind does not dry this. This cannot be cut, cannot be burned, cannot be wetted, cannot be dried; eternal, all-pervading, fixed, unmoving, everlasting. This is called unmanifest, unthinkable, unchangeable. Therefore, knowing this thus, you ought not to grieve.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Elemental immunity defines the Self against the war’s materials. Blade, fire, water, wind — the battlefield’s agents — fail. Positive epithets follow: eternal, all-going, pillar-firm, unmoving, anciently continuing. Then apophasis: unmanifest, unthinkable, unmodifiable. The contested conclusion is ethical-psychological: *therefore* you should not grieve. Knowledge (*viditvā*) is prescribed as grief’s solvent. Existentially, this is not a ban on tears; it is a ban on grieving as if the Real were subject to weapons. Learn the difference between mourning forms and despairing of being.

Elemental immunity is apophatic armor for the heart. Knowing this does not cancel care for bodies; it cancels despair that treats blade and fire as lords of being. Grief becomes precise when the Real is no longer imagined as cuttable.

Apophasis here is practical: if the Self is unthinkable and uncuttable, stop managing it like inventory. Manage duty; stop managing being. Grief ordered by that distinction becomes saner.

When elemental threats dominate imagination, return to what blade and fire cannot reach, then resume care for bodies.

### Key Terms
**acchedya (अच्छेद्य)** — uncuttable → immunity to weapon-partition → “indivisible” is related but more abstract than cut-resistance.

**sarvagata (सर्वगत)** — gone-to-all / all-pervading → ubiquity as ground of invulnerability → “omnipresent” is theological English approximation.

**avikārya (अविकार्य)** — unmodifiable → not subject to transformation → “unchanging” is close; the stress is non-susceptibility to *vikāra*.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Dao De Jing 4 / 6:** Both point to a reality not exhausted by elemental operations.
*Divergence:* Laozi stays poetic-apophatic about Dao; the Gītā applies apophasis directly to grief-discipline.

**Plotinus, Enneads III.6 (impassibility of the incorporeal):** Both deny that bodily affections reach the true self.
*Divergence:* Plotinus elaborates for metaphysical psychology; Kṛṣṇa compresses into martial consolation and command.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
When a cutting word lands today, notice the body flinch, then ask: “What in me is not cuttable by this?” Answer before retaliating.

---

## Even If You Think It Constantly Born and Constantly Dying
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.26

And if you think this to be constantly born and constantly dying, still, O mighty-armed, you ought not to grieve thus.

---

### Devanagari
अथ चैनं नित्यजातं नित्यं वा मन्यसे मृतम्।

तथापि त्वं महाबाहो नैवं शोचितुमर्हसि

### IAST
atha cainaṃ nityajātaṃ nityaṃ vā manyase mṛtam|

tathāpi tvaṃ mahābāho naivaṃ śocitumarhasi

### Pratibha Translation
“And if you hold this to be constantly born, or constantly dying — even then, mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve in this way.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Kṛṣṇa argues in the alternative. Even on the opponent’s premise — perpetual birth-death of the person — this style of grief is unfit. The contested move is dialectical generosity: I need not win the immortality thesis to defeat your paralysis. If becoming is endless, mourning each turn as absolute still misunderstands process. Existentially, this is a gift for plural audiences: whether you hold eternal Self or radical impermanence, compulsive *śoka* that freezes duty is still misplaced.

Arguing in the alternative is teacherly mercy. Whether you hold permanence or perpetual becoming, paralysis-grief still fails. The point is freedom to act without waiting for metaphysical consensus.

Dialectical mercy keeps the conversation moving when dogmas stall. You are not required to finish ontology before returning to responsibility. The unfit grief is the target under either map. The unfit grief is the real target; ontology is the means. Keep moving toward responsibility while the maps are still contested.

If metaphysics stalls agreement, still refuse the grief-style that freezes necessary action.

### Key Terms
**nitya-jāta (नित्यजात)** — constantly born → view of perpetual origination → “always being born” captures process metaphysics Kṛṣṇa brackets.

**tathāpi (तथापि)** — even so / nevertheless → concessive turn in argument → marks dialectical mercy.

**śocitum arhasi (शोचितुमर्हसि)** — you ought to grieve → negated: grief as unfit response → “should not mourn” is the ethical verdict under either ontology.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 18 / 24:** Both can release clinging whether one reifies permanence or annihilation.
*Divergence:* Nāgārjuna empties both extremes via emptiness; Kṛṣṇa uses either-or to unblock action.

**Epictetus, Discourses 1.27:** Both argue that correct response does not require settling every metaphysical dispute first.
*Divergence:* Stoicism centers judgment-training; here the aim is return to dharma-fight.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
State your working view of death in one sentence. Then ask: “Under this view, is my current freeze still justified?” Adjust one action accordingly.

---

## Death Is Certain for the Born, Birth Certain for the Dead
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.27

For the born, death is certain; for the dead, birth is certain. Therefore you should not grieve over an unavoidable matter.

---

### Devanagari
जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च।

तस्मादपरिहार्येऽर्थे न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि

### IAST
jātasya hi dhruvo mṛtyurdhruvaṃ janma mṛtasya ca|

tasmādaparihārye'rthe na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi

### Pratibha Translation
“For one who has been born, death is certain; and certain is birth for one who has died. Therefore over an unavoidable matter you ought not to grieve.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Certainty cuts both ways: *dhruva* death after birth, *dhruva* birth after death. The contested counsel is that *aparihārya* — the inescapable — is not a fit object of paralyzing grief. This is not cruelty; it is triage. Energy spent raging at structure cannot serve dharma within structure. Existentially, the verse asks you to stop negotiating with inevitables as if protest could repeal them, and to spend your freedom where choice still lives.

Inevitables are poor idols. Protest against structure can become a way to avoid the freedom still available beside structure. Spend yourself where choice lives.

Certainty of death and birth is meant to free attention, not to breed fatalism. The unavoidable is background; the choosable is foreground. Re-sort your day accordingly. Fatalism is the counterfeit twin of this verse. Certainty about death should increase care in the choosable, not decrease it.

Put inevitables in the background and choosables in the foreground; certainty should free care, not kill it.

### Key Terms
**dhruva (ध्रुव)** — fixed/certain → structural inevitability → “sure” is weaker than pole-star fixity implied.

**aparihārya (अपरिहार्य)** — unavoidable → that from which there is no escape → “inevitable” is right; the compound stresses non-circumventability.

**artha (अर्थ)** — matter/affair here → the issue at hand as unavoidable fact → not “meaning” in this use.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus:** Both aim to release life from mismanaged fear of death’s necessity.
*Divergence:* Epicurus denies post-mortem experience; the Gītā affirms cyclic return and later the deathless Self.

**Dao De Jing 50:** Both observe the tight binding of birth and death as human condition.
*Divergence:* Laozi points toward those who hold life loosely; Kṛṣṇa points toward non-grieving action in duty.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Write one unavoidable fact you are still bargaining with. Circle it, then list three choices that remain open beside it — and take one.

---

## Beings Are Unmanifest in Beginning and End — Why Lament the Middle
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.28–2.30

Beings are unmanifest in their beginnings, manifest in the middle, O Bhārata, and unmanifest again in their ends — what is there to lament in that? One sees it as wonder, another speaks of it as wonder, another hears of it as wonder — and even having heard, no one truly knows it. The embodied one is eternally indestructible in the body of all, Bhārata; therefore you ought not to grieve for any beings.

---

### Devanagari

अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना

आश्चर्यवत्पश्यति कश्चिदेन

माश्चर्यवद्वदति तथैव चान्यः।

आश्चर्यवच्चैनमन्यः श्रृणोति

श्रुत्वाप्येनं वेद न चैव कश्चित्

देही नित्यमवध्योऽयं देहे सर्वस्य भारत।

तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि

### IAST
avyaktādīni bhūtāni vyaktamadhyāni bhārata|

avyaktanidhanānyeva tatra kā paridevanā

āścaryavatpaśyati kaścidena

māścaryavadvadati tathaiva cānyaḥ|

āścaryavaccainamanyaḥ śrṛṇoti

śrutvāpyenaṃ veda na caiva kaścit

dehī nityamavadhyo'yaṃ dehe sarvasya bhārata|

tasmātsarvāṇi bhūtāni na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi

### Pratibha Translation
“Beings have the unmanifest as their beginning, are manifest in the middle, Bhārata, and have the unmanifest as their end — what lamentation is there in that? Someone sees this as wonder; another speaks of it likewise as wonder; another hears of it as wonder; and even having heard, no one truly knows it. This embodied one is eternally unslayable in the body of all, Bhārata; therefore you ought not to grieve for all beings.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Life appears as a bright middle between two unmanifests. *Paridevanā* — elaborate lament — is asked: for what, in such a structure? Then the wonder-paradox: seeing, speaking, hearing the Self as *āścarya* still does not equal knowing. The contested pairing is humility plus command: you will not master this by report, and still you must not grieve as if beings were slayable at the core. Existentially, let wonder replace possession of the doctrine. The point is not to own a theory of afterlives; it is to stop despairing over the manifest middle as if it were the whole.

Unmanifest–manifest–unmanifest makes elaborate lament look oversized. Wonder replaces possession of doctrine, and still the command holds: do not grieve beings as if their core were slayable. Humility and courage share the same verse.

Wonder without knowing protects against spiritual arrogance while still commanding non-despair. You can be astonished and steady. That combination is more adult than either clever certainty or theatrical lament.

### Key Terms
**avyakta (अव्यक्त)** — unmanifest → pre- and post-appearance phase of beings → “invisible” is sensory; unmanifest is ontological.

**paridevanā (परिदेवना)** — lamentation/wailing → circling grief-performance → “sorrow” is too mild for the theatrical mourning implied.

**āścarya (आश्चर्य)** — wonder/marvel → the Self as astonishment that exceeds secondhand knowing → “miracle” over-Christianizes; wonder is closer.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Dao De Jing 1 / 14:** Both place the manifest between returns to the nameless/unmanifest.
*Divergence:* Laozi warns against possessive naming; the Gītā warns against possessive grieving.

**Plotinus, Enneads V.5 / VI.9:** Both treat the One/Self as known more in wonder than in grasp.
*Divergence:* Plotinus culminates in contemplative union; here wonder coexists with the command not to grieve beings in war.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Contemplate one life as unmanifest–manifest–unmanifest for two minutes. Replace one sentence of lament with one sentence of wonder, without denying care.

---

## Look Also to Your Own Dharma — There Is No Better Than a Righteous Battle for a Kṣatriya
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.31–2.33

Looking also to your own dharma, you ought not to tremble. For a Kṣatriya, nothing better exists than a righteous battle. Happy are the Kṣatriyas, Pārtha, who obtain such a battle that comes of itself, an open door to heaven. But if you will not wage this righteous war, then abandoning your own dharma and fame, you will incur sin.

---

### Devanagari
स्वधर्ममपि चावेक्ष्य न विकम्पितुमर्हसि।

धर्म्याद्धि युद्धाछ्रेयोऽन्यत्क्षत्रियस्य न विद्यते

यदृच्छया चोपपन्नं स्वर्गद्वारमपावृतम्।

सुखिनः क्षत्रियाः पार्थ लभन्ते युद्धमीदृशम्

अथ चैत्त्वमिमं धर्म्यं संग्रामं न करिष्यसि।

ततः स्वधर्मं कीर्तिं च हित्वा पापमवाप्स्यसि

### IAST
svadharmamapi cāvekṣya na vikampitumarhasi|

dharmyāddhi yuddhāchreyo'nyatkṣatriyasya na vidyate

yadṛcchayā copapannaṃ svargadvāramapāvṛtam|

sukhinaḥ kṣatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddhamīdṛśam

atha caittvamimaṃ dharmyaṃ saṃgrāmaṃ na kariṣyasi|

tataḥ svadharmaṃ kīrtiṃ ca hitvā pāpamavāpsyasi

### Pratibha Translation
“Looking also to your own dharma, you ought not to tremble. For other than a righteous battle, nothing better exists for a Kṣatriya. Happy are the Kṣatriyas, Pārtha, who obtain such a battle come of itself — heaven’s door thrown open. But if you will not do this righteous war, then casting away your own dharma and fame, you will incur sin.”

### Pratibha Commentary
The argument shifts from metaphysics to vocation. *Svadharma* — one’s own holding-up — becomes the lens. For the Kṣatriya, a *dharmya yuddha* is not a sad necessity only; it is the excellent. The contested claim for modern readers is the varṇa framing; the transferable core is that role-responsibility can make refusal itself a moral failure. Heaven’s open door is epic incentive language; the sharper edge is *pāpa* from abandoning *svadharma* and *kīrti*. Existentially, ask whether your refusal protects the real or abandons the post only you can hold. Not every withdrawal is wisdom; some is desertion dressed as purity.

Vocation returns after metaphysics. Svadharma can make refusal itself a moral event. The transferable demand is to ask which post is yours when purity fantasies invite desertion.

Heaven-door rhetoric is incentive language inside an epic; the sharper edge is pāpa from abandoning the post. Translate carefully: what unique good fails if only you refuse? Answer without melodrama.

Translate svadharma without vanity: name the unique good that fails if only you walk away.

### Key Terms
**svadharma (स्वधर्म)** — one’s own dharma → role-specific responsibility that upholds the whole → “personal duty” is individualist; the term is vocational-cosmic.

**dharmya yuddha (धर्म्य युद्ध)** — righteous/battle aligned with dharma → war as dharma-occasion, not mere violence → “just war” is a partial Western analogue.

**yadṛcchā (यदृच्छा)** — chance/what comes of itself → unsought arrival of the decisive test → “by chance” captures spontaneity of the door’s opening.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Plato, Republic IV (each doing their own):** Both link justice to right performance of one’s function in the whole.
*Divergence:* Plato’s city-soul analogy aims at civic harmony; the Gītā binds vocation to liberation-teaching.

**Confucius, Analects 8.13 / 14.1:** Both warn that abandoning one’s proper post under danger can be moral failure, not virtue.
*Divergence:* Confucian courage is ritual-ethical; here courage is Kṣatriya dharma under open heaven-door imagery.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Name your current “post” in one concrete conflict. Ask: “If I withdraw, what exact good fails that is mine to uphold?” Answer before exiting.

## Dishonor Is Worse Than Death for One Long Honored
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.34–2.36

Beings will tell of your undying dishonor, and for one esteemed, dishonor is worse than death. The great chariot-warriors will think you withdrew from battle out of fear, and you who were highly regarded by them will come to lightness. Your enemies will speak many unspeakable words, scorning your capacity — what could be more painful than that?

---

### Devanagari
अकीर्तिं चापि भूतानि कथयिष्यन्ति तेऽव्ययाम्।

संभावितस्य चाकीर्तिर्मरणादतिरिच्यते

भयाद्रणादुपरतं मंस्यन्ते त्वां महारथाः।

येषां च त्वं बहुमतो भूत्वा यास्यसि लाघवम्

अवाच्यवादांश्च बहून् वदिष्यन्ति तवाहिताः।

निन्दन्तस्तव सामर्थ्यं ततो दुःखतरं नु किम्

### IAST
akīrtiṃ cāpi bhūtāni kathayiṣyanti te'vyayām|

saṃbhāvitasya cākīrtirmaraṇādatiricyate

bhayādraṇāduparataṃ maṃsyante tvāṃ mahārathāḥ|

yeṣāṃ ca tvaṃ bahumato bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam

avācyavādāṃśca bahūn vadiṣyanti tavāhitāḥ|

nindantastava sāmarthyaṃ tato duḥkhataraṃ nu kim

### Pratibha Translation
“Beings will also recount your undying dishonor; for one who has been esteemed, dishonor exceeds death. The great chariot-warriors will think you withdrew from battle out of fear, and having been highly regarded by them, you will come to lightness. Your enemies will speak many unsayable words, scorning your capacity — what could be more painful than that?”

### Pratibha Commentary
Kṛṣṇa uses honor-shame as medicinal rhetoric. For a *saṃbhāvita* — one long held in high regard — *akīrti* outweighs death. The contested move is appealing to reputation after teaching the deathless Self. The Gītā does not pretend Arjuna is already established in that vision; it meets him with the language his present identity still feels. Fear of being read as fear becomes part of the counsel. Existentially, this layer is double-edged: reputation can be ego-bondage, yet public trust is also a real good. Ask whether your withdrawal protects conscience or only manages image — and whether staying would be vanity or fidelity.

Honor-speech meets Arjuna where he still lives. Reputation is neither ultimate nor nothing. Sort image-fear from conscience-fear, or both will drive you and neither will free you.

Being taken lightly after being esteemed hurts because trust is real. Still, yoga will not let akīrti be ultimate. Hold reputation as secondary good under svadharma, not as a god.

Rank reputation below conscience without pretending public trust is unreal; sort image-fear from moral fear.

### Key Terms
**akīrti (अकीर्ति)** — dishonor/ill-fame → lasting social unmaking of name → “bad reputation” is thinner than undying un-glory.

**saṃbhāvita (संभावित)** — one held in honor/esteem → prior dignity that makes shame cut deeper → “respected person” misses the weight of being long regarded.

**lāghava (लाघव)** — lightness/triviality → fall from gravitas to being taken lightly → “disgrace” is related; the image is loss of weight.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (magnanimity and honor):** Both take honor seriously as a real human good for the excellent.
*Divergence:* Aristotle orders honor under virtue; the Gītā will soon relativize fruit and fame under yoga.

**Homeric shame-culture (Iliad, Hector and Achilles):** Both treat public reading of courage/cowardice as existentially heavy.
*Divergence:* Homer remains within kleos; the Gītā embeds honor-speech inside a turn toward Self-knowledge and non-possessive action.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Write the reputation-story you fear if you act, and the one you fear if you don’t. Mark which fear is conscience and which is image-management.

## Slain You Gain Heaven; Victorious You Enjoy the Earth — Therefore Stand
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.37–2.39

If slain you will gain heaven; if victorious you will enjoy the earth. Therefore stand up, son of Kuntī, resolved on battle. Holding pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal, then yoke yourself to battle; thus you will not incur sin. This understanding has been declared to you in Sāṅkhya; now hear it in Yoga. Yoked with understanding, Pārtha, you will cast off the bondage of action.

---

### Devanagari
हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम्।

तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौन्तेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चयः

सुखदुःखे समे कृत्वा लाभालाभौ जयाजयौ।

ततो युद्धाय युज्यस्व नैवं पापमवाप्स्यसि

एषा तेऽभिहिता सांख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां शृणु।

बुद्ध्यायुक्तो यया पार्थ कर्मबन्धं प्रहास्यसि

### IAST
hato vā prāpsyasi svargaṃ jitvā vā bhokṣyase mahīm|

tasmāduttiṣṭha kaunteya yuddhāya kṛtaniścayaḥ

sukhaduḥkhe same kṛtvā lābhālābhau jayājayau|

tato yuddhāya yujyasva naivaṃ pāpamavāpsyasi

eṣā te'bhihitā sāṃkhye buddhiryoge tvimāṃ śṛṇu|

buddhyāyukto yayā pārtha karmabandhaṃ prahāsyasi

### Pratibha Translation
“If slain, you will attain heaven; if victorious, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore stand up, son of Kuntī, with resolution made for battle. Holding pleasure and pain as equal, gain and loss, victory and defeat, then yoke yourself to battle; thus you will not incur sin. This understanding has been declared to you in Sāṅkhya; now hear it in Yoga. Yoked to this understanding, Pārtha, you will cast off the bondage of action.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Double assurance clears outcome-anxiety: death yields heaven, victory yields earth — so stand resolved. Then the deeper solvent: sameness across pleasure/pain, gain/loss, victory/defeat. Action without dualistic possession does not generate *pāpa* in the same way. The contested transition is named explicitly: this *buddhi* was given in Sāṅkhya; now hear it in Yoga — the turn from discriminative knowing toward yoking-in-action that releases *karma-bandha*. Existentially, resolution (*kṛta-niścaya*) plus equanimity is the pair: not frozen certainty, and not passive calm, but decided participation without outcome-possession.

Resolution plus equanimity opens karma-yoga. Sāṅkhya-buddhi becomes Yoga-buddhi when knowing yokes itself to action that can drop bondage. Stand decided without needing the fruit to complete your identity.

Equalizing the pairs does not erase preferences; it erases possessive identity fused to preferences. Then battle — or any hard duty — can be yoked without manufacturing sin through clinging.

Equalize the pairs in one hard effort today, then act with resolution that does not need applause to complete itself.

### Key Terms
**kṛta-niścaya (कृतनिश्चय)** — one who has made resolution → decidedness prior to action → “determined” is close; the compound stresses completed deciding.

**sāṅkhya / yoga (सांख्य / योग)** — discriminative enumeration vs. yoking practice → twin modes of the same *buddhi* → not later school labels only; here pedagogical phases.

**karma-bandha (कर्मबन्ध)** — bondage of action → binding appropriation of deeds → “karma bondage” must not be read as fatalism; it is sticky agency.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 1.2–1.3 / 2.1–2.2:** Both move from understanding toward yoking that releases binding patterns.
*Divergence:* YS systematizes eight limbs; Gītā 2.39 pivots from battlefield Sāṅkhya-view to karma-yoga.

**Epictetus, Discourses 1.1:** Both free action by equalizing what is not in our control (outcomes) while demanding commitment to what is.
*Divergence:* Stoicism brackets devotion and rebirth cosmology; the Gītā yokes equanimity to dharma and later bhakti.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Choose one contested effort today. Write success and failure as equal for the ego, then act with a single clear resolution sentence.

## No Effort on This Path Is Lost — Make the Understanding One-Pointed
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.40–2.42

On this path no effort is lost, no contrary result exists. Even a little of this dharma protects from great fear. The understanding whose essence is resolve is one here, joy of the Kurus; the understandings of the irresolute are many-branched and endless. The undiscerning speak this flowery speech, delighting in Veda-debate, saying there is nothing else.

---

### Devanagari
नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते।

स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात्

व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिरेकेह कुरुनन्दन।

बहुशाखा ह्यनन्ताश्च बुद्धयोऽव्यवसायिनाम्

यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः।

वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः

### IAST
nehābhikramanāśo'sti pratyavāyo na vidyate|

svalpamapyasya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt

vyavasāyātmikā buddhirekeha kurunandana|

bahuśākhā hyanantāśca buddhayo'vyavasāyinām

yāmimāṃ puṣpitāṃ vācaṃ pravadantyavipaścitaḥ|

vedavādaratāḥ pārtha nānyadastīti vādinaḥ

### Pratibha Translation
“Here there is no loss of unfinished effort, nor does contrary fruit exist. Even a little of this dharma protects from great fear. The understanding whose nature is resolve is one in this, joy of the Kurus; but the understandings of the unresolved are many-branched and endless. The undiscerning speak this flowery speech — devoted to Veda-debate, Pārtha, claiming nothing else exists.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Karma-yoga’s first consolation is non-waste: begun effort does not perish, and there is no *pratyavāya* backlash as in botched ritual. Even a little protects from great fear. The contested diagnostic follows: resolved *buddhi* is singular; unresolved *buddhi* proliferates branches without end. Flowery Veda-talk that says “nothing beyond this” is named as undiscerning. Existentially, the verse contrasts one-pointed commitment with the infinite subcommittee of preferences. Fear often multiplies options; this dharma reduces them to a resolute one.

Non-waste and one-pointedness answer fear’s proliferation. Flowery sacred talk that denies anything beyond desire-ritual is named as undiscerning for a reason: it keeps buddhi many-branched forever.

Many-branched buddhi feels like sophistication and functions like fear. Choose the one resolve that protects from great fear, and let the ornamental debates wait. Sophistication that multiplies options can be fear in costume. Prefer the resolve that actually protects.

Cut one ornamental debate branch and return to the single resolve that actually reduces fear.

### Key Terms
**abhikrama-nāśa (अभिक्रमनाश)** — destruction of begun undertaking → negated: no loss of started practice → “wasted effort” is the fear being removed.

**vyavasāyātmikā buddhi (व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धि)** — understanding whose essence is resolve → one-pointed decisive knowing → “determination” misses that it is a mode of *buddhi*, not mere grit.

**puṣpitā vāc (पुष्पिता वाच्)** — flowery speech → ornamented persuasion without liberating discernment → “eloquent words” understates the critique of seductive sacred talk.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 1.14:** Both insist practice becomes firm when pursued long, uninterrupted, with reverence — implying non-waste of sincere effort.
*Divergence:* YS specifies conditions of firmness; Gītā stresses even a little protects from fear.

**Zhuangzi, “Cutting open satchels” / critique of ornate knowing:** Both distrust proliferating clever speech that misses the one needful.
*Divergence:* Zhuangzi often dissolves purpose; here resolve is praised as singular *buddhi*.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Pick one practice. For seven days, refuse new “branches” of self-improvement and do only that one, even briefly, noting fear’s decrease.

## Desire-Selves Fixated on Heaven Lose Resolve in Samādhi
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.43–2.45

They are desire-selves, heaven-oriented, teaching rebirth as fruit of action — full of many special rites aimed at enjoyment and lordship. For those attached to enjoyment and lordship, their minds carried away by that speech, the resolve-natured understanding is not established in samādhi. The Vedas’ scope is the three guṇas; be without the three guṇas, Arjuna — free of dualities, abiding always in sattva, free of acquiring and keeping, possessed of the Self.

---

### Devanagari
कामात्मानः स्वर्गपरा जन्मकर्मफलप्रदाम्।

क्रियाविशेषबहुलां भोगैश्वर्यगतिं प्रति

भोगैश्वर्यप्रसक्तानां तयापहृतचेतसाम्।

व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिः समाधौ न विधीयते

त्रैगुण्यविषया वेदा निस्त्रैगुण्यो भवार्जुन।

निर्द्वन्द्वो नित्यसत्त्वस्थो निर्योगक्षेम आत्मवान्

### IAST
kāmātmānaḥ svargaparā janmakarmaphalapradām|

kriyāviśeṣabahulāṃ bhogaiśvaryagatiṃ prati

bhogaiśvaryaprasaktānāṃ tayāpahṛtacetasām|

vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ samādhau na vidhīyate

traiguṇyaviṣayā vedā nistraiguṇyo bhavārjuna|

nirdvandvo nityasattvastho niryogakṣema ātmavān

### Pratibha Translation
“Desire-selves, intent on heaven, [speak speech] that bestows birth as action’s fruit — crowded with many particular rites, aimed at the goal of enjoyment and lordship. For those attached to enjoyment and lordship, their minds carried off by that, the resolve-natured understanding is not established in samādhi. The Vedas have the triple guṇa as their scope; be without the triple guṇa, Arjuna — free of the pairs, always standing in sattva, free of getting-and-keeping, Self-possessed.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Ritual consumerism is diagnosed: *kāma-ātman* beings use sacred tech for heaven, enjoyment, and *aiśvarya*. Such speech hijacks the mind so resolve cannot seat in *samādhi*. Then the radical command: the Vedas’ range is *traiguṇya* — be *nistraiguṇya*. Free of dualities, established in sattva, without *yoga-kṣema* (acquiring and securing), be *ātmavān*. The contested move is not anti-Veda nihilism; it is refusal to let Veda-as-desire-manual own the whole of life. Existentially, notice which “spiritual” projects are still shopping for status and security. Liberation-talk that feeds acquisition cannot stabilize resolve.

When scripture becomes a shopping catalog for heaven and lordship, resolve cannot seat. Beyond-guṇa standing is not contempt for Veda; it is refusal to let acquisition own the sacred. Check your spiritual cart.

Niryoga-kṣema is the quiet revolution: stop living as acquire-and-secure. Self-possession begins when sacred projects stop being status engines. Then samādhi can host resolve.

Strip one sacred project of acquire-and-secure motive and watch whether it remains necessary.

### Key Terms
**kāma-ātman (कामात्मन्)** — one whose self is desire → identity organized as wanting → “sensual person” is narrower than desire-constituted selfhood.

**yoga-kṣema (योगक्षेम)** — getting and keeping / acquisition and security → the twin anxiety of obtain-and-protect → “welfare” in later usage softens the grasping pair here.

**nistraiguṇya (निस्त्रैगुण्य)** — beyond the three guṇas → not owned by Vedic guṇa-scope → “transcend the modes of nature” is interpretive but directionally right.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Mundaka Upaniṣad 1.1.4–1.2.13:** Both distinguish lower knowledge entangled in rites from higher knowledge that frees.
*Divergence:* Mundaka sharply ranks knowledges; the Gītā keeps action while stripping desire-framing.

**Augustine, Confessions X (concupiscence and curiositas):** Both expose how religious/intellectual appetite can still be desire in sacred dress.
*Divergence:* Augustine turns toward Christian caritas; the Gītā turns toward guṇa-free Self-possession and later karma-yoga.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Audit one spiritual or self-improvement habit: write whether it aims at enjoyment/status/security. If yes, practice it once today with no acquire-and-keep motive.
