## As Much Use as a Flooded Well Has for a Small Pond
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.46

As much use as there is in a water-well when water is flooding everywhere, so much is there in all the Vedas for a Brahmin who knows.

---

### Devanagari
यावानर्थ उदपाने सर्वतः संप्लुतोदके।

तावान्सर्वेषु वेदेषु ब्राह्मणस्य विजानतः

### IAST
yāvānartha udapāne sarvataḥ saṃplutodake|

tāvānsarveṣu vedeṣu brāhmaṇasya vijānataḥ

### Pratibha Translation
“As much purpose as a water reservoir has when water lies flooded on every side — that much is there in all the Vedas for a Brahmin who truly knows.”

### Pratibha Commentary
The simile is cool and exact. A pond matters when water is scarce; in flood, its *artha* shrinks. Likewise Vedic apparatus retains relative use, but for the one who knows (*vijānataḥ*), its urgency collapses. The contested claim is not contempt for Veda but scale: realization saturates what ritual partial-waters only locally supply. Existentially, tools that once saved you can become redundant without being evil. Knowing when a method has done its work is part of wisdom.

Flooded knowing relativizes local reservoirs without smashing them. Tools become optional when fullness arrives. Wisdom includes knowing when a method has finished its merciful work.

Relative use remains; absolute urgency departs. Keep gratitude for wells without digging new ones out of habit. Knowing includes right sizing of methods. Right-sizing methods is humility with gratitude, not contempt for what once saved you.

Thank a former method without digging another well from scarcity habit; right-size what still serves.

### Key Terms
**udapāna (उदपान)** — water place/well/reservoir → limited water-source → “well” is standard; the contrast with flood is the point.

**saṃpluta-udaka (संप्लुतोदक)** — water flooded all around → abundance rendering local storage minor → “flood” captures saturation of knowing.

**vijānat (विजानत्)** — one who discerns/knows fully → Brahmin as knower, not birth-label only → “learned” is too scholastic.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Dao De Jing 11 / 48:** Both suggest that as one approaches the real, needful apparatus lessens.
*Divergence:* Laozi emphasizes loss-as-gain; the Gītā keeps Veda’s relative *artha* while ranking knowing above it.

**Paul, 1 Corinthians 13:8–12:** Both image partial knowing superseded when fullness arrives.
*Divergence:* Paul frames through love and eschatology; the Gītā frames through Brahmin-knowing and Vedic scope.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Identify one practice you cling to from scarcity habit. Ask: “What fullness would make this optional?” Live one hour as if that fullness were already near.

---

## Your Claim Is to Action Alone, Never to Its Fruits
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.47

Your entitlement is to action alone, never to its fruits at any time. Do not become the cause of action’s fruits, and may you have no attachment to non-action.

---

### Devanagari
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन।

मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि

### IAST
karmaṇyevādhikāraste mā phaleṣu kadācana|

mā karmaphalaheturbhūrmā te saṅgo'stvakarmaṇi

### Pratibha Translation
“Your claim is to action alone, never at any time to the fruits. Do not become the reason for action’s fruits, and let there be no attachment in you to non-action.”

### Pratibha Commentary
This is the Gītā’s signature compression. *Adhikāra* — rightful claim/jurisdiction — extends to *karma*, not to *phala*. The contested triad: act; do not make yourself fruit-cause; do not cling to *akarma*. Detachment is not vacation from deeds. Bondage is pictured as turning yourself into the *hetu* of results — the one who must secure payoff. Existentially, this rewires work under uncertainty: integrity of action becomes the only honest success metric, while refusal to act is named as another attachment.

Jurisdiction over action, never over fruit, plus no cling to inaction: this triad is freedom’s practical grammar. Performance culture runs on the opposite. Rehearse the verse until your nervous system believes it.

The third clause matters as much as the first: attachment to non-action is still attachment. Freedom is precise participation without payoff-ownership. Drill all three together. Drill the triad until your body recognizes fruit-chasing as a category error rather than as motivation.

Run the triad end-to-end on one task: act fully, refuse fruit-ownership, refuse cling to inaction.

### Key Terms
**adhikāra (अधिकार)** — jurisdiction/entitlement/fitness for → what rightly falls in your sphere → “right” alone misses office-like claim.

**phala (फल)** — fruit/result → appropriated outcome that binds when claimed → “result” misses possessive ripeness.

**akarma (अकर्म)** — non-action → inaction as possible attachment-object → “not working” is behavioral; the term can also touch freedom-in-action later.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 8.5 / 9.6:** Both demand full right action without demand on outcomes.
*Divergence:* Marcus grounds in cosmopolis and logos; the Gītā grounds in yoga, dharma, and release from *karma-bandha*.

**Zhuozi, Cook Ding / non-possession of skill’s fruit:** Both show excellence without possessive hovering over results.
*Divergence:* Zhuangzi often dissolves deliberate duty; here duty remains while possession drops.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Choose one high-stakes task. Define completion only as “full integrity of the action,” write the feared fruit on paper, fold it away, and work.

---

## Established in Yoga, Do Actions — Equanimity Is Yoga
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.48

Established in yoga, perform actions, having abandoned attachment, Dhanaṃjaya. Having become equal toward success and failure, evenness is called yoga.

---

### Devanagari
योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय।

सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते

### IAST
yogasthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā dhanañjaya|

siddhyasiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṃ yoga ucyate

### Pratibha Translation
“Established in yoga, do actions, having abandoned attachment, Dhanaṃjaya. Having become equal in success and non-success, evenness is called yoga.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Yoga is defined as *samatva* — evenness — not as withdrawal or posture. The command is active: *kuru karmāṇi* while *yoga-stha*. Attachment (*saṅga*) is dropped; equality toward *siddhi/asiddhi* is taken up. The contested claim is that yoga equals a way of relating to outcomes while acting, not an alternative to acting. Existentially, this makes practice testable in email, conflict, and craft: can you stay even when the metric flips?

Evenness as yoga makes the definition testable at work. Success and failure become weather across which the yoked continue. If your yoga vanishes when metrics flip, it was preference, not yoga.

Samatva is verified under flip risk. Pre-commit to evenness, act, then inspect the body for clinging residue. That inspection is the yoga, not the slogan. Evenness under flip risk is the empirical definition. Slogan-evenness that collapses at outcomes is not yet yoga.

Inspect evenness after a metric flip; residue of clinging is the real score of whether yoga was present.

### Key Terms
**yoga-stha (योगस्थ)** — standing established in yoga → abiding in the yoked state while acting → “being in yoga” is vague; *stha* stresses stable station.

**saṅga (सङ्ग)** — attachment/sticking → adhesive bonding to fruit or role → “attachment” is right; stickiness is the feel.

**samatva (समत्व)** — evenness/equanimity → yoga’s definition here → “balance” can sound lifestyle; this is parity across success/failure.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 1.33:** Both cultivate even affective stance as yogic stabilization.
*Divergence:* YS lists friendliness etc. as mind-clarifiers; Gītā defines yoga itself as evenness in action’s results.

**Zhuangzi, “Fasting of the Mind”:** Both prize a non-stuck responsiveness.
*Divergence:* Zhuangzi empties toward spontaneous Dao; the Gītā evenness serves dharma-performance.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
On one task, pre-commit: “Success and failure are equal for my clinging.” Check your body at the end for evenness, not for the score.

---

## Far Inferior Is Action to the Yoga of Understanding
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.49

Far inferior is action to the yoga of understanding, Dhanaṃjaya. Seek refuge in understanding; the pitiful are those who are fruit-causes.

---

### Devanagari
दूरेण ह्यवरं कर्म बुद्धियोगाद्धनञ्जय।

बुद्धौ शरणमन्विच्छ कृपणाः फलहेतवः

### IAST
dūreṇa hyavaraṃ karma buddhiyogāddhanañjaya|

buddhau śaraṇamanviccha kṛpaṇāḥ phalahetavaḥ

### Pratibha Translation
“By far is action inferior to the yoga of understanding, Dhanaṃjaya. Seek refuge in understanding; pitiful are those who make themselves causes of fruit.”

### Pratibha Commentary
*Buddhi-yoga* outranks bare *karma*. This does not cancel 2.47; it ranks motive-structure. Fruit-causers are *kṛpaṇa* — wretched, pinched. Refuge (*śaraṇa*) is to be sought in *buddhi*. The contested move is calling outcome-obsession a poverty of spirit, not ambition. Existentially, notice the miser-logic of fruit-fixation: it never feels it has enough control. Refuge in understanding is wealth that does not depend on the quarter’s numbers.

Fruit-causers are called wretched because they live inside scarcity of control. Refuge in buddhi is the alternative wealth. Seek that shelter when the ledger of outcomes starts writing your self.

Calling fruit-causers kṛpaṇa is diagnostic kindness. It names poverty of spirit where culture sees drive. Take refuge in buddhi when drive becomes miser-logic. Refuge is practical: when the ledger writes your self, change the writing instrument to buddhi.

When drive turns miser-logic, take refuge in buddhi for five breaths before the next move. Let the contested move remain uncomfortable; comfort usually signals a softened reading.

### Key Terms
**buddhi-yoga (बुद्धियोग)** — yoga of understanding/discriminative intelligence → yoking through resolved knowing → “wisdom yoga” is approximate.

**kṛpaṇa (कृपण)** — pitiful/miserly → fruit-fixers as spiritually impoverished → “wretched” fits; miserly contraction is heard in the word.

**śaraṇa (शरण)** — refuge/shelter → *buddhi* as where one takes shelter → “take refuge” is right; it is relational, not merely cognitive assent.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Katha Upaniṣad 1.2.1–2 (śreyas vs preyas):** Both rank the truly better over the merely desired fruit.
*Divergence:* Katha stages choice via Yama; here ranking occurs inside karma-yoga instruction.

**Epictetus, Enchiridion 1:** Both treat clinging to outcomes outside one’s jurisdiction as the root of wretchedness.
*Divergence:* Stoicism stays with prohairesis; the Gītā names *buddhi-yoga* within dharma and devotion arc.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
When you catch yourself as *phala-hetu*, place a hand on the sternum and say: “Refuge in understanding,” then name the next right action only.

---

## The Yoked Leaves Both Good and Evil Deeds — Yoga Is Skill in Actions
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.50

The one yoked to understanding leaves behind both well-done and ill-done here. Therefore yoke yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in actions.

---

### Devanagari
बुद्धियुक्तो जहातीह उभे सुकृतदुष्कृते।

तस्माद्योगाय युज्यस्व योगः कर्मसु कौशलम्

### IAST
buddhiyukto jahātīha ubhe sukṛtaduṣkṛte|

tasmādyogāya yujyasva yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam

### Pratibha Translation
“The one yoked to understanding casts off both good and evil deeds here. Therefore yoke yourself to yoga; yoga is skillfulness in actions.”

### Pratibha Commentary
*Buddhi-yukta* abandons both *sukṛta* and *duṣkṛta* — not by becoming immoral, but by exiting the ledger of self-making through deeds. The famous definition follows: *yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam* — yoga is skill in actions. The contested claim is that highest skill includes non-binding. Clumsy action is not only inefficient; it is spiritually sticky. Existentially, skill means clean contact with the task without the extra motion of self-congratulation or self-loathing.

Leaving both good and evil ledgers frees skill to be clean contact. Kauśala is adeptness without sticky self-making. That is why yoga can be called skill in actions without becoming technique-worship.

Skill that still keeps a merit-demerit selfie is incomplete skill. Drop both ledgers in the midst of the task. Clean contact is the kauśala the verse means. Technique without non-binding is incomplete kauśala. Leave both ledgers while the hands still work.

Drop merit and demerit selfies mid-task and finish with clean contact alone — that is kauśala.

### Key Terms
**buddhi-yukta (बुद्धियुक्त)** — joined to understanding → person whose intelligence is yoked → “wise” is flatter than technical yoking.

**sukṛta / duṣkṛta (सुकृत / दुष्कृत)** — well-done / ill-done → merit-demerit pair left behind → “good and bad karma” is popular; the verse stresses leaving both.

**kauśala (कौशल)** — skillfulness/clever excellence → yoga as adeptness in deeds → “skill” must include non-binding, not mere technique.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Zhuangzi, Cook Ding:** Both make effortless rightness in action the mark of higher skill.
*Divergence:* Cook Ding forgets the ox in Dao-resonance; the Gītā’s skill still serves dharma and buddhi-yoga.

**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 2.1–2.2 (kriyā-yoga):** Both treat purified action-modes as yogic.
*Divergence:* YS lists tapas, study, īśvara-praṇidhāna; Gītā compresses into skill-as-yoga definition.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Do one ordinary action today as *kauśala*: full attention, no self-scoreboard during or after for five minutes.

---

## The Wise Abandon Action-Born Fruit and Go to the Soundless Place
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.51–2.53

The wise, yoked to understanding, having abandoned the fruit born of action, freed from the bondage of birth, go to the place beyond illness. When your understanding crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, then you will become indifferent to what has been heard and what is yet to be heard. When understanding, bewildered by revelation-conflicts, stands unmoving, unshaken in samādhi — then you will attain yoga.

---

### Devanagari
कर्मजं बुद्धियुक्ता हि फलं त्यक्त्वा मनीषिणः।

जन्मबन्धविनिर्मुक्ताः पदं गच्छन्त्यनामयम्

यदा ते मोहकलिलं बुद्धिर्व्यतितरिष्यति।

तदा गन्तासि निर्वेदं श्रोतव्यस्य श्रुतस्य च

श्रुतिविप्रतिपन्ना ते यदा स्थास्यति निश्चला।

समाधावचला बुद्धिस्तदा योगमवाप्स्यसि

### IAST
karmajaṃ buddhiyuktā hi phalaṃ tyaktvā manīṣiṇaḥ|

janmabandhavinirmuktāḥ padaṃ gacchantyanāmayam

yadā te mohakalilaṃ buddhirvyatitariṣyati|

tadā gantāsi nirvedaṃ śrotavyasya śrutasya ca

śrutivipratipannā te yadā sthāsyati niścalā|

samādhāvacalā buddhistadā yogamavāpsyasi

### Pratibha Translation
“For the wise, yoked to understanding, abandoning the fruit born of action, freed from birth-bondage, go to the untainted place. When your understanding crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, then you will reach dispassion toward what is to be heard and what has been heard. When your understanding, torn by conflicting revelations, stands unmoving, unshaken in samādhi — then you will attain yoga.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Fruit-abandonment leads to the *anāmaya pada* — the unailing place — and release from birth-bond. Then a phenomenology of maturity: *buddhi* crosses *moha-kalila* (delusion’s thicket), and *nirveda* arises toward the whole economy of hearing. Finally, when revelation-conflicts (*śruti-vipratipanna*) no longer shake understanding, and it stands unmoving in samādhi, yoga is attained. The contested claim is that more sacred information is not the goal; unshakability amid informational conflict is. Existentially, spiritual maturity looks like fewer arguments with podcasts and more seated clarity.

Crossing delusion’s thicket ends sacred FOMO. Conflicting revelations stop owning the mind when samādhi holds buddhi unmoving. Maturity prefers unshakability to another download of opinions.

Indifference to heard and to-be-heard is not anti-learning; it is end of compulsive seeking. When śruti-conflicts cannot shake you, yoga has somewhere to stand. Unshakability amid conflicting hearings is rarer than clever synthesis. Aim for the rarer thing.

Prefer one day of unshaken practice to another cycle of contested spiritual content.

### Key Terms
**moha-kalila (मोहकलिल)** — thicket/mire of delusion → dense confusion understanding must cross → “delusion” alone misses the tangled-obstacle image.

**nirveda (निर्वेद)** — dispassion/indifference → cooling toward heard and to-be-heard → “world-weariness” can misread; here it is freedom from sacred FOMO.

**śruti-vipratipanna (श्रुतिविप्रतिपन्न)** — conflicted by revelatory hearings → understanding pulled by opposing testimonies → “confused by scriptures” is close.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Mundaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8–2.2.9:** Both describe knowledge that cuts ignorance and ends restless seeking.
*Divergence:* Mundaka images the knot of the heart cut; Gītā images buddhi unmoving in samādhi amid śruti-conflict.

**Dao De Jing 48:** Both associate advance with decrease of restless acquiring (here, of hearings).
*Divergence:* Laozi decreases doing toward wuwei; the Gītā decreases hearing-thirst while keeping yoked action.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
For one day, impose a fast on new spiritual content. When urge arises, sit unmoving for one minute and return to your single practice.

---

## What Is the Speech of One Whose Wisdom Stands Firm
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.54

Arjuna said: What is the description of one whose wisdom stands firm, established in samādhi, Keśava? How does the firm-minded speak? How does he sit? How does he walk?

---

### Devanagari
अर्जुन उवाच

स्थितप्रज्ञस्य का भाषा समाधिस्थस्य केशव।

स्थितधीः किं प्रभाषेत किमासीत व्रजेत किम्

### IAST
arjuna uvāca

sthitaprajñasya kā bhāṣā samādhisthasya keśava|

sthitadhīḥ kiṃ prabhāṣeta kimāsīta vrajeta kim

### Pratibha Translation
Arjuna said: “What is the marking-description of one whose wisdom stands firm, who is established in samādhi, Keśava? How would the firm-minded speak? How would he sit? How would he go?”

### Pratibha Commentary
Arjuna requests phenomenology. *Sthita-prajña* is not only a metaphysical status; it must show in *bhāṣā*, speech, sitting, going. The contested hunger is for visible criteria — how shall I recognize the settled one, and become measurable to myself? The Gītā allows the question; the following verses answer with inner marks more than costume. Existentially, the wish to know how the wise walk is already the wish to stop taking turmoil as inevitable. Ask for marks, then be ready for answers that implicate desire, not gait alone.

Asking how the wise speak, sit, and go is already refusal of turmoil as fate. The following answers will implicate desire more than costume. Want marks that change you, not marks you can cosplay.

The question’s hunger for outer marks will be answered with inner physics. Accept that the curriculum will target kāma, not costume. That acceptance is already more sthita.

Want marks that change desire, not marks you can imitate for status; accept an inner curriculum.

### Key Terms
**sthita-prajña (स्थितप्रज्ञ)** — one whose wisdom/discernment stands firm → stable prajñā as identity → “man of steady wisdom” is traditional and apt.

**bhāṣā (भाषा)** — speech/description/mark → both how he is described and how speech works in him → “language” is too narrow.

**sthita-dhī (स्थितधी)** — firm-minded → stable intelligence → parallel to sthita-prajña with *dhī* emphasis.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 1.2–1.3:** Both imply that settled mind has recognizable abiding (*avasthāna*).
*Divergence:* YS is aphoristic definition; Arjuna asks for behavioral-linguistic marks in dialogue form.

**Analects 2.10:** Both suggest that watching how someone acts reveals what they are.
*Divergence:* Confucius watches to know persons in society; Arjuna asks the Lord for the type of the samādhi-established.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Observe one calm person today. Note speech, sitting, and moving without imitation; write which mark you most lack.

---

## When He Abandons All Desire-Wills and Is Content in the Self Alone
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.55

The Blessed Lord said: When he abandons all desires that enter the mind, Pārtha, and is contented in the Self by the Self, then he is called one whose wisdom stands firm.

---

### Devanagari
श्री भगवानुवाच

प्रजहाति यदा कामान् सर्वान् पार्थ मनोगतान्।

आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते

### IAST
śrī bhagavānuvāca

prajahāti yadā kāmān sarvān pārtha manogatān|

ātmanyevātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthitaprajñastadocyate

### Pratibha Translation
The Blessed Lord said: “When he abandons all desires that go in the mind, Pārtha, and is content in the Self by the Self, then he is called one whose wisdom stands firm.”

### Pratibha Commentary
The first mark is interior: all *kāmas* that move in mind are abandoned, and contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is in the Self by means of the Self. The contested claim is that firm wisdom is not primarily correct opinion; it is desire-release plus non-borrowed satisfaction. *Ātmany evātmanā tuṣṭaḥ* blocks the search for contentment in objects while using the Self as both locus and means. Existentially, this asks whether your calm depends on conditions aligning. If yes, prajñā is not yet *sthita*.

Self-contentment by the Self is the first standing-mark of prajñā. Desire-release without borrowed satisfaction is the test. If calm needs conditions, the standing is still conditional.

Contentment by the Self blocks the marketplace of soothing. Abandon mind-entered desires not by repression theater but by tasting a satisfaction that does not bill the world. Borrowed satisfaction always invoices the world. Self-contentment cancels the invoice.

Taste Self-contentment long enough that one mind-entered want loses urgency without theater of repression.

### Key Terms
**manogata kāma (मनोगत काम)** — desire gone-into-mind → wants as mental inhabitants → “desires of the heart” is softer; these are mind-entered claims.

**tuṣṭa (तुष्ट)** — content/satisfied → fullness without object-debt → “happy” is too broad.

**ātmanā (आत्मना)** — by the Self → instrumental Self-contentment → not contentment about the Self as topic only.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3–4.4:** Both locate true satisfaction in the Self rather than object quest.
*Divergence:* Bṛhadāraṇyaka unfolds through dream/deep-sleep dialectic; here the mark defines sthita-prajña for a warrior.

**Epicurus, Principal Doctrines on natural limits of desire:** Both link stable ease to dropping endless wants.
*Divergence:* Epicurus aims at bodily-attitudinal ataraxia; the Gītā aims at Self-contentment as wisdom’s standing.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
List three mind-entered desires active now. For each, ask: “Can the Self be enough without this?” Sit in that question for one minute per desire.

---

## Unshaken in Pain, Without Longing in Pleasure
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.56

Whose mind is unagitated in sorrows, who has gone beyond longing in pleasures, free of passion, fear, and anger — that steady-minded one is called a sage.

---

### Devanagari
दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः।

वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते

### IAST
duḥkheṣvanudvignamanāḥ sukheṣu vigataspṛhaḥ|

vītarāgabhayakrodhaḥ sthitadhīrmunirucyate

### Pratibha Translation
“Whose mind is not agitated in pains, who has left longing behind in pleasures, who has gone beyond passion, fear, and anger — that firm-minded one is called a muni.”

### Pratibha Commentary
The second mark is affective: no agitation (*anudvigna*) in *duḥkha*, no longing (*spṛhā*) in *sukha*, and freedom from the triad *rāga-bhaya-krodha*. The contested claim is that sagehood (*muni*) is readable in emotional physics, not only in silence or scripture. Pleasure’s danger is craving, not pleasure itself; pain’s danger is mental upheaval. Existentially, track one week’s spikes of passion, fear, anger: they map where *dhī* is not yet *sthita*.

Sagehood readable in emotional physics keeps spirituality honest. Pleasure’s trap is longing; pain’s trap is upheaval; both are joined by the triad passion-fear-anger. Track the triad and you track unsettled intelligence.

Muni is a name earned in weather. Unagitated in pain, unlonging in pleasure, beyond passion-fear-anger: these are lab criteria. Run the lab daily. Daily lab beats occasional admiration of sages. Collect your own data on agitation and longing.

Run the muni lab on today’s pain and pleasure; collect your own data rather than outsourcing admiration.

### Key Terms
**anudvigna-manas (अनुद्विग्नमनस्)** — mind not convulsed/agitated → stability under pain → “calm” is weaker than non-upheaval.

**vigata-spṛha (विगतस्पृह)** — longing departed → absence of acquisitive ache in pleasure → “without desire” can sound totalizing; here longing-in-pleasure specifically.

**vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodha (वीतरागभयक्रोध)** — beyond passion, fear, anger → classic affective liberation triad → each term is a distinct unseating force.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 1.33 / 2.3–2.9:** Both treat affective disturbances (including attachment, aversion, fear) as central obstacles.
*Divergence:* YS systematizes kleśas; Gītā packs the mark into a single portrait of the muni.

**Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 5.20 / 8.4:** Both train non-agitation under pains and non-enslavement to pleasures.
*Divergence:* Marcus uses Stoic assent; the Gītā names the muni within sthita-prajña pedagogy.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
At the next pleasure, watch for *spṛhā*’s reach beyond the moment. At the next pain, watch for *udvega*. Name which arises and take three slow breaths before acting.

---

## No Cling Anywhere — Tortoise-Wise Withdrawal — Taste Ceases When the Highest Is Seen
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.57–2.59

Who is without clinging anywhere, who neither rejoices nor hates on meeting the good or the bad — his wisdom is firmly set. When he draws in the senses from their objects on every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, his wisdom is firmly set. Objects turn away from the unfed embodied one — but not the taste; even the taste turns away for him who has seen the highest.

---

### Devanagari
यः सर्वत्रानभिस्नेहस्तत्तत्प्राप्य शुभाशुभम्।

नाभिनन्दति न द्वेष्टि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता

यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः।

इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता

विषया विनिवर्तन्ते निराहारस्य देहिनः।

रसवर्जं रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते

### IAST
yaḥ sarvatrānabhisnehastattatprāpya śubhāśubham|

nābhinandati na dveṣṭi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā

yadā saṃharate cāyaṃ kūrmo'ṅgānīva sarvaśaḥ|

indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyastasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā

viṣayā vinivartante nirāhārasya dehinaḥ|

rasavarjaṃ raso'pyasya paraṃ dṛṣṭvā nivartate

### Pratibha Translation
“Who is without clinging anywhere, who neither applauds nor hates on obtaining this or that fair or foul — his wisdom stands established. When he draws together the senses from their objects on every side, as a tortoise its limbs, his wisdom stands established. Objects turn away from the embodied one who does not feed on them — except for taste; even taste turns away for him who has seen the highest.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Three deepening marks: non-clinging through fair/foul outcomes; tortoise-withdrawal of senses; and the subtlety that fasting from objects removes objects but not *rasa* — residual taste — until the highest is seen. The contested claim is that behavioral restraint is necessary but incomplete. *Rasa* remains as ghost-appetite until *paraṃ dṛṣṭvā*. Existentially, white-knuckle abstinence without vision leaves the mouth watering in secret. Establish wisdom by contact with what outranks flavor.

Tortoise-withdrawal without vision leaves rasa hungry. Objects can leave while taste remains. Established wisdom needs a seeing of the highest that outranks flavor, or restraint stays brittle.

Behavioral fasting plus highest seeing is the pair. Without the second, rasa becomes a secret landlord. Seek a glimpse that makes flavor optional. Brittle restraint without higher seeing eventually bargains with rasa in secret. Seek the seeing.

Seek a higher seeing that makes residual rasa optional rather than secretly sovereign over restraint. Prefer the harder reading that still fits the Sanskrit over the easier reading that flatters you.

### Key Terms
**anabhisneha (अनभिस्नेह)** — without clinging/affectionate sticking → non-adhesion anywhere → “non-attachment” is close; *sneha*’s oily stickiness matters.

**kūrma (कूर्म)** — tortoise → model of voluntary sensory retraction → the image teaches agile withdrawal, not permanent hiding.

**rasa (रस)** — taste/flavor/relish → residual affective savor after objects withdraw → “desire” is blunter; taste can linger as aesthetic craving.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 2.54–2.55 (pratyāhāra):** Both use withdrawal of senses from objects as establishment of mastery.
*Divergence:* YS makes pratyāhāra a limb; Gītā adds that rasa remains until the highest is seen.

**John Cassian / desert asceticism on residual thoughts:** Both know that outer fasting can leave inner relish.
*Divergence:* Christian monasticism frames via grace and charity; the Gītā frames via seeing *para*.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Withdraw from one habitual sensory feed for a day. Watch what *rasa* remains, and give that longing one minute of honest seeing toward something higher than the object.

## Even the Discerning Man’s Mind Is Forcibly Carried Off by Storming Senses
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.60–2.61

The turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind, son of Kuntī, even of a striving, discerning person. Restraining them all, let him sit yoked, intent on Me; whose senses are under control, his wisdom stands established.

---

### Devanagari
यततो ह्यपि कौन्तेय पुरुषस्य विपश्चितः।

इन्द्रियाणि प्रमाथीनि हरन्ति प्रसभं मनः

तानि सर्वाणि संयम्य युक्त आसीत मत्परः।

वशे हि यस्येन्द्रियाणि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता

### IAST
yatato hyapi kaunteya puruṣasya vipaścitaḥ|

indriyāṇi pramāthīni haranti prasabhaṃ manaḥ

tāni sarvāṇi saṃyamya yukta āsīta matparaḥ|

vaśe hi yasyendriyāṇi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā

### Pratibha Translation
“The storming senses forcibly carry off the mind, son of Kuntī, even of a person who strives and discerns. Restraining them all, let him sit yoked, Me as the highest; for the one whose senses are in control, wisdom stands established.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Effort and intelligence are not enough. *Pramāthin* senses churn and seize the mind *prasabham* — by force. The remedy is *saṃyama* of all senses, seated yoked (*yukta*), with Kṛṣṇa as *mat-para* — the highest beyond. Here bhakti-orientation enters the sthita-prajña portrait: sense-control is stabilized by a supreme intentional object. Existentially, willpower without a “toward what” exhausts itself. Establish the senses by giving attention a worthy beyond.

Striving intelligence can still be kidnapped. Mat-para gives saṃyama a beyond, so restraint is not empty self-punishment. Seat the senses by giving attention a worthy highest.

Forced mind-theft humbles spiritual pride. Sit yoked with a highest, or willpower becomes brittle. Devotional orientation here is practical neuroscience of attention. Attention needs a beyond, or it will be owned by the nearest intense object. Choose the beyond deliberately.

When senses kidnap attention, re-seat it toward your highest before re-entering the stream of action. If your application no longer risks anything, you have likely replaced the claim with a slogan.

### Key Terms
**pramāthin (प्रमाथिन्)** — churning/turbulent/harassing → senses as agitative force → “violent” is partial; churning captures ongoing disturbance.

**prasabham (प्रसभम्)** — forcibly → seizure against resistance → marks the non-negotiable strength of sensory pull.

**mat-para (मत्पर)** — having Me as supreme → Kṛṣṇa as orienting highest → “devoted to God” is broad; *para* ranks the Lord above rival aims.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 1.30–1.32 / 2.54:** Both admit that even the practiced suffer mind-steal by distraction, and prescribe focused restraint.
*Divergence:* YS offers one-pointed principles and īśvara-praṇidhāna; here *mat-para* is explicit in the Gītā’s voice.

**Augustine, Confessions X (the senses and distraction):** Both confess the force of sensory seizure despite knowing better.
*Divergence:* Augustine turns to divine grace and ordered love; Arjuna is told to sit yoked with Kṛṣṇa as highest.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
When senses seize the mind today, sit for sixty seconds, name the sense, and re-aim attention toward your highest — then resume only one next action.

## Dwelling on Objects Births Attachment, Then Desire, Then Anger
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.62

For a person dwelling on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger is born.

---

### Devanagari
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते।

सङ्गात् संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते

### IAST
dhyāyato viṣayānpuṃsaḥ saṅgasteṣūpajāyate|

saṅgāt saṃjāyate kāmaḥ kāmātkrodho'bhijāyate

### Pratibha Translation
“For a person dwelling on objects, attachment to them arises. From attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger is born.”

### Pratibha Commentary
The causal chain is mercilessly clear: *dhyāna* on objects → *saṅga* → *kāma* → *krodha*. The contested claim is that anger’s root is not the world’s injustice alone but prior meditative sticking to objects. Brooding is already karma. Existentially, this verse makes thought-hygiene ethical: what you rehearse, you will eventually rage for when blocked. Interrupt the chain at dwelling — earliest and cheapest.

Dwelling is already deed. Interrupt rehearsal early and you interrupt anger’s feedstock. Thought-hygiene is ethics with a long fuse.

If dwelling births the chain, redesign your media and memory habits as ethical acts. What you rehearse, you will one day demand — and rage when denied. Media and memory are ethical infrastructure. Redesign them where the chain begins.

Redesign one rehearsal habit — feed, scroll, fantasy — as ethical interruption of the anger chain at dwelling. Check the verse against your next irreversible act before you file it as inspiration. Keep Arjuna’s crisis in view so the line cannot shrink into abstract uplift.

### Key Terms
**dhyāyat (ध्यायत्)** — dwelling/meditating upon → repeated mental inhabitation of objects → “thinking about” is weaker than meditative dwelling.

**saṅga (सङ्ग)** — attachment → adhesive relation born from dwelling → first sticky product of rehearsal.

**kāma → krodha (काम → क्रोध)** — desire to anger → blocked wanting’s heat → the sequence is law-like in this psychology.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 2.3–2.9:** Both map afflictive chains from cognitive-affective sticking.
*Divergence:* YS embeds in kleśa theory; Gītā gives a four-beat practical chain for interruption.

**Buddhist twelve nidānas (taṇhā–upādāna region):** Both show craving escalating from contact/attention patterns.
*Divergence:* Buddhism frames dependent origination toward cessation; here the chain warns a warrior toward sthita-prajña.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Catch one loop of dwelling on an object. Break it by naming: “dwelling → sticking,” and move attention to breath or duty for two minutes.

## From Anger, Delusion — From Delusion, Memory-Loss — Then Intelligence Falls, and One Is Lost
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.63

From anger comes delusion; from delusion, wandering of memory; from memory’s ruin, destruction of understanding; from destruction of understanding, one is lost.

---

### Devanagari
क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः।

स्मृतिभ्रंशाद् बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति

### IAST
krodhādbhavati saṃmohaḥ saṃmohātsmṛtivibhramaḥ|

smṛtibhraṃśād buddhināśo buddhināśātpraṇaśyati

### Pratibha Translation
“From anger arises delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from the fall of memory, destruction of understanding; from destruction of understanding, one perishes.”

### Pratibha Commentary
The chain continues to ruin: *krodha* → *saṃmoha* → *smṛti-vibhrama* → *buddhi-nāśa* → *praṇaśyati*. The contested claim is that perdition is psychological before it is cosmic. Lose memory of what matters, and intelligence cannot steer; without *buddhi*, the person is undone. Existentially, this is why anger management is spiritual practice: rage is not only heat; it is the beginning of forgetting who you are and what you know.

Anger is the beginning of forgetting what you know. Memory-ruin collapses buddhi, and the person is lost before any outer defeat. Treat rage as spiritual emergency, not as fuel.

Perishing begins as memory-scramble under heat. Protect smṛti of what matters when anger rises: names, vows, faces, the next clean act. That protection is buddhi-defense. Defend memory under heat as you would defend a friend. Vows and faces first, argument second.

Under heat, protect memory of vows and faces before protecting your argumentative advantage. Ask what identity the claim destabilizes in you; that instability is part of the medicine.

### Key Terms
**saṃmoha (संमोह)** — delusion/confounding → totalizing confusion born of anger → “bewilderment” is apt.

**smṛti-vibhrama (स्मृतिविभ्रम)** — wandering/confusion of memory → loss of formative recollection → “forgetting” understates the scramble of memory.

**buddhi-nāśa (बुद्धिनाश)** — destruction of understanding → collapse of discriminative intelligence → the decisive fall before *praṇaśyati*.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 6 (patience chapter):** Both treat anger as gateway to cascading mental ruin.
*Divergence:* Śāntideva trains patience for bodhisattva path; Gītā trains the chain-recognition for sthita-prajña.

**Epictetus, Discourses 1.18 / 2.18:** Both show how passion corrupts assent and character progressively.
*Divergence:* Stoicism focuses on impression-judgment; the Gītā sequences toward memory and buddhi explicitly.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
In the next anger spike, recite the chain aloud once (“anger–delusion–memory–buddhi–ruin”) before sending the message or speaking the wound.

## Moving Among Objects without Attraction and Aversion, Self-Governed, One Finds Clarity
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.64–2.66

But moving among objects with senses free of attraction and aversion, governed by the Self, the self-controlled attains clarity. In clarity, the destruction of all his sorrows is born; for the clear-minded, understanding soon becomes fully established. There is no understanding for the unyoked, and for the unyoked no becoming; for the non-becoming, no peace; for the peaceless, how should there be happiness?

---

### Devanagari
रागद्वेषवियुक्तैस्तु विषयानिन्द्रियैश्चरन्।

आत्मवश्यैर्विधेयात्मा प्रसादमधिगच्छति

प्रसादे सर्वदुःखानां हानिरस्योपजायते।

प्रसन्नचेतसो ह्याशु बुद्धिः पर्यवतिष्ठते

नास्ति बुद्धिरयुक्तस्य न चायुक्तस्य भावना।

न चाभावयतः शान्तिरशान्तस्य कुतः सुखम्

### IAST
rāgadveṣaviyuktaistu viṣayānindriyaiścaran|

ātmavaśyairvidheyātmā prasādamadhigacchati

prasāde sarvaduḥkhānāṃ hānirasyopajāyate|

prasannacetaso hyāśu buddhiḥ paryavatiṣṭhate

nāsti buddhirayuktasya na cāyuktasya bhāvanā|

na cābhāvayataḥ śāntiraśāntasya kutaḥ sukham

### Pratibha Translation
“But moving among objects with senses separated from attraction and aversion, self-controlled, the governed self attains clarity. In clarity, the loss of all his sorrows arises; for the clear-hearted, understanding quickly becomes fully established. There is no understanding for the unyoked, nor becoming for the unyoked; for one without becoming, no peace; for the peaceless, whence happiness?”

### Pratibha Commentary
The path is not flight from objects but movement among them with senses freed from *rāga-dveṣa*. Then *prasāda* — clarity/graceful lucidity — arises, and with it the waning of sorrows and the quick establishment of *buddhi*. The negative cascade seals it: unyoked → no buddhi → no *bhāvanā* → no śānti → no sukha. The contested claim is that happiness is structurally impossible without yoking; it is not a mood you can chase downstream. Existentially, stop hunting sukha while refusing the upstream work of non-reactive sensing.

Happiness cannot be hunted downstream of non-yoking. Move among objects without rāga-dveṣa until prasāda comes; then buddhi establishes and sorrow thins. Upstream work first.

The unyoked chase sukha and manufacture peacelessness. Reverse the order: yoke, gain prasāda, let buddhi establish, watch sorrow thin. Happiness arrives as side-effect of order. Order the causes correctly or happiness remains a mirage downstream of peacelessness.

Reverse the happiness hunt: yoke first, let clarity come, allow joy as side-effect of order.

### Key Terms
**prasāda (प्रसाद)** — clarity/lucidity/gracious clearness → settled clear mind-state → “grace” and “clarity” both resonate; here mental lucidity is primary.

**ayukta (अयुक्त)** — unyoked → one not joined in yoga → “undisciplined” is moralizing; the issue is non-yoking.

**bhāvanā (भावना)** — becoming/cultivation/meditative bringing-into-being → without which peace fails → “imagination” is misleading here.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra 1.33 / 1.47–1.48:** Both link clarified mind to stable right knowing.
*Divergence:* YS details samādhi grades; Gītā emphasizes movement-among-objects without rāga-dveṣa.

**Dao De Jing 16:** Both connect returning to clarity with capacity for right action/peace.
*Divergence:* Laozi stresses stillness and return to the root; Gītā stresses yoked sensing in the midst of objects.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Walk through a stimulating place for ten minutes practicing “see without sticking”: note one attraction and one aversion without acting either.

## The Mind That Follows Roaming Senses Steals Wisdom Like Wind Steals a Boat
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.67–2.69

When the mind is driven after the roaming senses, it carries off his wisdom as wind carries a boat on the waters. Therefore, mighty-armed, whose senses are withdrawn on every side from their objects — his wisdom stands established. What is night for all beings, in that the restrained one is awake; wherein beings are awake, that is night for the seeing sage.

---

### Devanagari
इन्द्रियाणां हि चरतां यन्मनोऽनुविधीयते।

तदस्य हरति प्रज्ञां वायुर्नावमिवाम्भसि

तस्माद्यस्य महाबाहो निगृहीतानि सर्वशः।

इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता

या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी।

यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः

### IAST
indriyāṇāṃ hi caratāṃ yanmano'nuvidhīyate|

tadasya harati prajñāṃ vāyurnāvamivāmbhasi

tasmādyasya mahābāho nigṛhītāni sarvaśaḥ|

indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyastasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā

yā niśā sarvabhūtānāṃ tasyāṃ jāgarti saṃyamī|

yasyāṃ jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśā paśyato muneḥ

### Pratibha Translation
“When the mind follows after the roaming senses, it carries off his wisdom as wind carries a boat on the water. Therefore, mighty-armed, whose senses are held back on every side from sense-objects — his wisdom stands established. What is night for all beings, in that the restrained one wakes; wherein beings wake, that is night for the seeing muni.”

### Pratibha Commentary
The boat image makes loss of prajñā kinetic: mind following senses is a sail catching every gust. Then the famous inversion: the *saṃyamin* is awake in what is night for creatures, and the crowd’s daylight is night for the seer. The contested claim is epistemic-ascetic: shared consensus wakefulness can be sleep regarding the Real. Existentially, notice which “obvious” concerns of your milieu put your deeper seeing to sleep — and which quiet hours are your true waking.

A mind after senses is a boat in wind. The seer’s night/day inversion warns that consensus wakefulness can be sleep. Choose your waking deliberately.

Choose waking that the crowd calls night if that waking sees. Protect it on the calendar. Consensus daylight is not automatically truth. Protect non-consensus waking on the calendar, or the crowd’s day will put your seeing to sleep.

Schedule the waking your culture calls night, and keep the appointment against consensus daylight.

### Key Terms
**anuvidhīyate (अनुविधीयते)** — is conformed after / follows as rule → mind taking senses as law → “follows” understates submission.

**saṃyamin (संयमिन्)** — the restrained/self-controlled one → awakens where others sleep → not merely “disciplined person.”

**niśā (निशा)** — night → metaphor for unknowing or for the sage’s indifference to worldly day → dual use is the verse’s brilliance.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Heraclitus, DK B1 / B73:** Both contrast the shared sleep of the many with the waking of the one who sees the logos.
*Divergence:* Heraclitus’ waking is to cosmic logos; the Gītā’s waking is yogic restraint and Self-seeing.

**Gospel of Thomas 11 / Matthew 25:1–13:** Both play waking/sleep as spiritual epistemic states.
*Divergence:* Christian texts frame eschatological readiness; Gītā frames ongoing muni-perception versus collective night.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Identify one “daytime” obsession of your world that deadens you. Schedule twenty minutes of your “night-waking” — quiet practice the culture does not reward.

## As Waters Enter the Full Sea without Disturbing It, So Desires Enter the One Who Finds Peace
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.70

As waters enter the ocean, filled from all sides, standing unmoved firm — so one whom all desires enter attains peace, not the one who desires desires.

---

### Devanagari
आपूर्यमाणमचलप्रतिष्ठं

समुद्रमापः प्रविशन्ति यद्वत्।

तद्वत्कामा यं प्रविशन्ति सर्वे

स शान्तिमाप्नोति न कामकामी

### IAST
āpūryamāṇamacalapratiṣṭhaṃ

samudramāpaḥ praviśanti yadvat|

tadvatkāmā yaṃ praviśanti sarve

sa śāntimāpnoti na kāmakāmī

### Pratibha Translation
“As waters enter the ocean, being filled from every side, standing in unmoved firmness — so one into whom all desires enter attains peace, not the desirer of desires.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Peace is not desirelessness as empty dryness; it is ocean-capacity. Desires may enter; the ocean does not lose *acala-pratiṣṭhā*. The *kāma-kāmī* — desirer of desires — never attains śānti because wanting has become recursive. The contested image allows influx without disturbance. Existentially, stop trying to build peace by damming every want; become deeper than what enters. Breadth without depth is swamp; depth that can receive is ocean.

Ocean-peace receives influx without losing stand. Recursive desire — wanting wanting — never arrives. Depth that can welcome is freer than dams that crack.

Receiving desires without becoming their desirer is ocean literacy. Feel influx; keep stand. Recursive craving is the only guaranteed non-arrival at śānti. Recursive wanting is a closed loop. Ocean literacy breaks the loop by receiving without chasing.

Practice ocean: receive influx, keep stand, refuse recursive wanting that never arrives at śānti. Refuse summaries that skip the hinge where agency and seeing are redefined.

### Key Terms
**acala-pratiṣṭha (अचलप्रतिष्ठ)** — unmoved establishment → stable standing of the ocean/self → “firm foundation” is close.

**kāma-kāmī (कामकामी)** — desirer of desires → meta-craving, wanting the state of wanting → “lustful person” is too narrow and moralizing.

**āpaḥ praviśanti (आपः प्रविशन्ति)** — waters enter → influx without ownership struggle → the grammar of entering without conquering.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Dao De Jing 4 / 32 / 34:** Both image the great as receiving the many without being disturbed.
*Divergence:* Laozi’s greatness is Dao-like emptiness-fullness; Gītā’s ocean is the person of peace versus the desire-desirer.

**Plotinus, Enneads VI.9:** Both suggest the Real’s fullness is not increased or harmed by what flows toward it.
*Divergence:* Plotinus speaks of the One; here the simile trains human śānti.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
When a desire enters today, practice ocean: let it be felt fully for thirty seconds without chasing or damming, then return to the next right action.

## Abandoning All Desires, Moving Free of Longing, Without Mine and I-Making
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.71

Abandoning all desires, the person who moves without longing, without sense of mine, without I-making — that one attains peace.

---

### Devanagari
विहाय कामान्यः सर्वान्पुमांश्चरति निःस्पृहः।

निर्ममो निरहंकारः स शांतिमधिगच्छति

### IAST
vihāya kāmānyaḥ sarvānpumāṃścarati niḥspṛhaḥ|

nirmamo nirahaṃkāraḥ sa śāṃtimadhigacchati

### Pratibha Translation
“Abandoning all desires, the person who moves without longing, without ‘mine,’ without I-making — that one attains peace.”

### Pratibha Commentary
Motion continues: *carati* — he goes about — but without *kāma*, without *spṛhā*, without *mama*, without *ahaṃkāra*. Peace is compatible with a life of walking; incompatible with possessive self-manufacturing. The contested claim is that *nirahaṃkāra* is not personality-erasure but release of the appropriating “I-am-the-doer/owner” reflex. Existentially, practice peace as a way of moving through tasks without the private stamp of mine and me.

Peace walks. Nirmama and nirahaṃkāra are how motion stays clean. Drop the private stamp of mine and me-making while the day continues.

Moving without mine and I-making is peace as locomotion. Try it in speech and errands. The day continues; the appropriating stamp does not have to. Peace that cannot walk is incomplete. Practice nirmama in motion until the stamp of mine goes quiet.

Move through an errand without mine-stamping; let peace prove itself as locomotion, not as escape. Return once more to the exact image the verse uses; images carry claims arguments alone miss.

### Key Terms
**niḥspṛha (निःस्पृह)** — without longing → absence of ache-to-obtain while moving → “desireless” is blunter.

**nirmama (निर्मम)** — without mine-ness → non-possessive field of experience → “unselfish” is moral; this is ontological de-mining.

**nirahaṃkāra (निरहंकार)** — without I-making → release of ego-construction → “egoless” is popular; the Sanskrit targets the fabricating function.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Īśā Upaniṣad 1:** Both pair moving in the world with non-grasping (*mā gṛdhaḥ*).
*Divergence:* Īśā opens with the Lord’s filling; Gītā specifies desire, mine, and I-making as the triad dropped for peace.

**Eckhart, talks on detachment (Abegescheidenheit):** Both make peace contingent on release of possessive self-reference.
*Divergence:* Eckhart aims at birth of the Word in the soul; Gītā aims at śānti as mark of sthita-prajña leading to brahma-nirvāṇa.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Complete one chore narrating silently without “my” and without self-credit: only verbs and objects. Notice the body’s quieter peace.

---

## This Is the Brahman-Standing — Attaining It, One Is Not Deluded; Fixed in It Even at Death, One Reaches Brahma-Nirvāṇa
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 2.72

This is the Brahman-standing, Pārtha; attaining it, one is not deluded. Standing in it even at the time of end, one reaches brahma-nirvāṇa.

---

### Devanagari
एषा ब्राह्मी स्थितिः पार्थ नैनां प्राप्य विमुह्यति।

स्थित्वाऽस्यामन्तकालेऽपि ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृच्छति

### IAST
eṣā brāhmī sthitiḥ pārtha naināṃ prāpya vimuhyati|

sthitvā'syāmantakāle'pi brahmanirvāṇamṛcchati

### Pratibha Translation
“This is the Brahman-standing, Pārtha; attaining it, one is not deluded. Abiding in it even at the hour of death, one reaches [brahma-nirvāṇa].”

### Pratibha Commentary
Chapter 2 closes by naming the portrait’s summit: *brāhmī sthiti* — standing as/in Brahman. Attaining it ends *vimoha*; abiding in it at *anta-kāla* yields *brahma-nirvāṇa*. The contested synthesis is that the whole psychology of desire-chains, sense-restraint, and ocean-peace is not merely coping — it is Brahman-mode. Death becomes a test of abiding, not a separate problem. Existentially, practice is rehearsal for the last hour by becoming undeceived now. The chapter that began with “stand up” ends with a standing that death cannot unsettle.

Brahman-standing gathers the chapter’s psychology into a mode of being undeceived. Rehearse it now so the last hour is not your first attempt at abiding. 'Stand up' completes itself as a standing death cannot unsettle.

Brahma-nirvāṇa is not an exit fantasy from duty; it is the fruit of undeceived abiding, including at the end. Practice undeception in small endings so the last hour recognizes its seat.

Rehearse undeceived abiding in a small ending so the last hour recognizes its seat.

### Key Terms
**brāhmī sthiti (ब्राह्मी स्थिति)** — Brahman-standing / state pertaining to Brahman → stable abiding in the absolute’s mode → “divine state” is vague; Brahman-specific standing is exact.

**vimuhyati (विमुह्यति)** — is deluded/led astray → negated upon attainment → delusion as preventable status, not fate.

**brahma-nirvāṇa (ब्रह्मनिर्वाण)** — extinguishing/blissful dissolution in Brahman → end-attainment from abiding → neither simple annihilation nor crude heaven; the compound holds Brahman and nirvāṇa together.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**Mandukya Upaniṣad (turiya):** Both point to a standing beyond waking delusion that refigures the sense of end.
*Divergence:* Mandukya maps states of consciousness; Gītā binds Brahman-standing to ethical-yogic marks and death-hour abiding.

**Nirvāṇa in early Buddhism (extinguishing of the fires):** Both use cessation-language for ultimate ease.
*Divergence:* Buddhist nirvāṇa centers cessation of greed-hatred-delusion without Brahman-metaphysics; *brahma-nirvāṇa* yokes extinguishing to Brahman-abiding.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Once today, sit as if rehearsing the last hour: drop one clinging narrative, rest in undeceived presence for three minutes, then return to duty without panic.

**Chapter:** 3 — Karma Yoga (the yoga of action)
**Units:** 19 (one per brief chunk)
**Sanskrit:** Devanagari and IAST taken verbatim from `bhagavad_gita_briefs/chapter_03_brief.md`
