## The Witness, the Permitter, the Great Lord
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 13.22–13.24

The person, seated in nature, indeed enjoys the guṇas born of nature. Attachment to the guṇas is the cause of his birth in good and evil wombs. The witness [upadraṣṭā], the permitter [anumantā], the supporter, the experiencer, the great Lord, and also called the supreme Self—thus is the highest person in this body. The one who thus knows the person and nature together with the guṇas is not born again, however he may live and act.

---

### Devanagari
पुरुषः प्रकृतिस्थो हि भुङ्क्ते प्रकृतिजान्गुणान्।कारणं गुणसङ्गोऽस्य सदसद्योनिजन्मसु
उपद्रष्टाऽनुमन्ता च भर्ता भोक्ता महेश्वरः।

परमात्मेति चाप्युक्तो देहेऽस्मिन्पुरुषः परः
य एवं वेत्ति पुरुषं प्रकृतिं च गुणैः सह।

सर्वथा वर्तमानोऽपि न स भूयोऽभिजायते

### IAST
puruṣaḥ prakṛtistho hi bhuṅkte prakṛtijānguṇān|kāraṇaṃ guṇasaṅgo'sya sadasadyonijanmasu
upadraṣṭā'numantā ca bhartā bhoktā maheśvaraḥ|

paramātmeti cāpyukto dehe'sminpuruṣaḥ paraḥ
ya evaṃ vetti puruṣaṃ prakṛtiṃ ca guṇaiḥ saha|

sarvathā vartamāno'pi na sa bhūyo'bhijāyate

### Pratibha Translation
The person, seated in nature, indeed enjoys the guṇas born of nature. Attachment to the guṇas is the cause of his birth in good and evil wombs. The witness [upadraṣṭā], the permitter [anumantā], the supporter, the experiencer, the great Lord, and also called the supreme Self—thus is the highest person in this body. The one who thus knows the person and nature together with the guṇas is not born again, however he may live and act.

### Pratibha Commentary
Bondage’s mechanism is named with precision: not the guṇas themselves, but guṇa-saṅga—attachment to them—causes rebirth across good and evil wombs. Then the chapter’s most compressed theology of immanence: in this very body the highest person is upadraṣṭā (over-seer), anumantā (one who permits), supporter, experiencer, Maheśvara, Paramātman. The contested move is to refuse a merely passive witness. The Self sees, allows, bears, tastes, and lords—without being reduced to the field’s turbulence. Knowing this—person, nature, and guṇas together—ends rebirth even while life continues in every way (sarvathā vartamānaḥ). Existentially, release is not behavioral disappearance; it is the end of misidentification while action continues.  The titles upadraṣṭā and anumantā keep witnessing from becoming dissociation: the Self is intimate, permitting, and sovereign—not checked out. Read as existential demand, the verse asks for a changed stance in the next difficult hour—not for ornamental agreement with a doctrine. Read as existential demand, the verse asks for a changed stance in the next difficult hour—not for ornamental agreement with a doctrine.

### Key Terms
**guṇa-saṅga (गुणसङ्ग)** — attachment to the strands -> the binding glue to prakṛti’s modes -> “liking qualities” understates karmic causality.
**upadraṣṭā (उपद्रष्टा)** — over-seer / witness nearby -> intimate witnessing presence -> “observer” can sound clinical and detached.
**anumantā (अनुमन्ता)** — permitter / consenter -> the one who allows processes to run -> “approver” wrongly moralizes permission.
**Maheśvara (महेश्वर)** — great Lord -> sovereign of the embodied field -> “God” without this embodied title loses the verse’s shock.
**Paramātman (परमात्मन्)** — supreme Self -> the highest person in the body -> “oversoul” can float outside incarnation.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Kaṭha Upaniṣad I.3.3–4]:** The Self as rider/lord of the bodily chariot parallels the highest person in the body.
*Divergence:* Kaṭha stresses yogic restraint of reins; here the titles emphasize witnessing, permitting, and lordship as already present.
**[Spanda tradition / Śiva as witness-agent]:** The Lord as both cognizer and dynamic allowability resonates with upadraṣṭā-anumantā.
*Divergence:* Kashmir Shaivism radicalizes world as Śiva’s vibration; the Gītā keeps prakṛti-guṇa analysis as the pedagogical frame.
**[Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy V]:** Providence as seeing and ordering parallels witness-permitter.
*Divergence:* Boethius works a Christian-Platonic providence; Krishna names the Lord as tasting and supporting within the body.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
For one difficult impulse today, practice the triad: “witnessed,” “permitted,” “not owned.” Act only after the third recognition.

## Many Paths, One Seeing
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 13.25–13.27

Some see the Self in the Self by meditation; others by Sāṃkhya-yoga; others by karma-yoga. Still others, not knowing thus, worship having heard from others; they too cross beyond death, devoted to what they have heard. Whatever being is born, moving or unmoving, know it as arising from the union of field and knower of the field, O best of Bharatas.

---

### Devanagari
ध्यानेनात्मनि पश्यन्ति केचिदात्मानमात्मना।अन्ये सांख्येन योगेन कर्मयोगेन चापरे
अन्ये त्वेवमजानन्तः श्रुत्वाऽन्येभ्य उपासते।तेऽपि चातितरन्त्येव मृत्युं श्रुतिपरायणाः
यावत्सञ्जायते किञ्चित्सत्त्वं स्थावरजङ्गमम्।क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञसंयोगात्तद्विद्धि भरतर्षभ

### IAST
dhyānenātmani paśyanti kecidātmānamātmanā|anye sāṃkhyena yogena karmayogena cāpare
anye tvevamajānantaḥ śrutvā'nyebhya upāsate|te'pi cātitarantyeva mṛtyuṃ śrutiparāyaṇāḥ
yāvatsañjāyate kiñcitsattvaṃ sthāvarajaṅgamam|kṣetrakṣetrajñasaṃyogāttadviddhi bharatarṣabha

### Pratibha Translation
Some see the Self in the Self by meditation; others by Sāṃkhya-yoga; others by karma-yoga. Still others, not knowing thus, worship having heard from others; they too cross beyond death, devoted to what they have heard. Whatever being is born, moving or unmoving, know it as arising from the union of field and knower of the field, O best of Bharatas.

### Pratibha Commentary
Pluralism here is not relativism. Meditation, Sāṃkhya, and karma-yoga are distinct disciplines that can yield the same seeing of ātman. Even those who do not know “thus” but live by trustworthy hearing can cross death—an extraordinary pastoral claim that dignifies receptive faith without collapsing it into anti-intellectualism. The contested move is to hold rigorous metaphysics and generous pedagogy together. Then the ontological punchline: every being arises from kṣetra-kṣetrajña-saṃyoga. Birth is union of field and knower. Existentially, this dissolves both crude materialism and disembodied spiritualism: life is always the coupling of terrain and awareness.  Pastoral pluralism here does not flatten standards; it refuses contempt for the hearer who lives by trust while the seer lives by vision. Read as existential demand, the verse asks for a changed stance in the next difficult hour—not for ornamental agreement with a doctrine. Read as existential demand, the verse asks for a changed stance in the next difficult hour—not for ornamental agreement with a doctrine.

### Key Terms
**dhyāna (ध्यान)** — meditation / sustained seeing -> Self seen in the Self by the Self -> “concentration” can sound merely attentional.
**Sāṃkhya-yoga (सांख्ययोग)** — yoga of discriminative enumeration -> path of tattva-discrimination -> “philosophy” misses its yogic force.
**śruti-parāyaṇa (श्रुतिपरायण)** — devoted to hearing -> liberation via receptive adherence to teaching -> “scriptural literalism” misreads the pastoral opening.
**saṃyoga (संयोग)** — union / conjunction -> field-knower coupling as birth’s condition -> “combination” is too mechanical.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 12.8–12]:** Multiple ranked practices with room for those of lesser capacity parallel this pluralism.
*Divergence:* Chapter 12 ranks by intimacy of devotion; chapter 13 centers the shared metaphysical seeing of field and knower.
**[Buddha, Magga / many approaches motif]:** Different temperaments, one liberation-oriented path ecology.
*Divergence:* Buddhism’s many doors open onto not-self and cessation; here doors open onto field-knower knowledge and the Lord.
**[Origen / early Christian pedagogy]:** Milk for beginners, meat for advanced echoes hearing-based worship versus direct seeing.
*Divergence:* Christian pedagogy aims at Christic union; Krishna’s horizon is crossing death via field-knower insight.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Identify your current primary door—meditation, study-discrimination, or selfless action. Practice it today without contempt for the other doors.

## Who Sees, Truly Sees
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 13.28–13.30

The one who sees the supreme Lord standing equally in all beings, the undying in the dying—he truly sees. Seeing the Lord established equally everywhere, one does not injure the Self by the self; then one goes to the highest goal. The one who sees that actions are done entirely by nature alone, and thus sees the Self as non-doer—he truly sees.

---

### Devanagari
समं सर्वेषु भूतेषु तिष्ठन्तं परमेश्वरम्।विनश्यत्स्वविनश्यन्तं यः पश्यति स पश्यति
समं पश्यन्हि सर्वत्र समवस्थितमीश्वरम्।न हिनस्त्यात्मनाऽऽत्मानं ततो याति परां गतिम्
प्रकृत्यैव च कर्माणि क्रियमाणानि सर्वशः।यः पश्यति तथाऽऽत्मानमकर्तारं स पश्यति

### IAST
samaṃ sarveṣu bhūteṣu tiṣṭhantaṃ parameśvaram|vinaśyatsvavinaśyantaṃ yaḥ paśyati sa paśyati
samaṃ paśyanhi sarvatra samavasthitamīśvaram|na hinastyātmanā''tmānaṃ tato yāti parāṃ gatim
prakṛtyaiva ca karmāṇi kriyamāṇāni sarvaśaḥ|yaḥ paśyati tathā''tmānamakartāraṃ sa paśyati

### Pratibha Translation
The one who sees the supreme Lord standing equally in all beings, the undying in the dying—he truly sees. Seeing the Lord established equally everywhere, one does not injure the Self by the self; then one goes to the highest goal. The one who sees that actions are done entirely by nature alone, and thus sees the Self as non-doer—he truly sees.

### Pratibha Commentary
“He who sees, sees” (sa paśyati) is the chapter’s refrain of authentic vision. Equal standing of Parameśvara in all beings—and the undying within the dying—redefines perception itself. From this seeing comes ethics: one does not strike the Self with the self. Violence is revealed as metaphysical suicide, not merely interpersonal harm. Then the non-doer teaching: actions are wrought wholly by prakṛti; the ātman is akartā. The contested move is to unite theistic equality-vision with Sāṃkhya non-doership without letting either cancel the other. Existentially, true seeing ends both cruelty and the anxious claim “I am the sole author of this life.”  Equal seeing is therefore the end of spiritual exceptionalism: if the Lord stands equally, your private drama of superiority loses its altar. Read as existential demand, the verse asks for a changed stance in the next difficult hour—not for ornamental agreement with a doctrine. Read as existential demand, the verse asks for a changed stance in the next difficult hour—not for ornamental agreement with a doctrine.

### Key Terms
**sama (सम)** — equal / even -> Lord’s equal presence in all beings -> “fairness” moralizes what is ontological.
**Parameśvara (परमेश्वर)** — supreme Lord -> the One standing in all fields -> “God” without equal immanence misses the ethical hinge.
**na hinasti (न हिनस्ति)** — does not injure -> non-injury as consequence of equal seeing -> “becomes nice” misses Self-on-Self stakes.
**akartā (अकर्ता)** — non-doer -> Self as not the agent of prakṛti’s actions -> “passive” wrongly implies limpness.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Īśā Upaniṣad 6–7]:** Seeing all beings in the Self and the Self in all ends grief and delusion—close ethical homology.
*Divergence:* Īśā is compact and ritual-renunciant; the Gītā explicitly ties equal seeing to non-doership of prakṛti’s actions.
**[Spinoza, Ethics IV–V]:** Seeing things under a species of eternity reduces harm born of partial passion.
*Divergence:* Spinoza’s God is substance known geometrically; Krishna’s Lord is personally addressed and equally stationed in beings.
**[Śāntideva, BCA VIII (exchange of self and other)]:** Equalizing vision undermines harm.
*Divergence:* Śāntideva uses imaginative exchange and emptiness; Krishna uses Lord-equality and prakṛti-agency.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Before speaking critically of someone, pause and see the undying in the dying field before you. Speak only after that seeing is even briefly available.

## Space Untouched, Self Untouched
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 13.31–13.33

When one sees the separate being of beings as abiding in the One, and from that alone their expansion, then one becomes Brahman. Because it is beginningless and without guṇas, this supreme Self is imperishable. Though dwelling in the body, O son of Kuntī, it neither acts nor is stained. As the all-pervading space is not stained because of its subtlety, so the Self, seated everywhere in the body, is not stained.

---

### Devanagari
यदा भूतपृथग्भावमेकस्थमनुपश्यति।तत एव च विस्तारं ब्रह्म सम्पद्यते तदा
अनादित्वान्निर्गुणत्वात्परमात्मायमव्ययः।शरीरस्थोऽपि कौन्तेय न करोति न लिप्यते
यथा सर्वगतं सौक्ष्म्यादाकाशं नोपलिप्यते।

सर्वत्रावस्थितो देहे तथाऽऽत्मा नोपलिप्यते

### IAST
yadā bhūtapṛthagbhāvamekasthamanupaśyati|tata eva ca vistāraṃ brahma sampadyate tadā
anāditvānnirguṇatvātparamātmāyamavyayaḥ|śarīrastho'pi kaunteya na karoti na lipyate
yathā sarvagataṃ saukṣmyādākāśaṃ nopalipyate|

sarvatrāvasthito dehe tathā''tmā nopalipyate

### Pratibha Translation
When one sees the separate being of beings as abiding in the One, and from that alone their expansion, then one becomes Brahman. Because it is beginningless and without guṇas, this supreme Self is imperishable. Though dwelling in the body, O son of Kuntī, it neither acts nor is stained. As the all-pervading space is not stained because of its subtlety, so the Self, seated everywhere in the body, is not stained.

### Pratibha Commentary
The climax of discrimination is unitive: separate beings are seen as established in the One, and their expansion as from that One alone—then one becomes Brahman. This is not metaphor; it is the fruit of seeing. The Paramātman, beginningless and nirguṇa, neither acts nor is stained though body-dwelling. The ākāśa analogy is exact: space pervades and is intimate with all forms yet unsoiled by them because of subtlety. The contested move is embodied non-staining: spirituality that needs to flee the body misunderstands subtlety. Existentially, guilt, praise, and defilement narratives can be felt as weather in space, not as tattoos on the Self.  The space analogy also disciplines guilt-spirituality: stains are real in the field, yet the Self’s subtlety is not improved by self-hate. Read as existential demand, the verse asks for a changed stance in the next difficult hour—not for ornamental agreement with a doctrine. Read as existential demand, the verse asks for a changed stance in the next difficult hour—not for ornamental agreement with a doctrine.

### Key Terms
**eka-stha (एकस्थ)** — abiding in the One -> multiplicity rooted in unity -> “oneness” as slogan misses located establishment.
**brahma sampadyate (ब्रह्म सम्पद्यते)** — becomes / attains Brahman -> realization as ontological fitting -> “goes to Brahman” can postpone what is present fruit.
**na lipyate (न लिप्यते)** — is not smeared / stained -> non-contamination amid embodiment -> “unaffected” can sound dissociative.
**ākāśa (आकाश)** — space / ether -> analogy for pervading unstained presence -> “sky” visualizes wrongly as overhead only.
**saukṣmya (सौक्ष्म्य)** — subtlety -> the reason space and Self remain unsoiled -> “thinness” is too physical.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Chāndogya Upaniṣad III.14 / VI]:** Becoming what one knows (Brahman) resonates with brahma sampadyate.
*Divergence:* Chāndogya often uses gradual teaching and metaphors of clay/gold; here the hinge is seeing multiplicity in the One.
**[Zhuangzi, “Fasting of the Mind”]:** Emptiness that receives the world without being soiled parallels ākāśa-like Self.
*Divergence:* Zhuangzi distrusts fixed metaphysical selves; the Gītā affirms Paramātman while using space as image of non-staining.
**[Meister Eckhart, on the ground of the soul]:** The soul’s ground remains virgin amid images.
*Divergence:* Eckhart pushes toward God beyond God; Krishna keeps the teaching inside body-dwelling non-action and non-stain.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Imagine awareness as space in the room of the body. Let sounds, thoughts, and sensations arise like birds through space. Note: space is not stained. Rest there for five minutes.

## The Sun of the Field, the Eye of Knowledge
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 13.34–13.35

As the one sun illumines this whole world, so the Lord of the field illumines the whole field, O Bhārata. Those who know, with the eye of knowledge, this distinction between field and knower of the field, and the liberation of beings from nature—they go to the Supreme.

---

### Devanagari
यथा प्रकाशयत्येकः कृत्स्नं लोकमिमं रविः।

क्षेत्रं क्षेत्री तथा कृत्स्नं प्रकाशयति भारत
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञयोरेवमन्तरं ज्ञानचक्षुषा।

भूतप्रकृतिमोक्षं च ये विदुर्यान्ति ते परम्

### IAST
yathā prakāśayatyekaḥ kṛtsnaṃ lokamimaṃ raviḥ|

kṣetraṃ kṣetrī tathā kṛtsnaṃ prakāśayati bhārata
kṣetrakṣetrajñayorevamantaraṃ jñānacakṣuṣā|

bhūtaprakṛtimokṣaṃ ca ye viduryānti te param

### Pratibha Translation
As the one sun illumines this whole world, so the Lord of the field illumines the whole field, O Bhārata. Those who know, with the eye of knowledge, this distinction between field and knower of the field, and the liberation of beings from nature—they go to the Supreme.

### Pratibha Commentary
The chapter closes with light. One sun, whole world; one kṣetrī, whole field. Illumination is not an extra act layered onto matter; it is the knower’s very presence as light. The eye of knowledge (jñāna-cakṣus) sees the antara—the difference—between field and knower, and also bhūta-prakṛti-mokṣa: liberation of beings from nature. The contested final claim is that discrimination and release belong together. Seeing the difference is already the beginning of freedom from prakṛti’s claim. Existentially, you do not wait to leave the world to be free of nature’s bondage; you learn to see the sun that was lighting the field all along, and in that seeing, go to the Supreme.  Going to the Supreme is thus not a travel plan after discrimination; discrimination itself is already sunlight learning to notice the sun. Read as existential demand, the verse asks for a changed stance in the next difficult hour—not for ornamental agreement with a doctrine.

### Key Terms
**kṣetrī (क्षेत्री)** — lord/owner of the field -> the illumining knower -> “soul” misses the solar metaphor’s public radiance.
**prakāśayati (प्रकाशयति)** — illumines -> knowing as lighting-up of the field -> “reveals” can sound merely informational.
**jñāna-cakṣus (ज्ञानचक्षुस्)** — eye of knowledge -> discriminative vision as organ of liberation -> “insight” can stay psychological.
**antara (अन्तर)** — distinction / interval / difference -> the liberating cut between field and knower -> “inner” mistranslates the philosophical sense here.
**prakṛti-mokṣa (प्रकृतिमोक्ष)** — liberation from nature -> release of beings from prakṛti’s binding -> “escape from matter” can sound dualistically crude.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Plato, Republic VI–VII (sun and cave)]:** The sun as analogue of the Good that lights knowables is structural kin.
*Divergence:* Plato’s sun serves dialectic ascent to forms; Krishna’s sun-knower illumines the field for discriminative release into the Supreme.
**[Kaṭha Upaniṣad II.2.15 / Śvetāśvatara VI.14]:** When That shines, all shines after it—light-of-lights homology.
*Divergence:* Those Upaniṣads climax in metaphysical radiance; the Gītā ties the solar image explicitly to kṣetra/kṣetrajña difference.
**[Dzogchen “self-knowing awareness” as lamp]:** Awareness lighting appearance without being identical to appearance.
*Divergence:* Dzogchen emphasizes primordial purity beyond effort; the Gītā still foregrounds the eye of knowledge and going to the Supreme.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
At sunset or beside a lamp, contemplate: “As this light shows the room, awareness shows the field.” Rest in the lighting, not in the furniture of experience.



**Corpus entry:** Bhagavad Gītā / Mahābhārata
**Units:** 12 (one per brief CHUNK)

---

## The Highest Knowledge Returns to Kinship
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.1–14.3

The Blessed Lord said: I will again declare the supreme knowledge, the best of knowings, knowing which all the sages have gone from here to the highest perfection. Those who take refuge in this knowledge and come to share My nature are not born even at the creation, nor do they tremble at the dissolution. My womb is the great Brahman; in it I place the seed. From that, O Bhārata, comes the birth of all beings.

---

### Devanagari
श्री भगवानुवाचपरं भूयः प्रवक्ष्यामि ज्ञानानां ज्ञानमुत्तमम्।यज्ज्ञात्वा मुनयः सर्वे परां सिद्धिमितो गताः
इदं ज्ञानमुपाश्रित्य मम साधर्म्यमागताः।सर्गेऽपि नोपजायन्ते प्रलये न व्यथन्ति च
मम योनिर्महद्ब्रह्म तस्मिन् गर्भं दधाम्यहम्।संभवः सर्वभूतानां ततो भवति भारत

### IAST
śrī bhagavānuvācaparaṃ bhūyaḥ pravakṣyāmi jñānānāṃ jñānamuttamam|yajjñātvā munayaḥ sarve parāṃ siddhimito gatāḥ
idaṃ jñānamupāśritya mama sādharmyamāgatāḥ|sarge'pi nopajāyante pralaye na vyathanti ca
mama yonirmahadbrahma tasmin garbhaṃ dadhāmyaham|saṃbhavaḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ tato bhavati bhārata

### Pratibha Translation
The Blessed Lord said: I will again declare the supreme knowledge, the best of knowings, knowing which all the sages have gone from here to the highest perfection. Those who take refuge in this knowledge and come to share My nature are not born even at the creation, nor do they tremble at the dissolution. My womb is the great Brahman; in it I place the seed. From that, O Bhārata, comes the birth of all beings.

### Pratibha Commentary
Krishna reopens teaching not with novelty but with intensification: this is jñānānāṃ jñānam uttamam—the highest among knowledges. The contested claim arrives immediately in its fruit: those who take refuge in this knowledge attain sādharmya, kinship of nature with the Lord, and stand beyond birth at creation and anguish at dissolution. Cosmology then turns parental: mahad-brahman is the womb, Krishna the seed-giver. The universe is not an accident of matter; it is a fertile field quickened by divine impregnation. In the Gītā’s arc, chapter 14 does not abandon earlier yoga; it names the qualitative weather that makes yoga necessary. Existentially, the verse relocates spiritual ambition from accumulating insights to entering a shared nature that does not panic when worlds end. Knowledge here is shelter (upāśritya), not ornament. The sage’s “perfection” is not technical mastery but passage into a mode of being that creation and destruction cannot commandeer. When you fear endings, the teaching asks whether you are clinging to a private timeline or resting in kinship with the seed-giver of all wombs.

### Key Terms
**jñānam uttamam (ज्ञानमुत्तमम्)** — highest knowledge -> knowledge whose fruit is divine kinship -> 'best philosophy' misses soteriological kinship.
**sādharmya (साधर्म्य)** — sameness of dharma/nature -> participation in the Lord's mode of being -> 'similarity' is too weak for ontological sharing.
**mahad-brahman (महद्ब्रह्म)** — great Brahman as womb -> prakṛti as cosmic matrix -> 'matter' erases sacred fertility.
**garbhaṃ dadhāmi (गर्भं दधामि)** — I place the seed/embryo -> divine seeding of the womb of nature -> 'create' is too generic.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Chāndogya Upaniṣad III.19 / cosmic egg motifs]:** Cosmic genesis through a fertile matrix resonates with womb-and-seed cosmology.
*Divergence:* Upaniṣadic eggs often remain impersonal; here Krishna is explicitly the seed-placing father.
**[Genesis 1 / impregnating Word traditions]:** World-birth through divine initiative parallels seed placed in a receptive matrix.
*Divergence:* Biblical creation is typically ex nihilo command; the Gītā uses sexual-cosmic metaphor inside guṇa psychology to come.
**[Dao De Jing 1 / 6]:** The gateway of the mysterious female as root of heaven and earth echoes womb-language.
*Divergence:* Daoist mystery resists a personal seed-giver; Krishna claims paternal agency within Brahman-womb.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
When anxiety about beginnings or endings arises, silently rest in kinship: 'Not my private timeline—shared nature.' Hold that for ten breaths.

---

## Father of Forms in Every Womb
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.4

Whatever forms are born in any womb, O son of Kuntī, the great Brahman is their womb, and I am the father who gives the seed.

---

### Devanagari
सर्वयोनिषु कौन्तेय मूर्तयः सम्भवन्ति याः।तासां ब्रह्म महद्योनिरहं बीजप्रदः पिता

### IAST
sarvayoniṣu kaunteya mūrtayaḥ sambhavanti yāḥ|tāsāṃ brahma mahadyonirahaṃ bījapradaḥ pitā

### Pratibha Translation
Whatever forms are born in any womb, O son of Kuntī, the great Brahman is their womb, and I am the father who gives the seed.

### Pratibha Commentary
The previous cosmology becomes universal law: every form, in every womb, has mahad-brahman as matrix and Krishna as seed-father. The contested move is to sacralize embodiment without romanticizing it. Birth is neither shame nor mere biology; it is the meeting of cosmic womb and divine seed. This undercuts both materialist reduction and world-rejecting spirituality. The verse also quietly universalizes dignity: no womb is outside this parentage, which means contempt for any form is a theological mistake. In classical commentary, this line anchors the Lord’s immanence inside prakṛti’s productivity rather than against it. Existentially, looking at any living form becomes a recognition scene: matrix and father are already at work. Ethics follows: cruelty toward bodies is hostility toward the Lord’s generative act. Wonder follows too: the ordinary face before you is not “just biology,” but a seeded form of the great womb. The parental metaphor also disciplines pride: if every form is womb-born and seed-given, spiritual status cannot be a private achievement trophy.

### Key Terms
**yoni (योनि)** — womb / source -> matrix of manifestation -> 'origin' loses embodied specificity.
**mūrti (मूर्ति)** — form / embodiment -> concrete appearance born of womb -> 'image' can sound merely representational.
**bīja-prada pitā (बीजप्रदः पिता)** — seed-giving father -> Krishna as impregnating principle -> 'creator god' flattens the parental metaphor.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad V–VI]:** God as source of beings resonates with father-of-seed language.
*Divergence:* Śvetāśvatara leans Rudra-theistic; the Gītā prepares a guṇa analysis of bondage within this parentage.
**[Plato, Timaeus]:** The demiurge and receptacle parallel seed and womb functions.
*Divergence:* Timaeus is craft-cosmology; Krishna’s parentage is intimate and immediately existential.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Look at one living being today and silently say: 'Great Brahman is the womb; the Lord is the seed-father.' Notice what hardness softens.

---

## The Guṇas Bind the Embodied
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.5

Sattva, rajas, and tamas—the guṇas born of nature—bind the imperishable embodied one to the body, O mighty-armed.

---

### Devanagari
सत्त्वं रजस्तम इति गुणाः प्रकृतिसंभवाः।निबध्नन्ति महाबाहो देहे देहिनमव्ययम्

### IAST
sattvaṃ rajastama iti guṇāḥ prakṛtisaṃbhavāḥ|nibadhnanti mahābāho dehe dehinamavyayam

### Pratibha Translation
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—the guṇas born of nature—bind the imperishable embodied one to the body, O mighty-armed.

### Pratibha Commentary
Here the chapter’s engine starts: the three guṇas, born of prakṛti, bind the imperishable embodied one (dehin) to the body. The contested claim is that what is avyaya—undecaying—can still be bound. Bondage is not damage to the Self’s essence; it is constraint of the embodied through qualitative modes. Sattva, rajas, and tamas are not moral teams first; they are ontological straps. This is why moralism alone fails: you can “be good” in a sattvic way and remain tightly bound. The Gītā’s psychology is cosmological; your moods are not merely private weather but expressions of prakṛti’s strands. Existentially, this explains why insight alone does not free: the straps are affective-behavioral climates, not mere opinions. The dehin remains imperishable while living as if perishable under guṇa-bondage. Freedom begins when binding is correctly named as binding, not as identity. Naming the straps correctly is already a sattvic act—so long as one does not cling to the naming as a new identity.

### Key Terms
**guṇa (गुण)** — strand / quality -> constitutive mode of prakṛti that binds -> 'quality' as adjective misses binding force.
**nibadhnanti (निबध्नन्ति)** — they bind -> active fastening of the embodied to body -> 'influence' softens captivity.
**dehin (देहिन्)** — embodied one -> the one possessing a body, imperishable yet bindable -> 'soul' can float free of embodiment.
**avyaya (अव्यय)** — imperishable -> undecaying subject of bondage -> 'eternal soul' can sound immune in the wrong way.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Sāṃkhya Kārikā 12–14]:** Tripartite guṇa theory is the direct structural ancestor.
*Divergence:* Classical Sāṃkhya aims at puruṣa’s isolation; the Gītā will teach transcendence into divine being through non-attachment and bhakti.
**[Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics on hexeis]:** Enduring dispositions shaping action parallel guṇa climates.
*Divergence:* Aristotelian ethics seeks virtuous mean; guṇas are cosmological binders before they are character styles.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
For one day, when you feel 'stuck,' ask: 'Which climate is binding me—clarity-attachment, restless drive, or dull concealment?' Name it without fixing it yet.

---

## How Each Guṇa Binds
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.6–14.8

Among them, sattva, being stainless, is luminous and healthy; it binds through attachment to joy and attachment to knowledge, O sinless one. Know rajas to be of the nature of passion, arising from thirst and attachment; it binds the embodied one through attachment to action, O son of Kuntī. Know tamas, born of ignorance, as the deluder of all embodied beings; it binds through negligence, indolence, and sleep, O Bhārata.

---

### Devanagari
तत्र सत्त्वं निर्मलत्वात्प्रकाशकमनामयम्।सुखसङ्गेन बध्नाति ज्ञानसङ्गेन चानघ
रजो रागात्मकं विद्धि तृष्णासङ्गसमुद्भवम्।तन्निबध्नाति कौन्तेय कर्मसङ्गेन देहिनम्
तमस्त्वज्ञानजं विद्धि मोहनं सर्वदेहिनाम्।प्रमादालस्यनिद्राभिस्तन्निबध्नाति भारत

### IAST
tatra sattvaṃ nirmalatvātprakāśakamanāmayam|sukhasaṅgena badhnāti jñānasaṅgena cānagha
rajo rāgātmakaṃ viddhi tṛṣṇāsaṅgasamudbhavam|tannibadhnāti kaunteya karmasaṅgena dehinam
tamastvajñānajaṃ viddhi mohanaṃ sarvadehinām|pramādālasyanidrābhistannibadhnāti bhārata

### Pratibha Translation
Among them, sattva, being stainless, is luminous and healthy; it binds through attachment to joy and attachment to knowledge, O sinless one. Know rajas to be of the nature of passion, arising from thirst and attachment; it binds the embodied one through attachment to action, O son of Kuntī. Know tamas, born of ignorance, as the deluder of all embodied beings; it binds through negligence, indolence, and sleep, O Bhārata.

### Pratibha Commentary
Each guṇa binds through what it makes lovable. Sattva binds by sukha-saṅga and jñāna-saṅga—attachment to joy and to knowing. The contested move is ruthless: even clarity and happiness are straps when clutched. Rajas binds through karma-saṅga, the addiction to doing born of thirst. Tamas binds through pramāda, ālasya, and nidrā—negligence, laziness, sleep—as forms of delusion. Spiritual culture often flees tamas and rajas into sattva, then worships luminous captivity as arrival. The Gītā refuses that bargain. In the sequence of the teaching, this triad prepares the later claim that transcendence is beyond all three, not an upgrade to the nicest strand. Existentially, watch what you defend most eloquently: if it is your calm, your insight, or your busy usefulness, you may be polishing a bind. Freedom is not upgrading your guṇa; it is seeing the binding mechanism in all three. The practical test is simple and severe: what happens when your favorite clarity is interrupted? If rage or despair follows, sattva was a strap.

### Key Terms
**sattva (सत्त्व)** — luminosity / purity-strand -> binds via joy-and-knowledge attachment -> 'goodness' moralizes a binder.
**rajas (रजस्)** — passion-strand -> binds via action-attachment -> 'energy' misses thirst-born compulsion.
**tamas (तमस्)** — darkness-strand -> binds via negligence, indolence, sleep -> 'laziness' shrinks cosmological delusion.
**saṅga (सङ्ग)** — attachment / adherence -> the actual strap within each guṇa -> 'liking' understates bondage.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Patañjali, YS II.3–9 (kleśas)]:** Afflictions that bind through attachment and ignorance parallel guṇa-binding.
*Divergence:* Kleśas are psychological; guṇas are also cosmic strands structuring rebirth.
**[Evagrius, eight thoughts]:** Passions that capture the monk resonate with rajas-tamas mechanisms; vainglory with sattvic binding.
*Divergence:* Evagrius aims at pure prayer; Krishna aims at guṇātīta freedom into divine being.
**[Zhuangzi on usefulness of useless]:** Suspicion of achievement-drive resonates with seeing rajas-binding.
*Divergence:* Zhuangzi dissolves fixed success metrics; the Gītā keeps a clear hierarchy toward transcendence of all three.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Catch one sattvic bind today (pride in insight or clinging to a calm mood). Soften the clutch while keeping the clarity.

---

## Dominance, Rotation, and the Signs of Sattva
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.9–14.11

Sattva causes attachment to joy, rajas to action, O Bhārata; but tamas, veiling knowledge, causes attachment to negligence. Sattva arises by overpowering rajas and tamas; rajas by overpowering sattva and tamas; likewise tamas by overpowering sattva and rajas. When light dawns through all the gates of this body, and knowledge as well—then one should know that sattva has increased.

---

### Devanagari
सत्त्वं सुखे सञ्जयति रजः कर्मणि भारत।ज्ञानमावृत्य तु तमः प्रमादे सञ्जयत्युत
रजस्तमश्चाभिभूय सत्त्वं भवति भारत।रजः सत्त्वं तमश्चैव तमः सत्त्वं रजस्तथा
सर्वद्वारेषु देहेऽस्मिन्प्रकाश उपजायते।ज्ञानं यदा तदा विद्याद्विवृद्धं सत्त्वमित्युत

### IAST
sattvaṃ sukhe sañjayati rajaḥ karmaṇi bhārata|jñānamāvṛtya tu tamaḥ pramāde sañjayatyuta
rajastamaścābhibhūya sattvaṃ bhavati bhārata|rajaḥ sattvaṃ tamaścaiva tamaḥ sattvaṃ rajastathā
sarvadvāreṣu dehe'sminprakāśa upajāyate|jñānaṃ yadā tadā vidyādvivṛddhaṃ sattvamityuta

### Pratibha Translation
Sattva causes attachment to joy, rajas to action, O Bhārata; but tamas, veiling knowledge, causes attachment to negligence. Sattva arises by overpowering rajas and tamas; rajas by overpowering sattva and tamas; likewise tamas by overpowering sattva and rajas. When light dawns through all the gates of this body, and knowledge as well—then one should know that sattva has increased.

### Pratibha Commentary
Guṇas are dynamic, not fixed personality tattoos. Each prevails by overpowering the others. Sattva attaches to joy, rajas to action, tamas—by veiling knowledge—to negligence. The diagnostic for rising sattva is concrete: prakāśa through all gates of the body, and jñāna dawning. The contested claim is that the body itself telegraphs ontology: luminous sense-doors are not merely good mood; they are evidence of sattva’s increase. This makes contemplative life empirical without becoming medicalized. You learn to read gates, not to obsess over labels. Existentially, this trains honest weather-reading without fatalism: climates rotate, and recognition is already a form of freedom’s beginning. When light increases, gratitude is appropriate; clutching the light as identity returns you to sattvic bondage named in the previous verses. Rotation also means compassion: the person lost in tamas today may stand in sattva tomorrow; contempt freezes a moving climate into a false essence. This is not ornamental theology; it is a demand that lived climate, ethical stance, and metaphysical claim stay braided in one practice of seeing.

### Key Terms
**sañjayati (सञ्जयति)** — causes to cling / attaches -> guṇa as binder to a domain -> 'leads to' is too mild.
**abhibhūya (अभिभूय)** — having overpowered -> rotational dominance among guṇas -> 'balance' wrongly implies stable equilibrium.
**sarva-dvāreṣu (सर्वद्वारेषु)** — in all gates -> sense-doors of the body as sites of light -> 'everywhere' misses embodied gates.
**prakāśa (प्रकाश)** — light / illumination -> sign of increased sattva -> 'happiness' conflates mood with luminosity.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Abhidharma / vipassanā mind-state diagnosis]:** Reading present qualities through signs parallels guṇa diagnostics.
*Divergence:* Buddhist reading aims at impermanence and non-self; here signs point to guṇa dominance and eventual transcendence.
**[Galenic temperaments]:** Humor climates shaping behavior are a loose Western cousin.
*Divergence:* Humors are medical; guṇas are soteriological binders tied to rebirth and liberation.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Three times today, scan the 'gates' of the body. If light and knowing are present, note 'sattva rising' without clinging to it.

---

## Signs of Rajas and Tamas, and Death in Sattva
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.12–14.14

Greed, activity, undertaking of actions, unrest, and longing arise when rajas increases, O best of Bharatas. Darkness, inactivity, negligence, and delusion arise when tamas increases, O joy of the Kurus. When the embodied one dies while sattva is dominant, then he attains the stainless worlds of those who know the highest.

---

### Devanagari
लोभः प्रवृत्तिरारम्भः कर्मणामशमः स्पृहा।रजस्येतानि जायन्ते विवृद्धे भरतर्षभ
अप्रकाशोऽप्रवृत्तिश्च प्रमादो मोह एव च।तमस्येतानि जायन्ते विवृद्धे कुरुनन्दन
यदा सत्त्वे प्रवृद्धे तु प्रलयं याति देहभृत्।तदोत्तमविदां लोकानमलान्प्रतिपद्यते

### IAST
lobhaḥ pravṛttirārambhaḥ karmaṇāmaśamaḥ spṛhā|rajasyetāni jāyante vivṛddhe bharatarṣabha
aprakāśo'pravṛttiśca pramādo moha eva ca|tamasyetāni jāyante vivṛddhe kurunandana
yadā sattve pravṛddhe tu pralayaṃ yāti dehabhṛt|tadottamavidāṃ lokānamalānpratipadyate

### Pratibha Translation
Greed, activity, undertaking of actions, unrest, and longing arise when rajas increases, O best of Bharatas. Darkness, inactivity, negligence, and delusion arise when tamas increases, O joy of the Kurus. When the embodied one dies while sattva is dominant, then he attains the stainless worlds of those who know the highest.

### Pratibha Commentary
Behavioral signatures clarify the climates: rajas shows as greed, initiation-fever, unrest, craving; tamas as darkness, non-activity, negligence, delusion. Then the chapter raises the stakes to death: dying in sattva yields stainless worlds of the highest knowers. The contested move is to treat the dying climate as decisive without reducing life to deathbed panic. One’s cultivated predominance at the end expresses a trajectory already rehearsed in ordinary days. Classical readers hear continuity between living practice and dying fruition; modern readers can hear a demand for honesty about the climate you feed. Existentially, this is not superstition; it is continuity: the weather you rehearse becomes the world you inherit. The teaching does not ask for perfection at the last minute; it asks for long apprenticeship in luminosity without making luminosity your prison. Therefore daily rehearsal matters more than emergency spirituality: the dying mind continues the groove already cut by living preference. This is not ornamental theology; it is a demand that lived climate, ethical stance, and metaphysical claim stay braided in one practice of seeing.

### Key Terms
**lobha (लोभ)** — greed -> rajasic signature -> 'ambition' can romanticize the same bind.
**aprakāśa (अप्रकाश)** — non-light / darkness -> tamasic signature -> 'confusion' is narrower than ontological darkening.
**pralaya (प्रलय)** — dissolution / death here as body's end -> transition keyed to guṇa dominance -> 'death' alone misses climate-continuity.
**amalān lokān (अमलान् लोकान्)** — stainless worlds -> sattvic postmortem fruition -> 'heaven' may import alien geography.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Tibetan bardos / dying awareness teachings]:** State at death shaping next arising is structurally homologous.
*Divergence:* Bardo teachings detail transitional visions; the Gītā compresses into guṇa predominance and world-attainment.
**[Plato, Phaedo]:** Philosophical life preparing a good death resonates with dying in sattva.
*Divergence:* Phaedo seeks pure soul freed from body; Krishna keeps guṇa cosmology and multiple postmortem tracks.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Ask once today: 'If this climate solidified, what world would it imply?' Let the answer sober your next indulgence of rajas or tamas.

---

## Fruits of the Guṇas
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.15–14.17

Dying in rajas, one is born among those attached to action; likewise, dying in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded. They say the fruit of good action is sattvic and stainless; the fruit of rajas is pain; the fruit of tamas is ignorance. From sattva, knowledge is born; from rajas, greed; from tamas arise negligence and delusion, and ignorance as well.

---

### Devanagari
रजसि प्रलयं गत्वा कर्मसङ्गिषु जायते।तथा प्रलीनस्तमसि मूढयोनिषु जायते
कर्मणः सुकृतस्याहुः सात्त्विकं निर्मलं फलम्।रजसस्तु फलं दुःखमज्ञानं तमसः फलम्
सत्त्वात्सञ्जायते ज्ञानं रजसो लोभ एव च।प्रमादमोहौ तमसो भवतोऽज्ञानमेव च

### IAST
rajasi pralayaṃ gatvā karmasaṅgiṣu jāyate|tathā pralīnastamasi mūḍhayoniṣu jāyate
karmaṇaḥ sukṛtasyāhuḥ sāttvikaṃ nirmalaṃ phalam|rajasastu phalaṃ duḥkhamajñānaṃ tamasaḥ phalam
sattvātsañjāyate jñānaṃ rajaso lobha eva ca|pramādamohau tamaso bhavato'jñānameva ca

### Pratibha Translation
Dying in rajas, one is born among those attached to action; likewise, dying in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded. They say the fruit of good action is sattvic and stainless; the fruit of rajas is pain; the fruit of tamas is ignorance. From sattva, knowledge is born; from rajas, greed; from tamas arise negligence and delusion, and ignorance as well.

### Pratibha Commentary
Postmortem destinations and present fruits are braided. Rajas leads to birth among karma-saṅgins; tamas into deluded wombs. Action’s fruit: sattvic stainlessness, rajasic pain, tamasic ignorance. Causally inverted and reinforced: sattva births knowledge, rajas greed, tamas negligence-delusion-ignorance. The contested claim is moral cosmology without cheap moralism—pain is not random punishment but rajas’s own yield. Ignorance is not an insult; it is tamas ripening. This loop explains why “trying harder” in a rajasic key often deepens pain, and why tamasic comfort deepens fog. Existentially, you can taste fruits now: the aftertaste of your actions already announces their guṇa. Liberation pedagogy uses that aftertaste as teacher before death makes the climate harder to revise. Watch especially the fruit that flatters you—stainlessness can intoxicate—and the fruit that shames you; both are teachers if not clutched. This is not ornamental theology; it is a demand that lived climate, ethical stance, and metaphysical claim stay braided in one practice of seeing.

### Key Terms
**karmasaṅgi (कर्मसङ्गि)** — one attached to action -> rajasic rebirth niche -> 'workaholic' shrinks the ontological claim.
**mūḍha-yoni (मूढयोनि)** — deluded womb -> tamasic birth matrix -> 'bad reincarnation' as cartoon misses epistemic darkness.
**phala (फल)** — fruit -> intrinsic yield of guṇa-shaped action -> 'reward/punishment' externalizes what is ripening.
**ajñāna (अज्ञान)** — ignorance -> tamas’s fruit and offspring -> 'not knowing facts' understates delusive closure.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Karma theory in Manu / Dharmaśāstra]:** Action-fruit continuity resonates, but here fruit is guṇa-coded.
*Divergence:* Dharmaśāstra often maps social duty; the Gītā maps psychological-cosmological ripening toward liberation.
**[Stoic doctrine of consequences in character]:** Actions shape the agent who then inherits their world.
*Divergence:* Stoicism centers assent and virtue; guṇa theory centers qualitative binders and rebirth.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
After one significant action today, taste its fruit immediately: stainless clarity, agitated pain, or fog. Name the guṇa of the fruit.

## Rising, Standing, Falling—and Seeing Beyond the Doer
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.18–14.20

Those established in sattva go upward; the rajasic remain in the middle; those established in the lowest guṇa-activity go downward. When the seer sees no doer other than the guṇas, and knows what is beyond the guṇas, he attains My being. Having transcended these three guṇas that arise from the body, the embodied one, freed from birth, death, age, and pain, tastes immortality.

---

### Devanagari
ऊर्ध्वं गच्छन्ति सत्त्वस्था मध्ये तिष्ठन्ति राजसाः।जघन्यगुणवृत्तिस्था अधो गच्छन्ति तामसाः
नान्यं गुणेभ्यः कर्तारं यदा द्रष्टानुपश्यति।गुणेभ्यश्च परं वेत्ति मद्भावं सोऽधिगच्छति
गुणानेतानतीत्य त्रीन्देही देहसमुद्भवान्।जन्ममृत्युजरादुःखैर्विमुक्तोऽमृतमश्नुते

### IAST
ūrdhvaṃ gacchanti sattvasthā madhye tiṣṭhanti rājasāḥ|jaghanyaguṇavṛttisthā adho gacchanti tāmasāḥ
nānyaṃ guṇebhyaḥ kartāraṃ yadā draṣṭānupaśyati|guṇebhyaśca paraṃ vetti madbhāvaṃ so'dhigacchati
guṇānetānatītya trīndehī dehasamudbhavān|janmamṛtyujarāduḥkhairvimukto'mṛtamaśnute

### Pratibha Translation
Those established in sattva go upward; the rajasic remain in the middle; those established in the lowest guṇa-activity go downward. When the seer sees no doer other than the guṇas, and knows what is beyond the guṇas, he attains My being. Having transcended these three guṇas that arise from the body, the embodied one, freed from birth, death, age, and pain, tastes immortality.

### Pratibha Commentary
Trajectory language becomes vertical: sattva upward, rajas middle, tamas downward. Then the decisive philosophical cut: the seer who sees no doer apart from the guṇas, and knows what is beyond them, attains madbhāva—Krishna’s being. Transcending the three yields immortality beyond birth-death-age-pain. The contested move is non-doership without nihilism: guṇas act; the seer knows the beyond. This is not permission for irresponsibility; it is the end of the fantasy that a separate ego authors the strands. In the Gītā’s theistic frame, seeing beyond the guṇas is not blank neutrality; it opens into divine being. Existentially, freedom is not becoming a better guṇa-bundle; it is seeing agency correctly and tasting the deathless while life continues. Madbhāva keeps the teaching from collapsing into blank witnessing: beyond the guṇas is not nowhere; it is kinship with the Lord. This is not ornamental theology; it is a demand that lived climate, ethical stance, and metaphysical claim stay braided in one practice of seeing.

### Key Terms
**ūrdhvam / madhye / adhaḥ (ऊर्ध्वम् / मध्ये / अधः)** — up / middle / down -> guṇa trajectories -> 'social mobility' parody misses cosmic psychology.
**draṣṭā (द्रष्टा)** — seer -> one who sees guṇas as sole doers -> 'observer' can sound detached in a clinical way.
**guṇātīta (गुणातीत)** — beyond the guṇas -> transcendence of the three binders -> 'above good and evil' can sound antinomian.
**amṛta (अमृत)** — immortality / deathless nectar -> fruit of transcending guṇas -> 'afterlife' postpones present tasting.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 3.27–28]:** Guṇas act among guṇas; the knower is not entangled—direct continuity.
*Divergence:* Chapter 3 emphasizes karma-yoga; chapter 14 thematizes transcendence into divine being.
**[Plotinus on rising above lower soul motions]:** Ascent beyond turbulent psychic modes resonates.
*Divergence:* Plotinus ascends toward the One; Krishna names attainment as madbhāva, personal-divine kinship.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
In one action today, watch the guṇas doing. Silently: 'No doer other than the strands—and there is the beyond.' Rest one breath in the beyond.

---

## Marks of One Who Has Gone Beyond
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.21–14.23

Arjuna said: By what marks is the one who has gone beyond these three guṇas known, O Lord? How does he conduct himself, and how does he transcend these three guṇas? The Blessed Lord said: Light, activity, and delusion alike—he does not hate them when they arise, O son of Pāṇḍu, nor longs for them when they cease. Seated as if indifferent, unmoved by the guṇas, he stands firm, knowing 'the guṇas alone are operating,' and does not waver.

---

### Devanagari
अर्जुन उवाचकैर्लिंगैस्त्रीन्गुणानेतानतीतो भवति प्रभो।किमाचारः कथं चैतांस्त्रीन्गुणानतिवर्तते
श्री भगवानुवाचप्रकाशं च प्रवृत्तिं च मोहमेव च पाण्डव।न द्वेष्टि सम्प्रवृत्तानि न निवृत्तानि काङ्क्षति
उदासीनवदासीनो गुणैर्यो न विचाल्यते।गुणा वर्तन्त इत्येव योऽवतिष्ठति नेङ्गते

### IAST
arjuna uvācakairliṃgaistrīnguṇānetānatīto bhavati prabho|kimācāraḥ kathaṃ caitāṃstrīnguṇānativartate
śrī bhagavānuvācaprakāśaṃ ca pravṛttiṃ ca mohameva ca pāṇḍava|na dveṣṭi sampravṛttāni na nivṛttāni kāṅkṣati
udāsīnavadāsīno guṇairyo na vicālyate|guṇā vartanta ityeva yo'vatiṣṭhati neṅgate

### Pratibha Translation
Arjuna said: By what marks is the one who has gone beyond these three guṇas known, O Lord? How does he conduct himself, and how does he transcend these three guṇas? The Blessed Lord said: Light, activity, and delusion alike—he does not hate them when they arise, O son of Pāṇḍu, nor longs for them when they cease. Seated as if indifferent, unmoved by the guṇas, he stands firm, knowing 'the guṇas alone are operating,' and does not waver.

### Pratibha Commentary
Arjuna asks for liṅgas—marks—and ācāra—conduct—of the guṇātīta. Krishna answers with non-reactivity across all three climates: he neither hates prakāśa, pravṛtti, and moha when they arise nor craves them when they cease. The contested image is udāsīnavad āsīnaḥ—seated as if indifferent—not numb, but unthrown. Knowing 'guṇā vartante'—the guṇas operate—he does not waver. This is the practical face of the previous metaphysics: if guṇas are the doers, hatred of a climate is still entanglement, and craving for a climate is still bondage. Existentially, transcendence looks like weather literacy without weather worship or weather war. The mark is not a costume of calm; it is unmoved intimacy with rising and ceasing alike. If you still need a particular mood to feel spiritual, you have not yet sat 'as if indifferent'; you have only switched allegiances among the strands. This is not ornamental theology; it is a demand that lived climate, ethical stance, and metaphysical claim stay braided in one practice of seeing.

### Key Terms
**liṅga (लिङ्ग)** — mark / sign -> recognizable traits of the transcender -> 'symptom' medicalizes liberation.
**udāsīna (उदासीन)** — seated as if aside / indifferent -> poised non-entanglement -> 'apathetic' is the failure mode of the translation.
**neṅgate (नेङ्गते)** — does not stir / waver -> stability amid guṇa rotation -> 'rigid' misreads as stiffness.
**guṇā vartante (गुणा वर्तन्ते)** — the guṇas operate -> mantra of non-doership -> 'stuff happens' is cynical counterfeit.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Patañjali, YS I.16 / para-vairāgya]:** Dispassion even toward the highest sattvic attainments resonates.
*Divergence:* Patañjali aims at aloneness of the seer; Krishna’s transcender is en route to unswerving bhakti (14.26).
**[Stoic phantasia and non-assent]:** Not being dragged by appearances parallels non-hate/non-craving toward guṇa-states.
*Divergence:* Stoicism trains rational assent; here the key cognition is 'guṇas alone operate.'

### Practice (Abhyasa)
When a mood arises or fades, practice the double refusal: do not hate its arrival; do not clutch its departure. Whisper: 'the guṇas operate.'

## Evenness That Names the Guṇātīta
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.24–14.25

Alike in pain and pleasure, self-abiding; regarding a clod, a stone, and gold as equal; the same toward liked and disliked, steadfast; the same in censure and praise of himself; the same in honor and dishonor; the same toward friend and foe parties; abandoning all undertakings—he is called one who has gone beyond the guṇas.

---

### Devanagari
समदुःखसुखः स्वस्थः समलोष्टाश्मकाञ्चनः।तुल्यप्रियाप्रियो धीरस्तुल्यनिन्दात्मसंस्तुतिः
मानापमानयोस्तुल्यस्तुल्यो मित्रारिपक्षयोः।सर्वारम्भपरित्यागी गुणातीतः स उच्यते

### IAST
samaduḥkhasukhaḥ svasthaḥ samaloṣṭāśmakāñcanaḥ|tulyapriyāpriyo dhīrastulyanindātmasaṃstutiḥ
mānāpamānayostulyastulyo mitrāripakṣayoḥ|sarvārambhaparityāgī guṇātītaḥ sa ucyate

### Pratibha Translation
Alike in pain and pleasure, self-abiding; regarding a clod, a stone, and gold as equal; the same toward liked and disliked, steadfast; the same in censure and praise of himself; the same in honor and dishonor; the same toward friend and foe parties; abandoning all undertakings—he is called one who has gone beyond the guṇas.

### Pratibha Commentary
The marks become a radical evenness: pain/pleasure, clod/stone/gold, dear/undear, blame/praise, honor/dishonor, friend-side/enemy-side. Sarvārambha-parityāgī—abandoning all egoic undertakings—completes the portrait. The contested claim is that equality is not flattened affect but freedom from guṇa-polarized valuation. Gold and clod differ conventionally; they do not differ as claimants on the Self. Friend and foe parties differ in the field; they do not own the knower. Existentially, this is training for a life not run by status meteorology. The renunciation of undertakings is not anti-work; it is anti-identity-project. When beginnings are no longer needed to prove the self, action can become clean—or fall silent—without panic. Evenness toward friend and foe parties is especially exacting in conflict: it does not deny justice; it denies possession of the Self by the party. This is not ornamental theology; it is a demand that lived climate, ethical stance, and metaphysical claim stay braided in one practice of seeing. This is not ornamental theology; it is a demand that lived climate, ethical stance, and metaphysical claim stay braided in one practice of seeing.

### Key Terms
**sama (सम)** — equal / even -> cross-polarity stability -> 'egalitarian politics' misses contemplative evenness.
**svastha (स्वस्थ)** — abiding in one’s own being -> self-restedness amid dualities -> 'self-confident' is a counterfeit.
**sarvārambha-parityāgī (सर्वारम्भपरित्यागी)** — renouncer of all undertakings -> dropping ego-initiated projects as identity -> 'lazy' is the parody.
**guṇātīta (गुणातीत)** — beyond the guṇas -> the one so even is so named -> 'transcendent person' can sound mythic rather than practical.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 2.56–57 / 12.18–19]:** Evenness toward dualities is a continuous Gītā signature.
*Divergence:* Earlier chapters link evenness to buddhi-yoga and bhakti traits; here it specifically indexes guṇa-transcendence.
**[Pyrrhonian ataraxia]:** Suspension amid conflicting valuations loosely resonates.
*Divergence:* Pyrrhonism suspends judgment for tranquility; Krishna’s evenness knows the guṇas and moves toward devotion.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Pick one polarity you obsess over (praise/blame or gain/loss). For twenty-four hours, practice sama: feel the wave, refuse the verdict.

## Unswerving Devotion Crosses the Guṇas
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.26

The one who serves Me with the yoga of devotion that does not stray crosses beyond these guṇas and becomes fit for becoming Brahman.

---

### Devanagari
मां च योऽव्यभिचारेण भक्ितयोगेन सेवते।स गुणान्समतीत्यैतान् ब्रह्मभूयाय कल्पते

### IAST
māṃ ca yo'vyabhicāreṇa bhakitayogena sevate|sa guṇānsamatītyaitān brahmabhūyāya kalpate

### Pratibha Translation
The one who serves Me with the yoga of devotion that does not stray crosses beyond these guṇas and becomes fit for becoming Brahman.

### Pratibha Commentary
Transcendence is not a DIY heroics of indifference. The one who serves Krishna with avyabhicāreṇa bhakti-yogena crosses the guṇas and becomes fit for brahma-bhūya—becoming Brahman. The contested move stitches bhakti into guṇa theory: love that does not stray is the ferry beyond qualitative bondage. Evenness without devotion can become sterile spectatorship; devotion without evenness can become another rajasic project. Together they ripen fitness for Brahman-being. In the chapter’s logic, this verse prevents a cold reading of guṇātīta as mere aloofness. Existentially, service becomes the way the transcender stays human and warm while unbound. The question is not “Have I achieved indifference?” but “Is my yoga of love still taking side doors?” Unstraying means the heart has one refuge even while the guṇas continue their weather in the body-field. This is not ornamental theology; it is a demand that lived climate, ethical stance, and metaphysical claim stay braided in one practice of seeing.

### Key Terms
**avyabhicāreṇa (अव्यभिचारेण)** — without straying -> fidelity of devotion -> 'loyalty' can sound merely institutional.
**bhakti-yoga (भक्तियोग)** — yoga of devotion -> service as crossing-means -> 'faith practice' understates yogic crossing.
**brahma-bhūya (ब्रह्मभूय)** — becoming Brahman -> fitness for Brahman-state -> 'union with God' may blur this exact idiom.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 12’s unswerving devotee]:** Same fidelity language now explicitly guṇa-crossing.
*Divergence:* Chapter 12 ranks paths; 14.26 makes non-straying devotion the engine past the three strands.
**[Bernard of Clairvaux on ordered love]:** Love rightly ordered liberates from disordered attachments.
*Divergence:* Cistercian love orders to Christ; here devotion fits one for Brahman-being beyond guṇas.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Offer one ordinary act today as unstraying service—no side altar of image-management. Let that be your guṇa-crossing practice.

---

## I Am the Ground of Brahman
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 14.27

For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the deathless and the imperishable, of everlasting dharma, and of absolute bliss.

---

### Devanagari
ब्रह्मणो हि प्रतिष्ठाऽहममृतस्याव्ययस्य च।शाश्वतस्य च धर्मस्य सुखस्यैकान्तिकस्य च

### IAST
brahmaṇo hi pratiṣṭhā'hamamṛtasyāvyayasya ca|śāśvatasya ca dharmasya sukhasyaikāntikasya ca

### Pratibha Translation
For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the deathless and the imperishable, of everlasting dharma, and of absolute bliss.

### Pratibha Commentary
The chapter’s final thunder: Krishna is the pratiṣṭhā—foundation—of Brahman, of the deathless and the imperishable, of everlasting dharma, and of aikāntika sukha—final, unalloyed joy. The contested claim is theistic grounding of the Absolute: Brahman is not bypassing Krishna; Krishna is Brahman’s ground. This blocks an escape hatch into impersonalism that abandons love, and blocks a piety that never tastes the deathless. It also reinterprets sattvic joy: guṇa-sukha was a bind; aikāntika sukha is grounded in the Lord. Existentially, the highest knowledge ends not in a diagram of strands but in a person who is the ground of the Absolute, of dharma, and of joy that does not trade on the guṇas. Refuge becomes metaphysical realism, not sentiment. To say Krishna is Brahman’s foundation is to refuse choosing between love and the Absolute; the Absolute is loved as ground. This is not ornamental theology; it is a demand that lived climate, ethical stance, and metaphysical claim stay braided in one practice of seeing.

### Key Terms
**pratiṣṭhā (प्रतिष्ठा)** — foundation / resting-place -> Krishna as ground of Brahman -> 'support' is too architectural-external.
**amṛta / avyaya (अमृत / अव्यय)** — deathless / imperishable -> grounded in Krishna -> 'eternity' can stay abstract.
**śāśvata dharma (शाश्वत धर्म)** — everlasting dharma -> grounded in the Lord -> 'religion' domesticates the claim.
**aikāntika sukha (ऐकान्तिक सुख)** — absolute / exclusive joy -> final bliss beyond guṇa-sukha -> 'happiness' is far too thin.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 7.7 / 10.8]:** Krishna as source and origin of all resonates with pratiṣṭhā of Brahman.
*Divergence:* Those chapters emphasize manifestation and vibhūti; 14.27 explicitly grounds Brahman, dharma, and absolute joy.
**[Rāmānuja’s viśiṣṭādvaita reading]:** The personal Lord as ground of Brahman is theologically decisive here.
*Divergence:* Non-dual readings stress identity; the verse’s 'I am the foundation' preserves a theistic asymmetry productive for devotion.
**[Pseudo-Dionysius on God as cause of being and good]:** Ground of deathless reality and joy resonates.
*Divergence:* Dionysius proceeds by ascent and negation; Krishna speaks as the foundation in first person to a friend in war.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Sit quietly and contemplate: 'The ground of the deathless and of joy is not a mood—it is the Lord.' Rest the mind there without argument.



**Corpus entry:** Bhagavad Gītā / Mahābhārata
**Units:** 10 (one per brief CHUNK)

## The Inverted Tree of Becoming
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 15.1

The Blessed Lord said: They speak of an eternal aśvattha tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns. Whoever knows it is a knower of the Veda.

---

### Devanagari
श्री भगवानुवाचऊर्ध्वमूलमधःशाखमश्वत्थं प्राहुरव्ययम्।छन्दांसि यस्य पर्णानि यस्तं वेद स वेदवित्

### IAST
śrī bhagavānuvācaūrdhvamūlamadhaḥśākhamaśvatthaṃ prāhuravyayam|chandāṃsi yasya parṇāni yastaṃ veda sa vedavit

### Pratibha Translation
The Blessed Lord said: They speak of an eternal aśvattha tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns. Whoever knows it is a knower of the Veda.

### Pratibha Commentary
The cosmos is imaged as an inverted sacred fig: roots above, branches below, leaves as Vedic chants. The contested move is epistemological and cosmological at once. Ordinary perception roots the world in the visible below; Krishna roots it in the unseen above. To know this tree is to be vedavit—not a technician of ritual sound, but one who understands what the hymns themselves are leaves of. The aśvattha is avyaya, enduring as saṃsāric process, yet knowable as a structure that can later be cut. Existentially, the verse asks whether you live as if meaning rises from sensory branches, or as if the nourishing root is above. The battlefield’s confusion is a canopy problem: too many leaves, forgotten root. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine.

### Key Terms
**aśvattha (अश्वत्थ)** — sacred fig / 'that which does not stand tomorrow' -> saṃsāra-tree -> 'world-tree' loses the name’s instability hint.
**ūrdhva-mūla (ऊर्ध्वमूल)** — root above -> transcendent sourceward orientation -> 'upside-down' as quirky image misses metaphysics.
**chandāṃsi (छन्दांसि)** — meters/Vedic hymns as leaves -> revelation as foliage of the tree -> 'poetry' understates liturgical cosmology.
**vedavit (वेदवित्)** — knower of Veda -> one who knows this tree -> 'scripture scholar' can miss the ontological knowing.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Kaṭha Upaniṣad II.3.1]:** The inverted aśvattha is near-direct source homology.
*Divergence:* Kaṭha emphasizes Brahman beyond; the Gītā will weaponize non-attachment as the axe.
**[Plato, cave allegory]:** Reversing the apparent source of reality resonates structurally.
*Divergence:* Plato ascends to forms; Krishna maps a cuttable tree of becoming.
**[Yggdrasil / world-tree myths]:** Cosmic tree as world-structure is cross-cultural.
*Divergence:* Those myths often stabilize cosmos; here the tree is to be known in order to be felled.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Visualize your worries as leaves. Ask once: 'Where is the root—below in events, or above?' Rest attention rootward for three minutes.

## Branches Everywhere, Axe of Non-Attachment
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 15.2–15.4

Its branches spread below and above, nourished by the guṇas, with sense-objects as twigs; and below, the roots extend into the world of humans, binding through action. Its form is not perceived here as such—no end, no beginning, no foundation. Having cut this deeply rooted aśvattha with the strong axe of non-attachment, one should then seek that goal from which, having gone, one does not return again, saying: 'I take refuge in that primal person from whom the ancient current streamed forth.'

---

### Devanagari
अधश्चोर्ध्वं प्रसृतास्तस्य शाखा     गुणप्रवृद्धा विषयप्रवालाः।अधश्च मूलान्यनुसन्ततानि     कर्मानुबन्धीनि मनुष्यलोके
न रूपमस्येह तथोपलभ्यते    नान्तो न चादिर्न च संप्रतिष्ठा।अश्वत्थमेनं सुविरूढमूल    मसङ्गशस्त्रेण दृढेन छित्त्वा
ततः पदं तत्परिमार्गितव्यम्

यस्मिन्गता न निवर्तन्ति भूयः।

तमेव चाद्यं पुरुषं प्रपद्ये

यतः प्रवृत्तिः प्रसृता पुराणी

### IAST
adhaścordhvaṃ prasṛtāstasya śākhā     guṇapravṛddhā viṣayapravālāḥ|adhaśca mūlānyanusantatāni     karmānubandhīni manuṣyaloke
na rūpamasyeha tathopalabhyate    nānto na cādirna ca saṃpratiṣṭhā|aśvatthamenaṃ suvirūḍhamūla    masaṅgaśastreṇa dṛḍhena chittvā
tataḥ padaṃ tatparimārgitavyam

yasmingatā na nivartanti bhūyaḥ|

tameva cādyaṃ puruṣaṃ prapadye

yataḥ pravṛttiḥ prasṛtā purāṇī

### Pratibha Translation
Its branches spread below and above, nourished by the guṇas, with sense-objects as twigs; and below, the roots extend into the world of humans, binding through action. Its form is not perceived here as such—no end, no beginning, no foundation. Having cut this deeply rooted aśvattha with the strong axe of non-attachment, one should then seek that goal from which, having gone, one does not return again, saying: 'I take refuge in that primal person from whom the ancient current streamed forth.'

### Pratibha Commentary
The tree thickens: guṇa-fed branches, sense-object shoots, and downward roots binding humans through karma. Yet its form cannot be grasped as a finished object—no end, beginning, or foundation available to ordinary seeing. The contested instruction is violent and precise: cut it with asaṅga-śastra, the axe of non-attachment, then seek the irreversible goal and take refuge in the primal person. Knowledge of the tree is not botanical tourism; it is preparatory to cutting and refuge. Existentially, non-attachment is not mood; it is a blade. Without refuge after the cut, one merely becomes homeless among falling leaves. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**asaṅga-śastra (असङ्गशस्त्र)** — weapon/axe of non-attachment -> cutting tool against the world-tree -> 'detachment' as vibe misses the blade.
**karmānubandhīni (कर्मानुबन्धीनि)** — binding through action -> downward roots in human world -> 'consequences' softens bondage.
**pada (पद)** — goal/standing-place -> that from which there is no return -> 'state' is too vague.
**prapadye (प्रपद्ये)** — I take refuge -> first-person surrender to the primal person -> 'believe in' is thinner than refuge.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 15.1 continuity with Kaṭha]:** Same tree, now explicitly cuttable by non-attachment.
*Divergence:* The Gītā adds karma-roots and explicit śaraṇa language.
**[John of the Cross, detachment]:** Cutting creaturely cling for God resonates.
*Divergence:* John’s nights are interior purification; Krishna’s axe follows a cosmological tree map.
**[Nagarjuna / pruning false establishments]:** Undoing falsely founded structures loosely parallels cutting the tree.
*Divergence:* Madhyamaka empties inherent existence; here one seeks a positive irreversible pada.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Name one clinging that feeds your tree. Practice one concrete cut today (a refusal), then immediately take refuge in the primal person for one minute.

## The Undying Place Beyond Sun and Fire
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 15.5–15.6

Without pride and delusion, having conquered the defect of attachment, constantly abiding in the Self, with desires turned away, freed from dualities called pleasure and pain—the undeluded go to that imperishable goal. That abode of Mine the sun does not light, nor the moon, nor fire; having gone there, they do not return. That is My supreme home.

---

### Devanagari
निर्मानमोहा जितसङ्गदोषा    अध्यात्मनित्या विनिवृत्तकामाः।द्वन्द्वैर्विमुक्ताः सुखदुःखसंज्ञै    र्गच्छन्त्यमूढाः पदमव्ययं तत्
न तद्भासयते सूर्यो न शशाङ्को न पावकः।यद्गत्वा न निवर्तन्ते तद्धाम परमं मम

### IAST
nirmānamohā jitasaṅgadoṣā    adhyātmanityā vinivṛttakāmāḥ|dvandvairvimuktāḥ sukhaduḥkhasaṃjñai    rgacchantyamūḍhāḥ padamavyayaṃ tat
na tadbhāsayate sūryo na śaśāṅko na pāvakaḥ|yadgatvā na nivartante taddhāma paramaṃ mama

### Pratibha Translation
Without pride and delusion, having conquered the defect of attachment, constantly abiding in the Self, with desires turned away, freed from dualities called pleasure and pain—the undeluded go to that imperishable goal. That abode of Mine the sun does not light, nor the moon, nor fire; having gone there, they do not return. That is My supreme home.

### Pratibha Commentary
The path-qualifications are listed as a single compound life: free of pride-delusion, attachment conquered, Self-abiding, desires quieted, freed from pleasure-pain dualities. Then the goal is imaged as Krishna’s supreme dhāman, which sun, moon, and fire do not illuminate. The contested claim is that the highest abode is not another lit object in the cosmos; it is the lighting-source beyond cosmic lamps. Non-return (na nivartante) seals irreversibility. Existentially, if your 'spiritual goals' still need the sun of status and the fire of intensity, you are still navigating branches. The supreme home is dark only to worldly lamps because it is too intimate to be their object. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**nir-māna-moha (निर्मानमोह)** — without pride and delusion -> purification before the goal -> 'humility' alone misses moha’s cognitive fog.
**padam avyayam (पदमव्ययम्)** — imperishable goal -> non-returning standing-place -> 'heaven' may mis-locate it.
**dhāman (धामन्)** — abode / home / light-sphere -> Krishna’s supreme dwelling -> 'place' can sound spatial-external.
**na nivartante (न निवर्तन्ते)** — they do not return -> irreversible liberation -> 'stay forever' can sound touristic.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Śvetāśvatara / Kaṭha light verses]:** Where sun/moon/fire do not shine is classic Upaniṣadic homology.
*Divergence:* The Gītā personalizes the abode as mama dhāma.
**[Pseudo-Dionysius, divine darkness]:** Beyond cosmic lights resonates with unknowing luminosity.
*Divergence:* Dionysius stresses negation; Krishna also lists ethical-yogic qualifications for entry.
**[Gītā 8.21]:** Non-returning supreme abode continues earlier teaching.
*Divergence:* Chapter 15 embeds it inside the tree-cutting sequence.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Sit in a darkened room. Contemplation: 'No sun, moon, or fire lights That.' Rest as the need for dramatic illumination softens.

## My Own Portion Become Living
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 15.7

A portion of Mine alone becomes the eternal living being in the world of the living, and draws to itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, that rest in nature.

---

### Devanagari
ममैवांशो जीवलोके जीवभूतः सनातनः।मनःषष्ठानीन्द्रियाणि प्रकृतिस्थानि कर्षति

### IAST
mamaivāṃśo jīvaloke jīvabhūtaḥ sanātanaḥ|manaḥṣaṣṭhānīndriyāṇi prakṛtisthāni karṣati

### Pratibha Translation
A portion of Mine alone becomes the eternal living being in the world of the living, and draws to itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, that rest in nature.

### Pratibha Commentary
The jīva is not an alien spark kidnapped by matter; it is mamaiva aṃśa—Krishna’s own portion—become living in the living world, eternal (sanātana). This portion draws the senses and mind (the sixth) that are stationed in prakṛti. The contested move is simultaneous intimacy and tension: you are the Lord’s portion, and you are the one yanking prakṛti’s instruments into a private drama. Bondage is not that an aṃśa exists; it is how it appropriates mind-senses. Existentially, this blocks both self-contempt and self-deification. You are not trash, and you are not the whole; you are a portion that can either clutch instruments or remember source. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**aṃśa (अंश)** — portion / share -> jīva as the Lord’s portion -> 'piece of God' can become crude pantheism.
**jīva-bhūta (जीवभूत)** — become a living being -> portion as embodied life -> 'soul incarnate' may smuggle foreign anthropology.
**karṣati (कर्षति)** — draws / drags -> appropriation of mind-senses -> 'uses' softens the dragging violence.
**manaḥ-ṣaṣṭha (मनःषष्ठ)** — mind as sixth -> mind grouped with senses as drawn instruments -> 'mind and five senses' as list misses the dragging.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 7.5 / 13.22]:** Jīva amid prakṛti continues the field-person analysis.
*Divergence:* 15.7 makes the jīva explicitly the Lord’s portion.
**[Rāmānuja on aṃśa-śeṣa]:** The soul as mode/portion of the Lord is theistic homology.
*Divergence:* Advaita readings stress apparent limitation; the verse’s 'draws the senses' keeps psychological realism.
**[Paul, 'body of Christ' membership]:** Portion-of-the-whole anthropology loosely resonates.
*Divergence:* Pauline membership is ecclesial; here the portion is metaphysical and sense-dragging.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
When craving pulls hard, note: 'A portion is dragging instruments.' Soften the drag for five breaths and remember the whole.

## Wind Taking Scents: The Traveler of Bodies
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 15.8–15.10

When the lord acquires a body and when he departs, he carries these and goes, as wind carries scents from their seat. Presiding over hearing, sight, touch, taste, and smell, and over the mind, he enjoys the sense-objects. The deluded do not see him departing, staying, or enjoying, endowed with the guṇas; those with the eye of knowledge see.

---

### Devanagari
शरीरं यदवाप्नोति यच्चाप्युत्क्रामतीश्वरः।गृहीत्वैतानि संयाति वायुर्गन्धानिवाशयात्
श्रोत्रं चक्षुः स्पर्शनं च रसनं घ्राणमेव च।अधिष्ठाय मनश्चायं विषयानुपसेवते
उत्क्रामन्तं स्थितं वापि भुञ्जानं वा गुणान्वितम्।विमूढा नानुपश्यन्ति पश्यन्ति ज्ञानचक्षुषः

### IAST
śarīraṃ yadavāpnoti yaccāpyutkrāmatīśvaraḥ|gṛhītvaitāni saṃyāti vāyurgandhānivāśayāt
śrotraṃ cakṣuḥ sparśanaṃ ca rasanaṃ ghrāṇameva ca|adhiṣṭhāya manaścāyaṃ viṣayānupasevate
utkrāmantaṃ sthitaṃ vāpi bhuñjānaṃ vā guṇānvitam|vimūḍhā nānupaśyanti paśyanti jñānacakṣuṣaḥ

### Pratibha Translation
When the lord acquires a body and when he departs, he carries these and goes, as wind carries scents from their seat. Presiding over hearing, sight, touch, taste, and smell, and over the mind, he enjoys the sense-objects. The deluded do not see him departing, staying, or enjoying, endowed with the guṇas; those with the eye of knowledge see.

### Pratibha Commentary
Transmigration is imaged with sensory precision: the īśvara of the body carries mind-senses as wind carries fragrance from a seat. Embodiment is not a hard reset; it is transport of subtle instruments. While staying, he enjoys objects through the senses and mind. The deluded do not see departing, staying, or enjoying; jñāna-cakṣus does. The contested claim is that what is most intimate—enjoyership and migration—is invisible to confusion and obvious to knowledge’s eye. Existentially, this trains seeing the traveler in living faces, including your own: not a corpse-to-be only, but a fragrance-bearing lord of a temporary seat. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**utkrāmati (उत्क्रामति)** — goes up/out / departs -> leaving the body with instruments -> 'dies' erases the carrying.
**vāyur gandhān iva (वायुर्गन्धानिव)** — like wind with scents -> migration analogy -> 'spirit rises' is vaguer than scent-transport.
**guṇānvita (गुणान्वित)** — endowed with guṇas -> enjoyer as guṇa-clothed -> 'having qualities' misses binding dress.
**jñāna-cakṣus (ज्ञानचक्षुस्)** — eye of knowledge -> seeing the traveler -> 'insight' can stay psychological.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad IV.4]:** Departure carrying knowledge/karma is homologous.
*Divergence:* The Gītā’s wind-scent image and guṇa-clothing sharpen the phenomenology.
**[Tibetan subtle-body migration imagery]:** Continuity of subtle faculties across deaths resonates.
*Divergence:* Bardo systems detail channels and visions; Krishna compresses to scent-wind and seeing/not-seeing.
**[Plato, Phaedrus chariot]:** Soul traveling with powers loosely parallels carrying senses-mind.
*Divergence:* Plato mythologizes wings and heaven; Krishna emphasizes delusion versus knowledge-eye in ordinary living.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
In meditation, watch a sensation arise and fade like scent in wind. Then notice the enjoyer-function without denying it or becoming it.
