## Yogins See; the Unready Do Not
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 15.11–15.13

Striving yogins also see him established in the Self; but the unready, even though striving, do not see him, lacking awareness. Know that brilliance in the sun that lights the whole world, and that in the moon and in fire, to be Mine. Entering the earth, I support beings with strength, and having become soma, savor itself, I nourish all plants.

---

### Devanagari
यतन्तो योगिनश्चैनं पश्यन्त्यात्मन्यवस्थितम्।यतन्तोऽप्यकृतात्मानो नैनं पश्यन्त्यचेतसः
यदादित्यगतं तेजो जगद्भासयतेऽखिलम्।यच्चन्द्रमसि यच्चाग्नौ तत्तेजो विद्धि मामकम्
गामाविश्य च भूतानि धारयाम्यहमोजसा।पुष्णामि चौषधीः सर्वाः सोमो भूत्वा रसात्मकः

### IAST
yatanto yoginaścainaṃ paśyantyātmanyavasthitam|yatanto'pyakṛtātmāno nainaṃ paśyantyacetasaḥ
yadādityagataṃ tejo jagadbhāsayate'khilam|yaccandramasi yaccāgnau tattejo viddhi māmakam
gāmāviśya ca bhūtāni dhārayāmyahamojasā|puṣṇāmi cauṣadhīḥ sarvāḥ somo bhūtvā rasātmakaḥ

### Pratibha Translation
Striving yogins also see him established in the Self; but the unready, even though striving, do not see him, lacking awareness. Know that brilliance in the sun that lights the whole world, and that in the moon and in fire, to be Mine. Entering the earth, I support beings with strength, and having become soma, savor itself, I nourish all plants.

### Pratibha Commentary
Effort alone does not guarantee seeing. Yogins who strive see the Self-established one; those with unready selves (akṛtātmanaḥ), even striving, do not—because they are acetasaḥ, not truly aware. Then Krishna widens identity into cosmic energies: solar, lunar, and fiery brilliance are his; he supports beings by entering the earth; as rasa-natured soma he nourishes plants. The contested pairing is interior seeing and exterior cosmology: the same Lord missed by unreadiness is the brilliance and the soil-strength you already live from. Existentially, unreadiness is not lack of hours on the cushion; it is an unworked self that can perform effort while remaining opaque. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**akṛtātman (अकृतात्मन्)** — whose self is unready/unmade -> effort without maturation -> 'undisciplined' is narrower.
**tejas (तेजस्)** — brilliance / energy -> solar-lunar-fire splendor as the Lord’s -> 'light' can become merely visual.
**ojas (ओजस्)** — vital strength -> supporting power in the earth -> 'force' misses living vigor.
**soma / rasātmaka (सोम / रसात्मक)** — soma as savor-nature -> nourishing essence of plants -> 'moon-plant juice' only is too botanical-literal.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Īśā / Śvetāśvatara cosmic pervasion]:** Lord as energy in sun/fire resonates.
*Divergence:* Here unreadiness explains why pervasion is missed.
**[Gītā 7.8–9]:** Krishna as taste, light, life continues.
*Divergence:* 15.11–13 ties that cosmology to who can see the indwelling one.
**[Gregory of Nyssa on spiritual senses]:** Needing formed senses to perceive God parallels readiness.
*Divergence:* Gregory’s formation is Christic; here readiness is yogic self-work amid cosmic theism.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Ask honestly: 'Is my effort paired with readiness, or with opacity?' Do one act of self-work (sleep, apology, or restraint) that increases readiness.

## I Digest as the Fire in All
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 15.14

Having become vaiśvānara, seated in the bodies of living beings, joined with in-breath and out-breath, I digest the fourfold food.

---

### Devanagari
अहं वैश्वानरो भूत्वा प्राणिनां देहमाश्रितः।प्राणापानसमायुक्तः पचाम्यन्नं चतुर्विधम्

### IAST
ahaṃ vaiśvānaro bhūtvā prāṇināṃ dehamāśritaḥ|prāṇāpānasamāyuktaḥ pacāmyannaṃ caturvidham

### Pratibha Translation
Having become vaiśvānara, seated in the bodies of living beings, joined with in-breath and out-breath, I digest the fourfold food.

### Pratibha Commentary
The Lord is not only sun and soil; he is vaiśvānara, the digestive fire in every body, married to prāṇa and apāna, cooking the four kinds of food. The contested intimacy is extreme: transcendence is metabolically immanent. Spirituality that despises digestion despises a divine act. Classical readers hear Agni-Vaiśvānara theology; modern readers can hear a refusal of body-rejecting mysticism. Existentially, each meal is already a theophany of sorts—not sentimental gratitude theater, but recognition that the cooker of food is the same Lord the unreadiness misses. The battlefield body Arjuna fears is also a hearth of the Lord. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**vaiśvānara (वैश्वानर)** — universal fire / digestive fire -> Lord as metabolizer in all -> 'stomach acid' parodies the theology.
**prāṇa-apāna (प्राणापान)** — forward and downward breaths -> respiratory pair joined to digestion -> 'breathing' alone misses the pair’s metabolic yoga.
**pacāmi (पचामि)** — I cook/digest -> first-person divine digestion -> 'nature digests' erases the claim.
**caturvidha anna (चतुर्विध अन्न)** — fourfold food -> all edible modes -> 'meals' is too casual.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Bṛhadāraṇyaka / Chāndogya Vaiśvānara]:** Upaniṣadic cosmic digestive fire is direct homology.
*Divergence:* The Gītā personalizes: ahaṃ ... pacāmi.
**[Christian Eucharist metabolisms of divine life]:** God feeding and being intimate with bodies resonates loosely.
*Divergence:* Eucharist is sacramental memorial/presence; here digestion itself is the Lord’s ongoing act.
**[Daoist body-gods / alchemy]:** Divinity in visceral processes has cross-tradition echoes.
*Divergence:* Daoist maps are many-spirited; Krishna asserts one Lord as the fire.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Before eating once today, silently: 'You digest this as the fire in me.' Eat slowly enough to mean it.

## I Am Seated in Every Heart
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 15.15

And I am seated in the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. I alone am to be known by all the Vedas; I am the author of Vedānta and the knower of the Veda.

---

### Devanagari
सर्वस्य चाहं हृदि सन्निविष्टो    मत्तः स्मृतिर्ज्ञानमपोहनं च।वेदैश्च सर्वैरहमेव वेद्यो    वेदान्तकृद्वेदविदेव चाहम्

### IAST
sarvasya cāhaṃ hṛdi sanniviṣṭo    mattaḥ smṛtirjñānamapohanaṃ ca|vedaiśca sarvairahameva vedyo    vedāntakṛdvedavideva cāham

### Pratibha Translation
And I am seated in the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. I alone am to be known by all the Vedas; I am the author of Vedānta and the knower of the Veda.

### Pratibha Commentary
The center shifts to the heart: Krishna is seated in all hearts; from him come smṛti, jñāna, and apohana—memory, knowledge, and removal/loss. The contested completeness is stunning: not only illumination but forgetting issues from the same source. Then the Veda claim: he alone is the knowable of all Vedas, maker of Vedānta, and knower of Veda. Scripture circles back into the heart-dweller. Existentially, this reinterprets both insight and amnesia as not merely neural accidents. The question becomes relational: what in my knowing and forgetting is refuge, and what is flight from the heart’s occupant? In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**hṛdi sanniviṣṭa (हृदि सन्निविष्ट)** — seated firmly in the heart -> intimate indwelling -> 'in my feelings' psychologizes the heart.
**apohana (अपोहन)** — removal / loss / negation -> forgetting as from the Lord -> 'amnesia' as pathology only misses the theological net.
**vedya (वेद्य)** — to be known -> Krishna as Veda’s knowable -> 'topic of scripture' is too academic.
**vedānta-kṛt (वेदान्तकृत्)** — maker of Vedānta -> author of the Veda’s end/teaching -> 'Vedānta philosopher' invents a schoolroom.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Kaṭha / Śvetāśvatara heart-dweller]:** Thumb-sized Self in the heart is homologous.
*Divergence:* The Gītā adds memory/knowledge/loss and Veda-authorship.
**[Augustine on God as inner teacher]:** Illumination from within resonates.
*Divergence:* Augustine includes forgetting differently; here apohana is explicitly from the Lord.
**[Gītā 10.20]:** Self as indwelling one continues.
*Divergence:* 15.15 intensifies by claiming Veda’s knowability and Vedānta’s authorship.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
When you forget something important, pause before self-attack: 'From Him also is loss.' Then ask what the heart is teaching through the gap.

---

## The Highest Person Beyond Perishable and Imperishable
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 15.16–15.18

There are two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable is all beings; the imperishable is called the unchanging. But there is another, the highest person, called the supreme Self, who, entering the three worlds, supports them as the undying Lord. Because I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Person Supreme.

---

### Devanagari
द्वाविमौ पुरुषौ लोके क्षरश्चाक्षर एव च।क्षरः सर्वाणि भूतानि कूटस्थोऽक्षर उच्यते
उत्तमः पुरुषस्त्वन्यः परमात्मेत्युदाहृतः।यो लोकत्रयमाविश्य बिभर्त्यव्यय ईश्वरः
यस्मात्क्षरमतीतोऽहमक्षरादपि चोत्तमः।अतोऽस्मि लोके वेदे च प्रथितः पुरुषोत्तमः

### IAST
dvāvimau puruṣau loke kṣaraścākṣara eva ca|kṣaraḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni kūṭastho'kṣara ucyate
uttamaḥ puruṣastvanyaḥ paramātmetyudāhṛtaḥ|yo lokatrayamāviśya bibhartyavyaya īśvaraḥ
yasmātkṣaramatīto'hamakṣarādapi cottamaḥ|ato'smi loke vede ca prathitaḥ puruṣottamaḥ

### Pratibha Translation
There are two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable is all beings; the imperishable is called the unchanging. But there is another, the highest person, called the supreme Self, who, entering the three worlds, supports them as the undying Lord. Because I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Person Supreme.

### Pratibha Commentary
A triad replaces a duality. Kṣara is all beings; akṣara is the kūṭastha, the unchanging. Beyond both is uttama puruṣa / Paramātman / Puruṣottama, who enters and supports the three worlds. Krishna’s claim is comparative and absolute: transcending perishable and higher than imperishable, he is celebrated as Puruṣottama. The contested move is against two reductions: reducing the divine to changing nature, or to a static impersonal absolute that cannot love or support. Existentially, refuge aims not at becoming a frozen unchanging principle, nor at surfing perishability forever, but at the highest person who holds both. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**kṣara / akṣara (क्षर / अक्षर)** — perishable / imperishable -> two persons of the world -> 'mortal/immortal' is too coarse.
**kūṭastha (कूटस्थ)** — standing at the peak/anvil-fixed -> unchanging person -> 'immutable soul' may miss the technical term.
**Puruṣottama (पुरुषोत्तम)** — Person Supreme -> beyond both kṣara and akṣara -> 'God' without the triad loses the claim’s precision.
**bibharti (बिभर्ति)** — supports / bears -> active sustaining of three worlds -> 'exists behind' is too passive.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Śvetāśvatara III–VI]:** Higher than the perishable/imperishable motif appears in Upaniṣadic theism.
*Divergence:* The Gītā crystallizes the title Puruṣottama.
**[Rāmānuja’s tattva-traya]:** God, souls, matter as structured reality resonates.
*Divergence:* Exact mappings differ; the verse’s hinge is Krishna’s transcendence of both persons.
**[Christian Trinity debates on personhood]:** Personal Absolute beyond impersonal abstraction resonates loosely.
*Divergence:* Trinitarian grammar differs; here the triad is kṣara/akṣara/Puruṣottama.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Contemplate three layers in experience: changing beings, witnessing stillness, and the Lord who supports both. Rest in the third for two minutes.

---

## Knowing Me as Puruṣottama Completes the Work
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 15.19–15.20

Whoever, undeluded, thus knows Me as the Person Supreme, knows all and worships Me with his whole being, O Bhārata. This most secret teaching has been declared by Me, O sinless one; knowing this, one becomes wise and has done what is to be done.

---

### Devanagari
यो मामेवमसम्मूढो जानाति पुरुषोत्तमम्।स सर्वविद्भजति मां सर्वभावेन भारत
इति गुह्यतमं शास्त्रमिदमुक्तं मयाऽनघ।एतद्बुद्ध्वा बुद्धिमान्स्यात्कृतकृत्यश्च भारत

### IAST
yo māmevamasammūḍho jānāti puruṣottamam|sa sarvavidbhajati māṃ sarvabhāvena bhārata
iti guhyatamaṃ śāstramidamuktaṃ mayā'nagha|etadbuddhvā buddhimānsyātkṛtakṛtyaśca bhārata

### Pratibha Translation
Whoever, undeluded, thus knows Me as the Person Supreme, knows all and worships Me with his whole being, O Bhārata. This most secret teaching has been declared by Me, O sinless one; knowing this, one becomes wise and has done what is to be done.

### Pratibha Commentary
Undeluded knowing of Krishna as Puruṣottama yields sarva-vid—knowing all—and whole-being worship (sarva-bhāvena). The most secret śāstra ends in a completion formula: becoming buddhimān and kṛta-kṛtya, one who has done what needed doing. The contested claim is that metaphysical recognition and total devotion are one act, and that human incompleteness ends there—not in endless self-improvement. Existentially, 'knowing all' is not trivia mastery; it is knowing the One who ranks above perishable and imperishable, and letting that knowledge become worship with every bhāva. The secret is not information; it is undeluded recognition that finishes the task. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**asammūḍha (असम्मूढ)** — undeluded -> clarity required for Puruṣottama-knowing -> 'smart' is irrelevant.
**sarva-vid (सर्वविद्)** — all-knower -> fruit of knowing Puruṣottama -> 'omniscient' can sound mythic-inflated.
**sarva-bhāvena (सर्वभावेन)** — with one’s whole being/mode -> total worship -> 'enthusiastically' is too thin.
**kṛta-kṛtya (कृतकृत्य)** — one who has done what is to be done -> completion of human task -> 'successful' is worldly counterfeit.
**guhyatama śāstra (गुह्यतम शास्त्र)** — most secret teaching -> climax disclosure -> 'esoteric doctrine' can become clubbish.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 18.50–55 / 18.65–66]:** Completion and whole-being devotion foreshadow the finale.
*Divergence:* Chapter 15’s secret is Puruṣottama; chapter 18’s is refuge beyond all dharmas.
**[Muṇḍaka’s para vidyā]:** Highest knowledge completing the aim of life resonates.
*Divergence:* Muṇḍaka aims at Brahman; here completion is knowing and worshipping Puruṣottama.
**[Ignatius, 'take, Lord, receive']:** Whole-being offering parallels sarva-bhāva worship.
*Divergence:* Ignatian offering is Christic-mission; here the hinge is undeluded Puruṣottama recognition.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
At day’s end ask: 'What remains undone if I have not worshipped with my whole being?' Offer the residue in one honest bow.



**Corpus entry:** Bhagavad Gītā / Mahābhārata
**Units:** 10 (one per brief CHUNK)

## The Inventory of Divine Wealth
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 16.1–16.3

The Blessed Lord said: Fearlessness, purity of sattva, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, giving, self-restraint, sacrifice, study, austerity, uprightness; non-harming, truth, absence of anger, renunciation, peace, absence of slander, compassion for beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty, absence of restlessness; vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, absence of malice, absence of excessive pride—these belong to one born to the divine endowment, O Bhārata.

---

### Devanagari
श्री भगवानुवाच

अभयं सत्त्वसंशुद्धिः ज्ञानयोगव्यवस्थितिः।

दानं दमश्च यज्ञश्च स्वाध्यायस्तप आर्जवम्
अहिंसा सत्यमक्रोधस्त्यागः शान्तिरपैशुनम्।दया भूतेष्वलोलुप्त्वं मार्दवं ह्रीरचापलम्
तेजः क्षमा धृतिः शौचमद्रोहो नातिमानिता।

भवन्ति सम्पदं दैवीमभिजातस्य भारत

### IAST
śrī bhagavānuvāca

abhayaṃ sattvasaṃśuddhiḥ jñānayogavyavasthitiḥ|

dānaṃ damaśca yajñaśca svādhyāyastapa ārjavam
ahiṃsā satyamakrodhastyāgaḥ śāntirapaiśunam|dayā bhūteṣvaloluptvaṃ mārdavaṃ hrīracāpalam
tejaḥ kṣamā dhṛtiḥ śaucamadroho nātimānitā|

bhavanti sampadaṃ daivīmabhijātasya bhārata

### Pratibha Translation
The Blessed Lord said: Fearlessness, purity of sattva, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, giving, self-restraint, sacrifice, study, austerity, uprightness; non-harming, truth, absence of anger, renunciation, peace, absence of slander, compassion for beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty, absence of restlessness; vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, absence of malice, absence of excessive pride—these belong to one born to the divine endowment, O Bhārata.

### Pratibha Commentary
The chapter opens not with metaphysics but with a catalogue of daivī sampad—divine endowment as a constellation of traits. Fearlessness stands first: terror is not a private feeling only but a spiritual climate. The contested move is to treat ethics as ontology of birth into a divine inheritance, without reducing freedom to genetics. These qualities are recognizable, trainable, and diagnostic. In the Gītā’s war setting, divine wealth is not softness; it includes tejas and dhṛti. Existentially, the list is a mirror: which items are living in you, which are costumes, which are absent? The teaching will soon contrast this endowment with the āsuric, so honesty now is mercy later. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**daivī sampad (दैवी सम्पद्)** — divine endowment/wealth -> constellation of liberating traits -> 'being nice' misses vigor and fearlessness.
**abhaya (अभय)** — fearlessness -> first divine mark -> 'confidence' can be egoic counterfeit.
**jñāna-yoga-vyavasthiti (ज्ञानयोगव्यवस्थिति)** — steadfast standing in knowledge-yoga -> stable knowing -> 'having beliefs' is weaker.
**hrī (ह्री)** — modesty/shame before wrong -> delicate moral sensitivity -> 'embarrassment' psychologizes it.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Patañjali yama-niyama]:** Virtue lists as yoga foundation are homologous.
*Divergence:* Patañjali systematizes limbs; Krishna frames traits as divine vs āsuric endowments.
**[Paul, fruits of the Spirit]:** Catalogues of Spirit-born traits resonate.
*Divergence:* Pauline fruits are Christic; here traits index daivī sampad toward liberation.
**[Confucian virtue clusters]:** Recognizable ethical constellations shaping the person.
*Divergence:* Confucian cultivation aims at social harmony; the Gītā aims at mokṣa-oriented endowment.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Choose one trait from the list you lack. Practice it once today in a concrete scene, as endowment rather than self-improvement theater.

## Two Births, One Consolation
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 16.4–16.6

Hypocrisy, arrogance, excessive pride, anger, harshness, and ignorance belong to one born to the demonic endowment, O Pārtha. The divine endowment is for liberation; the demonic is considered for bondage. Do not grieve: you are born to the divine endowment, O son of Pāṇḍu. There are two kinds of created beings in this world: the divine and the demonic. The divine has been spoken of at length; hear from Me of the demonic, O Pārtha.

---

### Devanagari
दम्भो दर्पोऽभिमानश्च क्रोधः पारुष्यमेव च।अज्ञानं चाभिजातस्य पार्थ सम्पदमासुरीम्
दैवी सम्पद्विमोक्षाय निबन्धायासुरी मता।मा शुचः सम्पदं दैवीमभिजातोऽसि पाण्डव
द्वौ भूतसर्गौ लोकेऽस्मिन् दैव आसुर एव च।दैवो विस्तरशः प्रोक्त आसुरं पार्थ मे श्रृणु

### IAST
dambho darpo'bhimānaśca krodhaḥ pāruṣyameva ca|ajñānaṃ cābhijātasya pārtha sampadamāsurīm
daivī sampadvimokṣāya nibandhāyāsurī matā|mā śucaḥ sampadaṃ daivīmabhijāto'si pāṇḍava
dvau bhūtasargau loke'smin daiva āsura eva ca|daivo vistaraśaḥ prokta āsuraṃ pārtha me śrṛṇu

### Pratibha Translation
Hypocrisy, arrogance, excessive pride, anger, harshness, and ignorance belong to one born to the demonic endowment, O Pārtha. The divine endowment is for liberation; the demonic is considered for bondage. Do not grieve: you are born to the divine endowment, O son of Pāṇḍu. There are two kinds of created beings in this world: the divine and the demonic. The divine has been spoken of at length; hear from Me of the demonic, O Pārtha.

### Pratibha Commentary
The āsuric list is short and sharp: hypocrisy, pride, anger, harshness, ignorance. Then the teleology: daivī sampad leads to liberation; āsurī to bondage. Krishna’s pastoral thunder follows: mā śucaḥ—do not grieve; Arjuna is born to the divine endowment. The contested move is typology without fatalism: two created streams exist, yet consolation is possible, and listening still matters. Existentially, the verse refuses both despair (“I am demonic”) and complacency (“I am divine, so I am done”). Classification is pedagogical; the next verses will expose āsuric philosophy so it can be recognized and refused. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**āsurī sampad (आसुरी सम्पद्)** — demonic endowment -> traits that bind -> 'evil personality' cartoonishly essentializes.
**vimokṣāya / nibandhāya (विमोक्षाय / निबन्धाय)** — for liberation / for bondage -> teleology of endowments -> 'good/bad vibes' misses destiny-logic.
**mā śucaḥ (मा शुचः)** — do not grieve -> pastoral reassurance -> 'cheer up' trivializes the battlefield grief.
**bhūta-sarga (भूतसर्ग)** — creation of beings -> two streams of creatures -> 'personality types' shrinks cosmology.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 9.11–12]:** Āsuric disregard of the Lord’s embodiment foreshadows this typology.
*Divergence:* Chapter 16 expands into a full anthropology of the āsuric mind.
**[Augustine, two cities]:** Two loves making two cities resonates structurally.
*Divergence:* Augustine’s cities are eschatological-historical; here endowments are ethical-psychological streams.
**[Buddhist loka / gati mappings]:** Beings oriented toward higher/lower rebirths loosely parallel.
*Divergence:* Buddhist maps are karmic-intentional; Krishna’s consolation to Arjuna personalizes the teaching.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
When shame says 'I am āsuric,' answer with honest inventory and the refusal of despair. When pride says 'I am divine,' inventory again.

## The World Without a Lord
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 16.7–16.9

Demonic people do not know engagement or withdrawal; purity, right conduct, and truth are not found in them. They say the world is without truth, without foundation, without a Lord, not produced by regular causation, having desire as its only cause—what else? Holding this view, with lost selves and little understanding, they rise with fierce deeds as enemies for the destruction of the world.

---

### Devanagari
प्रवृत्तिं च निवृत्तिं च जना न विदुरासुराः।न शौचं नापि चाचारो न सत्यं तेषु विद्यते
असत्यमप्रतिष्ठं ते जगदाहुरनीश्वरम्।अपरस्परसम्भूतं किमन्यत्कामहैतुकम्
एतां दृष्टिमवष्टभ्य नष्टात्मानोऽल्पबुद्धयः।प्रभवन्त्युग्रकर्माणः क्षयाय जगतोऽहिताः

### IAST
pravṛttiṃ ca nivṛttiṃ ca janā na vidurāsurāḥ|na śaucaṃ nāpi cācāro na satyaṃ teṣu vidyate
asatyamapratiṣṭhaṃ te jagadāhuranīśvaram|aparasparasambhūtaṃ kimanyatkāmahaitukam
etāṃ dṛṣṭimavaṣṭabhya naṣṭātmāno'lpabuddhayaḥ|prabhavantyugrakarmāṇaḥ kṣayāya jagato'hitāḥ

### Pratibha Translation
Demonic people do not know engagement or withdrawal; purity, right conduct, and truth are not found in them. They say the world is without truth, without foundation, without a Lord, not produced by regular causation, having desire as its only cause—what else? Holding this view, with lost selves and little understanding, they rise with fierce deeds as enemies for the destruction of the world.

### Pratibha Commentary
Āsuric cognition is first a failure to know pravṛtti and nivṛtti—when to act and when to refrain—then a collapse of purity, custom, and truth. Their metaphysics follows: the world is asatya, apratiṣṭha, anīśvara—untrue, unfounded, lordless—born of mutual appetite, desire-caused only. The contested claim is that bad metaphysics births fierce world-destroying action. This is not anti-intellectualism; it is insistence that worldview has teeth. Existentially, whenever you reduce the world to appetite plus accident, watch what permissions open in your speech and strategy. The Gītā links nihilism to ugra-karma with alarming clarity. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**pravṛtti / nivṛtti (प्रवृत्ति / निवृत्ति)** — engagement / withdrawal -> knowing when to act or refrain -> 'busy/rest' misses ethical discernment.
**anīśvara (अनीश्वर)** — without a Lord -> lordless cosmos -> 'atheism' as modern identity may miss the ethical fallout named here.
**kāma-haituka (कामहेतुक)** — desire-caused -> appetite as sole causality -> 'psychological explanation' can be the same reduction.
**ugra-karman (उग्रकर्मन्)** — fierce deeds -> destructive action from that view -> 'intensity' romanticizes harm.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Dostoevsky’s 'if no God…']:** Moral consequences of lordless worlds resonate in modern key.
*Divergence:* Dostoevsky dramatizes conscience; Krishna maps a full āsuric psychology next.
**[Madhyamaka vs nihilism warnings]:** Emptiness misunderstood as nothingness parallels asatya-world talk.
*Divergence:* Nāgārjuna rejects nihilism; āsuric doctrine asserts desire-only causality as positive claim.
**[Nietzschean critiques of truth (contrast)]:** World as unfounded can be read as liberation or as license.
*Divergence:* The Gītā reads the lordless claim as binding and destructive, not emancipatory.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Catch one sentence today that reduces a person or situation to 'just appetite/politics/accident.' Revise it toward foundation and responsibility.

## Insatiable Desire as Religion
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 16.10–16.12

Clinging to insatiable desire, full of hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance, holding false views through delusion, they proceed with impure resolves. Giving themselves to immeasurable cares ending only at dissolution, taking gratification of desire as the highest, convinced that this is all; bound by a hundred snares of hope, devoted to desire and anger, they seek to accumulate wealth by unjust means for the sake of sense-enjoyment.

---

### Devanagari
काममाश्रित्य दुष्पूरं दम्भमानमदान्विताः।मोहाद्गृहीत्वासद्ग्राहान्प्रवर्तन्तेऽशुचिव्रताः
चिन्तामपरिमेयां च प्रलयान्तामुपाश्रिताः।कामोपभोगपरमा एतावदिति निश्िचताः
आशापाशशतैर्बद्धाः कामक्रोधपरायणाः।ईहन्ते कामभोगार्थमन्यायेनार्थसञ्चयान्

### IAST
kāmamāśritya duṣpūraṃ dambhamānamadānvitāḥ|mohādgṛhītvāsadgrāhānpravartante'śucivratāḥ
cintāmaparimeyāṃ ca pralayāntāmupāśritāḥ|kāmopabhogaparamā etāvaditi niśicatāḥ
āśāpāśaśatairbaddhāḥ kāmakrodhaparāyaṇāḥ|īhante kāmabhogārthamanyāyenārthasañcayān

### Pratibha Translation
Clinging to insatiable desire, full of hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance, holding false views through delusion, they proceed with impure resolves. Giving themselves to immeasurable cares ending only at dissolution, taking gratification of desire as the highest, convinced that this is all; bound by a hundred snares of hope, devoted to desire and anger, they seek to accumulate wealth by unjust means for the sake of sense-enjoyment.

### Pratibha Commentary
The āsuric life is revealed as a counterfeit religion: kāma is refuge, enjoyment is ultimate, cares stretch to pralaya, and unjust wealth-gathering is liturgy. Hypocrisy and pride are not side traits; they are structural. The contested insight is that “this is all” (etāvad iti) is a metaphysical creed, not a casual mood. Existentially, modern busyness ending only at burnout is already sketched: immeasurable cintā until dissolution. The snares of āśā—hope as rope—bind more efficiently than open despair. Liberation begins when “this is all” is heard as a prison slogan rather than realism. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**duṣpūra kāma (दुष्पूर काम)** — desire hard to fill -> insatiable craving -> 'ambition' may mask the same.
**etāvad iti (एतावदिति)** — 'this much is all' -> creed of appetite-finality -> 'realism' is its flattering name.
**āśā-pāśa (आशापाश)** — snares of hope -> binding expectations -> 'optimism' can be the same rope.
**anyāyena (अन्यायेन)** — by injustice -> wealth for enjoyment via wrong means -> 'hustle' romanticizes it.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Buddha on taṇhā]:** Insatiable craving as world-driver is strong homology.
*Divergence:* Buddhism ends craving toward nibbāna; Krishna exposes craving as āsuric creed before teaching śāstra-refuge.
**[Ecclesiastes on vanity]:** Endless striving under the sun resonates.
*Divergence:* Qoheleth’s skepticism can open to fear of God; here the creed 'this is all' hardens into unjust accumulation.
**[Capitalist capture of desire (modern reading)]:** Insatiable consumption as ultimate loosely echoes etāvad iti.
*Divergence:* The Gītā’s frame remains theological-ethical, not merely sociological critique.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Name your current 'this is all.' Fast from it for one hour and watch the snare of hope tighten or loosen.

---

## The Litany of the Inflated I
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 16.13–16.15

'This has been gained by me today; this desire I will obtain; this is mine, and this wealth too will be mine again. That enemy has been slain by me, and I will slay others as well. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am perfect, powerful, happy. I am wealthy and high-born; who else is like me? I will sacrifice, I will give, I will rejoice'—thus they are deluded by ignorance.

---

### Devanagari
इदमद्य मया लब्धमिमं प्राप्स्ये मनोरथम्।इदमस्तीदमपि मे भविष्यति पुनर्धनम्
असौ मया हतः शत्रुर्हनिष्ये चापरानपि।ईश्वरोऽहमहं भोगी सिद्धोऽहं बलवान्सुखी
आढ्योऽभिजनवानस्मि कोऽन्योऽस्ति सदृशो मया।यक्ष्ये दास्यामि मोदिष्य इत्यज्ञानविमोहिताः

### IAST
idamadya mayā labdhamimaṃ prāpsye manoratham|idamastīdamapi me bhaviṣyati punardhanam
asau mayā hataḥ śatrurhaniṣye cāparānapi|īśvaro'hamahaṃ bhogī siddho'haṃ balavānsukhī
āḍhyo'bhijanavānasmi ko'nyo'sti sadṛśo mayā|yakṣye dāsyāmi modiṣya ityajñānavimohitāḥ

### Pratibha Translation
'This has been gained by me today; this desire I will obtain; this is mine, and this wealth too will be mine again. That enemy has been slain by me, and I will slay others as well. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am perfect, powerful, happy. I am wealthy and high-born; who else is like me? I will sacrifice, I will give, I will rejoice'—thus they are deluded by ignorance.

### Pratibha Commentary
Krishna ventriloquizes the āsuric interior monologue until it becomes unbearable to hear as one’s own. The contested pedagogical move is exposure by quotation: theology of the inflated I is not refuted first by argument but by being displayed. “I am īśvara” here is not Gītā theology; it is ego’s parody of lordship. Sacrifice and giving appear even here, but as self-celebration. Existentially, read the litany slowly and mark every clause that has passed through your mind this month. The demonic is often not monstrous; it is the ordinary first-person empire. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**īśvaro’ham (ईश्वरोऽहम्)** — I am the lord -> egoic counterfeit of divine lordship -> 'empowerment' can be its modern gloss.
**aham bhogī (अहं भोगी)** — I am the enjoyer -> identity as consumer of experience -> 'I deserve nice things' is the soft version.
**ajñāna-vimohita (अज्ञानविमोहित)** — deluded by ignorance -> the litany’s cause -> 'confident' may hide the same delusion.
**manoratha (मनोरथ)** — wish-chariot / desire -> projected obtainables -> 'goals' can be neutral or āsuric.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Luke 12, rich fool]:** Self-talk of barns and security resonates strongly.
*Divergence:* The parable ends in divine summons; Krishna continues into karmic-āsuric consequences.
**[Buddhist asmi-māna]:** Conceit 'I am' as deep bind is homologous.
*Divergence:* Buddhism dismantles I-making; the Gītā contrasts false 'I am lord' with true refuge in the Lord.
**[Stirner / egoist philosophy (contrast)]:** Ownness as ultimate is the modern cousin of this litany.
*Divergence:* The Gītā names it ignorance-delusion, not emancipation.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Write your own three-line version of this litany honestly. Then rewrite each line without the imperial I.

## Hell’s Net and Hatred of the Indwelling Lord
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 16.16–16.18

Led astray by many thoughts, caught in the net of delusion, attached to gratification of desires, they fall into an unclean hell. Self-conceited, stubborn, drunk on wealth-pride, they sacrifice in name only, out of hypocrisy, not according to ordinance. Clinging to egoism, power, pride, desire, and anger, these resentful ones hate Me in their own and others’ bodies.

---

### Devanagari
अनेकचित्तविभ्रान्ता मोहजालसमावृताः।प्रसक्ताः कामभोगेषु पतन्ति नरकेऽशुचौ
आत्मसम्भाविताः स्तब्धा धनमानमदान्विताः।यजन्ते नामयज्ञैस्ते दम्भेनाविधिपूर्वकम्
अहङ्कारं बलं दर्पं कामं क्रोधं च संश्रिताः।मामात्मपरदेहेषु प्रद्विषन्तोऽभ्यसूयकाः

### IAST
anekacittavibhrāntā mohajālasamāvṛtāḥ|prasaktāḥ kāmabhogeṣu patanti narake'śucau
ātmasambhāvitāḥ stabdhā dhanamānamadānvitāḥ|yajante nāmayajñaiste dambhenāvidhipūrvakam
ahaṅkāraṃ balaṃ darpaṃ kāmaṃ krodhaṃ ca saṃśritāḥ|māmātmaparadeheṣu pradviṣanto'bhyasūyakāḥ

### Pratibha Translation
Led astray by many thoughts, caught in the net of delusion, attached to gratification of desires, they fall into an unclean hell. Self-conceited, stubborn, drunk on wealth-pride, they sacrifice in name only, out of hypocrisy, not according to ordinance. Clinging to egoism, power, pride, desire, and anger, these resentful ones hate Me in their own and others’ bodies.

### Pratibha Commentary
The cascade continues into naraka, namedyajña, and the deepest crime: hatred of Krishna in one’s own and others’ bodies. The contested claim is that āsuric egoism is not merely horizontal harm; it is enmity toward the indwelling Lord. Self-conceit and wealth-drunk ritual produce sacrifice as branding. Existentially, this verse makes contempt for bodies—your own or others’—theologically charged. If the Lord is in bodies, then harshness is not “just personality”; it is pradviṣantah, active hatred of the One in the field of flesh. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**moha-jāla (मोहजाल)** — net of delusion -> entanglement structure -> 'confusion' is too mild.
**nāma-yajña (नामयज्ञ)** — sacrifice in name only -> hypocritical ritual -> 'performative religion' is the modern cousin.
**pradviṣantaḥ (प्रद्विषन्तः)** — hating / resenting -> enmity toward the Lord in bodies -> 'dislike' understates.
**ātma-para-deheṣu (आत्मपरदेहेषु)** — in own and others’ bodies -> locus of the hated Lord -> 'people' misses indwelling.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 13.28 / non-injury of Self by self]:** Hatred in bodies reverses equal seeing.
*Divergence:* 16.18 shows the āsuric form of that injury as hatred of the Lord.
**[1 John on hating the brother]:** Hatred of the seen as hatred of God resonates.
*Divergence:* Johannine logic is Christic love; here hatred targets Krishna-in-bodies amid ego-power.
**[Levinas on violence to the face]:** Assault on the other as metaphysical event resonates loosely.
*Divergence:* Levinas is phenomenological-ethical; Krishna names explicit theological hatred.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Notice one harsh judgment on a body (yours or another’s). Soften it as refusal to hate the indwelling One.

## Thrown Again into Demonic Wombs
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 16.19–16.20

Those hateful, cruel, lowest of humans in the worlds of change I cast continually into demonic wombs. Entering demonic wombs, deluded birth after birth, not reaching Me, O son of Kuntī, they then go to the lowest way.

---

### Devanagari
तानहं द्विषतः क्रूरान्संसारेषु नराधमान्।क्षिपाम्यजस्रमशुभानासुरीष्वेव योनिषु
आसुरीं योनिमापन्ना मूढा जन्मनि जन्मनि।

मामप्राप्यैव कौन्तेय ततो यान्त्यधमां गतिम्

### IAST
tānahaṃ dviṣataḥ krūrānsaṃsāreṣu narādhamān|kṣipāmyajasramaśubhānāsurīṣveva yoniṣu
āsurīṃ yonimāpannā mūḍhā janmani janmani|

māmaprāpyaiva kaunteya tato yāntyadhamāṃ gatim

### Pratibha Translation
Those hateful, cruel, lowest of humans in the worlds of change I cast continually into demonic wombs. Entering demonic wombs, deluded birth after birth, not reaching Me, O son of Kuntī, they then go to the lowest way.

### Pratibha Commentary
The tone is severe: Krishna as the one who casts the cruel and hateful into āsuric wombs again and again. The contested difficulty is theistic participation in karmic consequence without making God a sadist. In the Gītā’s frame, this is the universe’s refusal to let hatred of the indwelling Lord become a successful strategy. Not reaching Me (mām aprāpya) is both cause and doom. Existentially, the verse is a warning against romanticizing cruelty as strength. The lowest gati is not a scare-illustration only; it is the trajectory of entrenched hatred. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**kṣipāmi (क्षिपामि)** — I cast/throw -> divine role in consequence -> 'they reincarnate' erases the first person.
**āsurī yoni (आसुरी योनि)** — demonic womb -> birth-matrix of the āsuric -> 'bad life circumstances' is too sociological.
**adhamā gati (अधमा गति)** — lowest way/destination -> end of the trajectory -> 'hell' may import alien maps.
**mām aprāpya (मामप्राप्य)** — not reaching Me -> failure of attainment as hinge -> 'not religious' is too shallow.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Dharmaśāstra karmic rebirth mappings]:** Cruel deeds to lower births is homologous.
*Divergence:* The Gītā centers hatred of the Lord in bodies as the decisive crime.
**[Dante’s contrapasso (literary)]:** Fitting destinies for hatred/cruelty resonate imaginatively.
*Divergence:* Dante’s Christian topography differs; here the engine is āsuric wombs and non-attainment.
**[Buddhist niraya warnings]:** Ethical causality toward lower realms resonates.
*Divergence:* Buddhist hells are impersonal-karmic; here Krishna speaks as caster.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Where you are tempted to admire cruelty (in politics, art, or yourself), name the trajectory this verse warns toward—and choose another strength.

## The Triple Gate of Hell
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 16.21

This is the triple gate of hell that destroys the self: desire, anger, and greed. Therefore one should abandon these three.

---

### Devanagari
त्रिविधं नरकस्येदं द्वारं नाशनमात्मनः।कामः क्रोधस्तथा लोभस्तस्मादेतत्त्रयं त्यजेत्

### IAST
trividhaṃ narakasyedaṃ dvāraṃ nāśanamātmanaḥ|kāmaḥ krodhastathā lobhastasmādetattrayaṃ tyajet

### Pratibha Translation
This is the triple gate of hell that destroys the self: desire, anger, and greed. Therefore one should abandon these three.

### Pratibha Commentary
The chapter compresses into a portable diagnostic: kāma, krodha, lobha—desire, anger, greed—are naraka’s triple gate and ātman’s destroyer. The contested simplicity is merciful. After long anthropology, the practical hinge is tiny and exact. Tyajet—one should abandon—these three. Existentially, most elaborate self-stories are cover for one of the three gates. The verse does not ask you to solve your whole biography; it asks you to stop walking through these doors. Hell here is not only postmortem; it is the self-destroying passage already available in ordinary craving, rage, and grab. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**trividhaṃ dvāram (त्रिविधं द्वारम्)** — triple gate -> three entrances to hell -> 'bad habits' understates the gate image.
**nāśanam ātmanaḥ (नाशनमात्मनः)** — destruction of the self -> what the gates do -> 'unhealthy' is too soft.
**kāma-krodha-lobha (कामक्रोधलोभ)** — desire-anger-greed -> the triad to abandon -> 'passions' is less precise.
**tyajet (त्यजेत्)** — one should abandon -> imperative of renunciation -> 'manage' is a weaker modern substitute.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 3.37–41]:** Desire-anger as enemies continues into this triad with greed.
*Divergence:* 16.21 makes them explicitly hell’s gate.
**[Christian capital vices (lust/wrath/avarice)]:** Overlap in the moral triad is clear.
*Divergence:* Christian lists expand; Krishna compresses to a triple gate with mokṣa at stake.
**[Buddhist lobha-dosa-moha]:** Close homology, though moha/ignorance is the third there.
*Divergence:* Here greed stands third; delusion was already thematized as āsuric worldview.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
For twenty-four hours, label each spike: desire, anger, or greed. Abandon one spike mid-course by a concrete refusal.

## Freed from the Dark Gates, Bound to Śāstra
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 16.22–16.23

Released from these three gates of darkness, O son of Kuntī, a person practices what is good for the self and then goes to the highest goal. But the one who discards the injunctions of scripture and acts under the impulse of desire does not attain perfection, nor happiness, nor the highest goal.

---

### Devanagari
एतैर्विमुक्तः कौन्तेय तमोद्वारैस्त्रिभिर्नरः।आचरत्यात्मनः श्रेयस्ततो याति परां गतिम्
यः शास्त्रविधिमुत्सृज्य वर्तते कामकारतः।न स सिद्धिमवाप्नोति न सुखं न परां गतिम्

### IAST
etairvimuktaḥ kaunteya tamodvāraistribhirnaraḥ|ācaratyātmanaḥ śreyastato yāti parāṃ gatim
yaḥ śāstravidhimutsṛjya vartate kāmakārataḥ|na sa siddhimavāpnoti na sukhaṃ na parāṃ gatim

### Pratibha Translation
Released from these three gates of darkness, O son of Kuntī, a person practices what is good for the self and then goes to the highest goal. But the one who discards the injunctions of scripture and acts under the impulse of desire does not attain perfection, nor happiness, nor the highest goal.

### Pratibha Commentary
Freedom from the triple gate enables ātmanaḥ śreyas—what is truly better for the self—and the highest path. Then a hard edge: discarding śāstra-vidhi and acting kāmakārataḥ yields neither siddhi nor sukha nor the highest goal. The contested claim is that desire-impulse is not authentic freedom. In a culture that equates authenticity with impulse, this verse is abrasive on purpose. Existentially, the question is whether your “I have to” is hell’s gate dressed as honesty. Śāstra here is not paperwork; it is measured norm that protects the self from self-destruction. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**tamo-dvāra (तमोद्वार)** — gate of darkness -> the triad as dark entries -> 'negative patterns' is weaker.
**ātmanaḥ śreyas (आत्मनः श्रेयस्)** — the better/good of the self -> true self-interest -> 'self-care' can be a counterfeit.
**śāstra-vidhi (शास्त्रविधि)** — scriptural injunction -> normative measure -> 'rules' misses liberative function.
**kāmakārataḥ (कामकारतः)** — from desire’s doing -> impulse-agency -> 'following your heart' may be the soft gloss.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 2.52–53 / buddhi settled in śāstra-sāṃkhya]:** Norm-guided discernment continues.
*Divergence:* 16.22–23 make desire-against-śāstra explicitly fruitless.
**[Halakhic / rule-of-life traditions]:** Measured practice freeing from impulse resonates.
*Divergence:* Specific canons differ; the structural claim is impulse ≠ liberation.
**[Aristotle on akrasia]:** Acting from appetite against right measure resonates.
*Divergence:* Aristotle aims at virtue; Krishna aims at highest gati via śāstra-aligned good.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Identify one impulse you call 'authentic.' Test it against a trusted ethical measure before acting.

## Therefore Let Śāstra Be Your Measure
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 16.24

Therefore let scripture be your measure in establishing what is to be done and what is not to be done. Knowing the scriptural ordinance, you should perform action here.

---

### Devanagari
तस्माच्छास्त्रं प्रमाणं ते कार्याकार्यव्यवस्थितौ।ज्ञात्वा शास्त्रविधानोक्तं कर्म कर्तुमिहार्हसि

### IAST
tasmācchāstraṃ pramāṇaṃ te kāryākāryavyavasthitau|jñātvā śāstravidhānoktaṃ karma kartumihārhasi

### Pratibha Translation
Therefore let scripture be your measure in establishing what is to be done and what is not to be done. Knowing the scriptural ordinance, you should perform action here.

### Pratibha Commentary
The chapter closes with a clear criterion: śāstraṃ pramāṇam—scripture as measure for kārya and akārya. Knowing what is taught, one should act. The contested modern discomfort is authority. Yet within the Gītā’s argument, this is medicine after the āsuric creed of desire-only causality. Existentially, “I alone measure” was already quoted as demonic litany. The alternative is not mindless conformity; it is pramāṇa—reliable measure—against the triple gate’s distortions. Action remains; arbitrariness does not. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**pramāṇa (प्रमाण)** — measure / valid means of knowing -> śāstra as criterion -> 'authority' as domination mishears it.
**kāryākārya (कार्याकार्य)** — to-be-done / not-to-be-done -> ethical discernment field -> 'tasks' is too managerial.
**śāstra-vidhāna (शास्त्रविधान)** — scriptural ordinance -> enacted measure -> 'tradition' can become vague nostalgia.
**iha (इह)** — here / in this world -> act here, not in fantasy -> 'someday spirituality' is refused.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Nyāya on pramāṇa]:** Concern for valid measure resonates intellectually.
*Divergence:* Here the measure is specifically śāstra for action amid āsuric temptation.
**[Benedictine rule as measure]:** A rule ordering do/don’t for liberation-adjacent peace resonates.
*Divergence:* Benedictine rule is monastic-Christian; Krishna’s śāstra addresses Arjuna in war-duty.
**[Gītā 17’s opening]:** The next chapter problematizes those who abandon śāstra yet sacrifice with śraddhā—teaching continues.
*Divergence:* 16.24 sets the measure; 17 investigates faith’s guṇas when measure is dropped.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Before a morally loaded choice today, name your pramāṇa explicitly. If it is only desire, pause and consult a trusted measure.



**Corpus entry:** Bhagavad Gītā / Mahābhārata
**Units:** 11 (one per brief CHUNK)

## Faith Has Three Climates
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 17.1–17.2

Arjuna said: Those who discard scriptural injunction yet sacrifice filled with faith—what is their standing, Kṛṣṇa? Sattva, or rajas, or tamas? The Blessed Lord said: Faith in embodied beings is threefold, born of their own nature: sattvic, rajasic, and also tamasic. Hear of it.

---

### Devanagari
अर्जुन उवाचये शास्त्रविधिमुत्सृज्य यजन्ते श्रद्धयाऽन्विताः।तेषां निष्ठा तु का कृष्ण सत्त्वमाहो रजस्तमः
श्री भगवानुवाचत्रिविधा भवति श्रद्धा देहिनां सा स्वभावजा।सात्त्विकी राजसी चैव तामसी चेति तां श्रृणु

### IAST
arjuna uvācaye śāstravidhimutsṛjya yajante śraddhayā'nvitāḥ|teṣāṃ niṣṭhā tu kā kṛṣṇa sattvamāho rajastamaḥ
śrī bhagavānuvācatrividhā bhavati śraddhā dehināṃ sā svabhāvajā|sāttvikī rājasī caiva tāmasī ceti tāṃ śrṛṇu

### Pratibha Translation
Arjuna said: Those who discard scriptural injunction yet sacrifice filled with faith—what is their standing, Kṛṣṇa? Sattva, or rajas, or tamas? The Blessed Lord said: Faith in embodied beings is threefold, born of their own nature: sattvic, rajasic, and also tamasic. Hear of it.

### Pratibha Commentary
Arjuna’s question is pastorally exact: what of sincere people who abandon śāstra yet sacrifice with śraddhā? Krishna refuses a binary of “faith good / lawlessness bad.” Śraddhā itself is trividhā and svabhāva-jā—threefold, born of one’s nature. The contested move is to subject faith to guṇa analysis. Sincerity does not automatically sanctify; climate colors trust. Existentially, this protects against two errors: condemning all extra-canonical devotion, and romanticizing intensity as truth. The next verses will show faith’s object and style as diagnostic of its guṇa. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**śraddhā (श्रद्धा)** — faith / trustful placing-of-heart -> threefold, nature-born -> 'belief' as assent understates lived trust.
**niṣṭhā (निष्ठा)** — standing / orientation -> Arjuna’s question about their stance -> 'denomination' is too institutional.
**svabhāva-jā (स्वभावजा)** — born of own nature -> faith arising from constitution -> 'personality preference' shrinks ontology.
**śāstra-vidhiṃ utsṛjya (शास्त्रविधिमुत्सृज्य)** — discarding scriptural injunction -> the problem-case -> 'spiritual but not religious' is a modern echo.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 16.23–24]:** Śāstra as measure sets up Arjuna’s question about faithful discarders.
*Divergence:* 17 opens the guṇa-internal analysis of faith itself.
**[Luther / sola fide debates (contrast)]:** Faith’s primacy is affirmed yet here faith is guṇa-qualified.
*Divergence:* Christian debates differ; Krishna will not treat all śraddhā as equal.
**[William James on varieties of religious experience]:** Varieties of faith-temperament resonate loosely.
*Divergence:* James is psychological-pragmatic; the Gītā maps varieties onto sattva/rajas/tamas.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Name your current faith-object (what you actually trust). Ask which climate it breathes: clarity, restless gain, or dark compulsion.

## A Person Is Made of Faith
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 17.3

The faith of each is in accordance with their essence, O Bhārata. A person is made of faith; whatever one’s faith is, that one verily is.

---

### Devanagari
सत्त्वानुरूपा सर्वस्य श्रद्धा भवति भारत।श्रद्धामयोऽयं पुरुषो यो यच्छ्रद्धः स एव सः

### IAST
sattvānurūpā sarvasya śraddhā bhavati bhārata|śraddhāmayo'yaṃ puruṣo yo yacchraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ

### Pratibha Translation
The faith of each is in accordance with their essence, O Bhārata. A person is made of faith; whatever one’s faith is, that one verily is.

### Pratibha Commentary
This is among the Gītā’s most compressed anthropologies: śraddhāmayo’yaṃ puruṣaḥ—this person is made of faith. Yo yacchraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ—as is one’s faith, so is one. The contested claim collapses the gap between “having beliefs” and “being.” You do not merely hold śraddhā; you are shaped as it. Existentially, this makes faith-diagnosis identity-diagnosis without freezing people into types. If you want to know who you are becoming, inspect what you entrust yourself to when pressed. The verse also explains conversion’s depth: changing faith is changing the person. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**sattva (सत्त्व)** — here as essence/being -> faith according to one’s sattva -> 'mood' is far too thin.
**śraddhāmaya (श्रद्धामय)** — made of faith -> person as faith-constituted -> 'faithful type' misses constitution.
**sa eva saḥ (स एव सः)** — that one verily is -> identity with one’s faith -> 'you are what you believe' is a rough cousin.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Proverbs / 'as a man thinketh' traditions]:** Inner trust shaping the person resonates.
*Divergence:* Biblical lines vary; here faith is explicitly guṇa-correlated.
**[Buddhism on saddhā]:** Faith as a faculty shaping the path resonates.
*Divergence:* Buddhist saddhā is clarified by wisdom; Krishna analyzes śraddhā by guṇas.
**[Tillich’s 'ultimate concern']:** Being shaped by what one ultimately trusts is homologous.
*Divergence:* Tillich’s ontology of concern differs; the Gītā keeps guṇa typology concrete.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Complete the sentence: 'I am becoming what I trust about ___.' Change one trust-practice today to match who you intend to be.

## Whom One Worships Reveals the Guṇa
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 17.4–17.6

The sattvic sacrifice to the gods; the rajasic to yakṣas and rākṣasas; others, the tamasic people, sacrifice to ghosts and hosts of spirits. Those who practice horrific austerities not enjoined by scripture, given to hypocrisy and egoism, powered by desire and passion, starving the aggregate of elements in the body, and Me within the body as well—know them as of demonic resolve.

---

### Devanagari
यजन्ते सात्त्विका देवान्यक्षरक्षांसि राजसाः।प्रेतान्भूतगणांश्चान्ये यजन्ते तामसा जनाः
अशास्त्रविहितं घोरं तप्यन्ते ये तपो जनाः।दम्भाहङ्कारसंयुक्ताः कामरागबलान्विताः
कर्षयन्तः शरीरस्थं भूतग्राममचेतसः।मां चैवान्तःशरीरस्थं तान्विद्ध्यासुरनिश्चयान्

### IAST
yajante sāttvikā devānyakṣarakṣāṃsi rājasāḥ|pretānbhūtagaṇāṃścānye yajante tāmasā janāḥ
aśāstravihitaṃ ghoraṃ tapyante ye tapo janāḥ|dambhāhaṅkārasaṃyuktāḥ kāmarāgabalānvitāḥ
karṣayantaḥ śarīrasthaṃ bhūtagrāmamacetasaḥ|māṃ caivāntaḥśarīrasthaṃ tānviddhyāsuraniścayān

### Pratibha Translation
The sattvic sacrifice to the gods; the rajasic to yakṣas and rākṣasas; others, the tamasic people, sacrifice to ghosts and hosts of spirits. Those who practice horrific austerities not enjoined by scripture, given to hypocrisy and egoism, powered by desire and passion, starving the aggregate of elements in the body, and Me within the body as well—know them as of demonic resolve.

### Pratibha Commentary
Worship-targets become diagnostics: gods, yakṣas-rākṣasas, pretas-bhūtas. Then a severe portrait of aśāstra austerity: ghora tapas driven by dambha and ahaṅkāra, starving the body-elements and the indwelling Lord. The contested claim is that extreme asceticism can be āsuric. Intensity is not holiness. Existentially, any practice that harms the body-host while inflating the ego is already named. The Lord within the body makes self-starvation as display a theological offense, not a badge. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**yajante (यजन्ते)** — they sacrifice/worship -> guṇa shown by object of worship -> 'pray to' understates sacrificial orientation.
**ghora tapas (घोर तपस्)** — horrific austerity -> violent asceticism outside ordinance -> 'hardcore discipline' may be its glamor name.
**āsuraniścaya (आसुरनिश्चय)** — demonic resolve/conclusion -> their determination -> 'toxic mindset' is thinner.
**antaḥ-śarīrastha (अन्तःशरीरस्थ)** — stationed inside the body -> the Lord harmed by abusive tapas -> 'inner self' psychologizes.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 16.17–18]:** Hypocritical sacrifice and hatred in bodies continues into abusive tapas.
*Divergence:* 17.5–6 shows the ascetic form of āsuric resolve.
**[Desert Father warnings on vainglorious asceticism]:** Extreme practice as pride resonates.
*Divergence:* Christian warnings aim at charity/prayer; here the Lord in the body is explicitly starved.
**[Modern eating-mortification / biohacking extremes]:** Body-harm as spiritual/optimized identity echoes the pattern.
*Divergence:* The Gītā’s criterion remains śāstra and non-harm of the indwelling One.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Audit one 'discipline' you perform. Does it honor the body-dwelling One, or starve it for ego’s theater? Adjust accordingly.

## Food Preference as Guṇa Mirror
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 17.7–17.9

Even food dear to all is of three kinds, as are sacrifice, austerity, and giving; hear this distinction among them. Foods that increase life, sattva, strength, health, joy, and cheer, that are savory, smooth, substantial, and agreeable—these are dear to the sattvic. Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning—dear to the rajasic—produce pain, grief, and disease.

---

### Devanagari
आहारस्त्वपि सर्वस्य त्रिविधो भवति प्रियः।यज्ञस्तपस्तथा दानं तेषां भेदमिमं श्रृणु
आयुःसत्त्वबलारोग्यसुखप्रीतिविवर्धनाः।रस्याः स्निग्धाः स्थिरा हृद्या आहाराः सात्त्विकप्रियाः
कट्वम्ललवणात्युष्णतीक्ष्णरूक्षविदाहिनः।आहारा राजसस्येष्टा दुःखशोकामयप्रदाः

### IAST
āhārastvapi sarvasya trividho bhavati priyaḥ|yajñastapastathā dānaṃ teṣāṃ bhedamimaṃ śrṛṇu
āyuḥsattvabalārogyasukhaprītivivardhanāḥ|rasyāḥ snigdhāḥ sthirā hṛdyā āhārāḥ sāttvikapriyāḥ
kaṭvamlalavaṇātyuṣṇatīkṣṇarūkṣavidāhinaḥ|āhārā rājasasyeṣṭā duḥkhaśokāmayapradāḥ

### Pratibha Translation
Even food dear to all is of three kinds, as are sacrifice, austerity, and giving; hear this distinction among them. Foods that increase life, sattva, strength, health, joy, and cheer, that are savory, smooth, substantial, and agreeable—these are dear to the sattvic. Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning—dear to the rajasic—produce pain, grief, and disease.

### Pratibha Commentary
The teaching descends into the plate. Food preferences express and reinforce guṇas: sattvic foods foster life and gladness; rajasic foods, extreme and burning, yield pain, grief, disease. The contested move is refusing neutrality of appetite. Desire for food is already philosophical. Existentially, this is not a grocery purity cult; it is weather literacy. What you find “dear” (priya) is a clue to the climate you are feeding. The same triad will map onto yajña, tapas, and dāna, so food is the introductory pedagogy of discernment. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**āhāra (आहार)** — food / intake -> first triad illustration -> 'diet' can become lifestyle branding.
**priya (प्रिय)** — dear / beloved -> preference as diagnostic -> 'guilty pleasure' already half-understands.
**rasyāḥ snigdhāḥ sthirāḥ (रस्याः स्निग्धाः स्थिराः)** — savory, unctuous, steady -> sattvic food qualities -> 'comfort food' may or may not fit.
**duḥkha-śoka-āmaya (दुःखशोकामय)** — pain, grief, disease -> rajasic food fruits -> 'inflammation' is a partial modern echo.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Āyurvedic guṇa/food mappings]:** Direct cultural homology with sattva-rajas-tamas foods.
*Divergence:* The Gītā subordinates food lore to liberation pedagogy.
**[Monastic fasting rules]:** Intake shaped for clarity resonates.
*Divergence:* Monastic aims vary; here preference itself is guṇa-indexed.
**[Feuerbach 'you are what you eat' (loose)]:** Intake shaping the person resonates popularly.
*Divergence:* The Gītā’s claim is guṇa-soteriological, not materialist anthropology.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
At your next meal, notice what you find dear and what fruit it typically leaves in body-mind. Choose one sattvic preference deliberately.

## Tamasic Food, Sattvic and Rajasic Sacrifice
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 17.10–17.12

Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid, leftover, and also impure is dear to the tamasic. Sacrifice offered by those who desire no fruit, as prescribed, with the mind resolved 'this must be offered'—that is sattvic. But sacrifice offered with a view to fruit, and also for ostentation, O best of Bharatas—know that to be rajasic.

---

### Devanagari
यातयामं गतरसं पूति पर्युषितं च यत्।उच्छिष्टमपि चामेध्यं भोजनं तामसप्रियम्
अफलाकाङ्क्षिभिर्यज्ञो विधिदृष्टो य इज्यते।यष्टव्यमेवेति मनः समाधाय स सात्त्विकः
अभिसंधाय तु फलं दम्भार्थमपि चैव यत्।इज्यते भरतश्रेष्ठ तं यज्ञं विद्धि राजसम्

### IAST
yātayāmaṃ gatarasaṃ pūti paryuṣitaṃ ca yat|ucchiṣṭamapi cāmedhyaṃ bhojanaṃ tāmasapriyam
aphalākāṅkṣibhiryajño vidhidṛṣṭo ya ijyate|yaṣṭavyameveti manaḥ samādhāya sa sāttvikaḥ
abhisaṃdhāya tu phalaṃ dambhārthamapi caiva yat|ijyate bharataśreṣṭha taṃ yajñaṃ viddhi rājasam

### Pratibha Translation
Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid, leftover, and also impure is dear to the tamasic. Sacrifice offered by those who desire no fruit, as prescribed, with the mind resolved 'this must be offered'—that is sattvic. But sacrifice offered with a view to fruit, and also for ostentation, O best of Bharatas—know that to be rajasic.

### Pratibha Commentary
Tamasic dearness is decay and impurity; then yajña splits by intention. Sattvic sacrifice: vidhi-aligned, fruit-not-craved, mind settled that it ought to be done. Rajasic sacrifice: fruit-aimed and/or dambha-aimed. The contested claim is that identical outer rites differ absolutely by interior contract. Existentially, audit your “good deeds”: are they ought-to-be-done offerings, or investments and advertisements? The Gītā’s sattvic mind does not negotiate the rite as a deal. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**yātayāma (यातयाम)** — past its time / stale -> tamasic food -> 'meal prep leftover' is not automatically tamasic; the cluster matters.
**aphalākāṅkṣin (अफलाकाङ्क्षिन्)** — not craving fruit -> sattvic sacrificer -> 'unmotivated' misreads freedom from bargaining.
**vidhi-dṛṣṭa (विधिदृष्ट)** — seen in ordinance -> prescribed rite -> 'traditional' can be vague.
**dambhārtham (दम्भार्थम्)** — for ostentation -> rajasic aim -> 'visibility' as branding is the modern form.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 2.47]:** Non-attachment to fruit continues into sacrificial typology.
*Divergence:* 17.11–12 apply it specifically to yajña.
**[Gospel critique of trumpet-almsgiving]:** Ostentatious piety as invalid resonates.
*Divergence:* Matthew aims at Father’s reward secrecy; Krishna maps ostentation as rajasic guṇa.
**[Mīmāṃsā on ritual fruit]:** Debate on fruits of sacrifice is the scholastic background.
*Divergence:* The Gītā ethicizes and guṇa-codes the fruit-desire itself.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Perform one small obligatory good with the mind: 'this is to be done'—no audience, no bargain. Feel the difference.

## Tamasic Sacrifice and the Triple Austerity
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 17.13–17.15

Sacrifice without ordinance, without food offered, without mantras, without gifts, and without faith is declared tamasic. Worship of gods, of the twice-born, of teachers, and of the wise; purity, uprightness, continence, and non-harming are called austerity of the body. Speech that causes no agitation, that is true, pleasant, and beneficial, and also practice of sacred study—these are called austerity of speech.

---

### Devanagari
विधिहीनमसृष्टान्नं मन्त्रहीनमदक्षिणम्।श्रद्धाविरहितं यज्ञं तामसं परिचक्षते
देवद्विजगुरुप्राज्ञपूजनं शौचमार्जवम्।ब्रह्मचर्यमहिंसा च शारीरं तप उच्यते
अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत्।स्वाध्यायाभ्यसनं चैव वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते

### IAST
vidhihīnamasṛṣṭānnaṃ mantrahīnamadakṣiṇam|śraddhāvirahitaṃ yajñaṃ tāmasaṃ paricakṣate
devadvijaguruprājñapūjanaṃ śaucamārjavam|brahmacaryamahiṃsā ca śārīraṃ tapa ucyate
anudvegakaraṃ vākyaṃ satyaṃ priyahitaṃ ca yat|svādhyāyābhyasanaṃ caiva vāṅmayaṃ tapa ucyate

### Pratibha Translation
Sacrifice without ordinance, without food offered, without mantras, without gifts, and without faith is declared tamasic. Worship of gods, of the twice-born, of teachers, and of the wise; purity, uprightness, continence, and non-harming are called austerity of the body. Speech that causes no agitation, that is true, pleasant, and beneficial, and also practice of sacred study—these are called austerity of speech.

### Pratibha Commentary
Tamasic yajña is defined by absences: no vidhi, no food-sharing, no mantra, no dakṣiṇā, no śraddhā. Then tapas is redeemed from ghora parody by a threefold humane map. Body-tapas: reverence, purity, continence, non-harm. Speech-tapas: non-agitating, true, kind, useful speech plus svādhyāya. The contested move is relocating austerity into ethics of relation and speech. Existentially, your harshest “honesty” may fail speech-tapas; your flashiest fast may fail body-tapas. The Gītā prefers reverence and non-harm to self-violence. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**dakṣiṇā (दक्षिणा)** — ritual gift -> absence marks tamasic yajña -> 'tip' trivializes reciprocal offering.
**śārīraṃ tapaḥ (शारीरं तपः)** — bodily austerity -> reverence/purity/continence/non-harm -> 'workout' is a parody.
**vāṅmayaṃ tapaḥ (वाङ्मयं तपः)** — austerity of speech -> truth joined to kindness and benefit -> 'radical candor' often fails this.
**svādhyāya (स्वाध्याय)** — self-study / recitation -> part of speech-tapas -> 'reading about spirituality' can counterfeit it.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 17.5–6 contrast]:** Abusive tapas vs ethical tapas is intentional pedagogy.
*Divergence:* 17.14–15 redefine austerity after exposing demonic austerity.
**[James 3 on the tongue]:** Speech ethics as spiritual crucible resonates.
*Divergence:* James is ecclesial-wisdom; Krishna places speech inside guṇa-coded tapas.
**[Confucian rectification of speech/rite]:** Right speaking and rite without hollowness resonate.
*Divergence:* Aims differ; both refuse empty ceremony and harmful speech.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Practice speech-tapas for one conversation: true, non-agitating, pleasant, and beneficial. If you cannot meet all four, choose silence.

## Mental Austerity and Its Guṇa-Colors
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 17.16–17.18

Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, purification of disposition—these are called austerity of the mind. This threefold austerity practiced with highest faith by people joined to yoga, not craving fruit, is declared sattvic. Austerity practiced for esteem, honor, and reverence, and also with hypocrisy—said to be rajasic, unstable and impermanent.

---

### Devanagari
मनःप्रसादः सौम्यत्वं मौनमात्मविनिग्रहः।भावसंशुद्धिरित्येतत्तपो मानसमुच्यते
श्रद्धया परया तप्तं तपस्तत्ित्रविधं नरैः।अफलाकाङ्क्षिभिर्युक्तैः सात्त्विकं परिचक्षते
सत्कारमानपूजार्थं तपो दम्भेन चैव यत्।क्रियते तदिह प्रोक्तं राजसं चलमध्रुवम्

### IAST
manaḥprasādaḥ saumyatvaṃ maunamātmavinigrahaḥ|bhāvasaṃśuddhirityetattapo mānasamucyate
śraddhayā parayā taptaṃ tapastatitravidhaṃ naraiḥ|aphalākāṅkṣibhiryuktaiḥ sāttvikaṃ paricakṣate
satkāramānapūjārthaṃ tapo dambhena caiva yat|kriyate tadiha proktaṃ rājasaṃ calamadhruvam

### Pratibha Translation
Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, purification of disposition—these are called austerity of the mind. This threefold austerity practiced with highest faith by people joined to yoga, not craving fruit, is declared sattvic. Austerity practiced for esteem, honor, and reverence, and also with hypocrisy—said to be rajasic, unstable and impermanent.

### Pratibha Commentary
Mind-tapas completes the triad: prasāda, gentleness, mauna, restraint, bhāva-purity. Then the same threefold tapas is guṇa-colored by motive. Sattvic: highest faith, yogic, fruit-free. Rajasic: for satkāra-māna-pūjā, and with dambha—unstable. The contested claim is that mental calm pursued for applause is already rajasic. Existentially, ask what audience lives in your head when you practice serenity. If an admirer is watching, the tapas is already trembling. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**manaḥ-prasāda (मनःप्रसाद)** — clarity/serenity of mind -> mental austerity -> 'chill' understates luminous gladness.
**mauna (मौन)** — silence -> mental/verbal restraint -> 'not talking' can be sulking counterfeit.
**bhāva-saṃśuddhi (भावसंशुद्धि)** — purification of inner disposition -> deep tapas -> 'positive attitude' is thin.
**calam adhruvam (चलमध्रुवम्)** — unsteady, impermanent -> rajasic tapas fruit -> 'inconsistent practice' is the surface symptom.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Patañjali on citta-prasādana]:** Serenity practices resonate.
*Divergence:* Patañjali aims at samādhi; Krishna guṇa-codes tapas motives.
**[Sermon on the Mount on secret fasting]:** Against display-austerity is strong homology.
*Divergence:* Matthew emphasizes Father-secret; Krishna labels display rajasic and unstable.
**[Stoic inner citadel]:** Mental austerity as sovereignty resonates loosely.
*Divergence:* Stoicism centers rational assent; here faith-yoga and non-fruiting define sattvic tapas.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Do one unnoticed austerity of mind today (gentle restraint, silence, or softening a disposition) with no report to anyone.

## Tamasic Austerity and the Three Givings
**Source:** Bhagavad Gītā 17.19–17.21

Austerity done with deluded grasping, with self-torture, or in order to destroy another is declared tamasic. Giving that is given because it ought to be given, to one who cannot give back, in right place, time, and to a worthy recipient—that giving is remembered as sattvic. But giving given for return favor, or with fruit in view, or given grudgingly—that giving is remembered as rajasic.

---

### Devanagari
मूढग्राहेणात्मनो यत्पीडया क्रियते तपः।परस्योत्सादनार्थं वा तत्तामसमुदाहृतम्
दातव्यमिति यद्दानं दीयतेऽनुपकारिणे।देशे काले च पात्रे च तद्दानं सात्त्विकं स्मृतम्
यत्तु प्रत्युपकारार्थं फलमुद्दिश्य वा पुनः।दीयते च परिक्लिष्टं तद्दानं राजसं स्मृतम्

### IAST
mūḍhagrāheṇātmano yatpīḍayā kriyate tapaḥ|parasyotsādanārthaṃ vā tattāmasamudāhṛtam
dātavyamiti yaddānaṃ dīyate'nupakāriṇe|deśe kāle ca pātre ca taddānaṃ sāttvikaṃ smṛtam
yattu pratyupakārārthaṃ phalamuddiśya vā punaḥ|dīyate ca parikliṣṭaṃ taddānaṃ rājasaṃ smṛtam

### Pratibha Translation
Austerity done with deluded grasping, with self-torture, or in order to destroy another is declared tamasic. Giving that is given because it ought to be given, to one who cannot give back, in right place, time, and to a worthy recipient—that giving is remembered as sattvic. But giving given for return favor, or with fruit in view, or given grudgingly—that giving is remembered as rajasic.

### Pratibha Commentary
Tamasic tapas is named without romance: deluded fixation, self-torture, or harm of another. Then dāna enters the triad. Sattvic giving: ought-to-give, to non-reciprocators, right place-time-recipient. Rajasic giving: for return, for fruit, or with pain. The contested move makes generosity ethically precise. Existentially, many “kindnesses” are rajasic contracts. Sattvic dāna breaks the economy of return without becoming contemptuous of recipients. In the Gītā’s pedagogy, concept without existential cut becomes another ornament of bondage; therefore the verse must be read as a demand on perception, desire, and refuge, not as a museum label on a doctrine. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics. The existential stake is that this teaching must change how you inhabit the next hour, not only how you narrate metaphysics.

### Key Terms
**mūḍha-grāha (मूढग्राह)** — deluded grasping -> tamasic tapas motive -> 'stubborn discipline' may hide it.
**parasyotsādana (परस्योत्सादन)** — destroying another -> tapas as weapon -> 'competitive self-denial' is a soft form.
**anupakārin (अनुपकारिन्)** — one who does not return help -> sattvic recipient criterion -> 'networking charity' fails it.
**parikliṣṭa (परिक्लिष्ट)** — given with pain/grudge -> rajasic giving tone -> 'duty donation' can sour into this.

### Cross-Tradition Resonances
**[Gītā 17.5–6 / 17.19]:** Demonic and tamasic austerity form a continuous warning.
*Divergence:* Motive to destroy another makes tapas explicitly violent.
**[Luke 14 on inviting those who cannot repay]:** Strong homology with anupakārin giving.
*Divergence:* Luke’s banquet ethic is Kingdom-shaped; Krishna maps it as sattvic dāna.
**[Seneca on benefits]:** Giving and return calculus is a classical parallel.
*Divergence:* Seneca philosophizes benefits; the Gītā guṇa-codes giving for liberation pedagogy.

### Practice (Abhyasa)
Give once this week where return is unlikely, in a fitting way, without announcement. Protect the sattvic conditions.
